A. Aspiration pneumonitis: Occurs immediately after aspiration with focal infiltrates and fever. No aspiration history; CT shows diffuse ground-glass, not focal.

B. Cardiogenic pulmonary edema: Seen in heart failure with crackles, JVD, cardiomegaly. Young patient with trauma + neuro symptoms → unlikely.

C. Drug hypersensitivity: Would cause rash, fever, eosinophilia. None present.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: 42-year-old woman comes to the AIIMS OPD due to right knee pain for the past 3 days. She was carrying a heavy backpack on a muddy trail when she tripped, twisting her leg. The next morning, she had swelling at the knee and significant medial knee pain with stairs and squatting. Which of the following is most likely to be found on examination of this patient's knee?
options: Anterior laxity of the tibia relative to the femur
Excessive valgus deviation with lower leg abduction
Painful click during knee extension and external rotation
Tenderness at the medial knee below the joint line
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Painful click during knee extension and external rotation

Case scenario:

• Twisting injury while weight-bearing ✔
• Swelling next morning ✔ (delayed effusion → meniscus, not ligament)
• Medial knee pain, worse with squatting & stairs ✔

Points towards meniscal injury

Examination finding:

Painful click during knee extension and external rotation -McMurray test for medial meniscus tear.

Why others are wrong?

A) Anterior laxity → ACL tear (positive Lachman/anterior drawer) ❌

B) Excessive valgus deviation → MCL injury ❌

D) Tenderness below joint line → Pes anserine bursitis ❌

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: 6-year-old boy is brought to the office for evaluation of leg pain. The pain has been constant for the last 2 weeks and keeps the patient from playing with his friends. It is worse at night and has made it difficult for the child to fall asleep. He wakes up several times nightly to void and has had episodes of incontinence as the leg pain prevents him from walking to the bathroom. The patient has had no recent fever or dysuria. Temperature is 36.7⁰C (98⁰F). Cardiac examination reveals tachycardia; no murmurs are present. A soft, non-fluctuant, tender, 5-cm mass over the right anterior distal thigh without overlying erythema is noted. The right knee has full range of motion, and no effusion is noted. An erythematous, popular rash is present over the chest, trunk, and groin. Hip X-ray is shown here. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Langerhans cell histiocytosis

A child with persistent bone pain (worse at night)

Tender bony mass

• An erythematous papular rash suggests Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH).
• LCH is characterized by ~~“\~~clonal proliferation of Langerhans cells.~~\~~
• Common in children.
•

Frequently involves:

o    Long bones (lytic lesions in diaphysis)

o    Skull, ribs, pelvis

•

May present with:

o    Bone pain and swelling

o    Papular seborrheic-like rash (trunk, scalp, groin)

o    Possible systemic features (lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly)

X-ray findings:

• Well-defined lytic lesion
• Possible cortical thinning or endosteal scalloping

Pathology hallmark:

• CD1a+, Langerin (CD207)+ cells
• Birbeck granules (“tennis racket” appearance) on EM

Why not others:

B. McCune-Albright syndrome → café-au-lait spots + fibrous dysplasia + endocrine abnormalities.

C. Mazabraud syndrome → fibrous dysplasia + intramuscular myxomas.

D. Osteoid osteoma → night pain relieved by NSAIDs; no rash.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: 6-year-old girl is brought to the clinic for evaluation of knee pain. The patient first had soreness in her right knee 4 days ago, after her first gymnastics class. Her mother gave her PCM and massaged her knee, but this did not help. The patient also developed a limp over the past 2 days. She has no chronic medical conditions and does not take daily medications. Height is at the 50th percentile and weight is at the 90th percentile. Temperature is 37.9⁰C (100.2⁰F). When walking, she limits weight-bearing on her right side. When supine, the right hip is held flexed with the knee pointed laterally. There is limited internal rotation and extension of the right hip. The right knee has full range of motion and there is no tenderness on palpation around the knee. Laboratory evaluation shows leukocyte count of 11,500/mm3 and C-reactive protein of 8 mg/L (normal: <10). Ultrasound of the hips shows small, bilateral effusions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Transient synovitis

A child with acute limp, hip held in flexion & external rotation, limited internal rotation, mild fever, normal/mildly elevated inflammatory markers, and small hip effusion on ultrasound is most consistent with Transient synovitis.

• Most common cause of acute hip pain and limp in children (3–10 years)
• Often follows minor trauma or recent viral illness
•

Presents with:

o Refusal to bear weight or limp

o Hip held in flexion, abduction, external rotation

o Pain referred to knee

•

Labs:

o Normal or mildly elevated WBC

o Normal or mildly elevated CRP

•

Ultrasound:

o Small hip joint effusion

Why not others:

A. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis → chronic symptoms (>6 weeks), morning stiffness.

B. Perthes disease → insidious onset, no fever, avascular necrosis of femoral head.

C. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) → obese adolescents (10–16 yrs), not typical in a 6-year-old.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 1-year-old child with DDH has failed closed reduction. What is the next best step in treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Open reduction

Why Open Reduction is Correct

Open reduction means surgically exposing the hip joint and removing obstacles preventing reduction, such as:

• Tight capsule
• Pulvinar tissue
• Ligamentum teres
• Inverted labrum

After that, the femoral head is placed properly in the acetabulum and stabilized. (Early anatomical reduction is essential for normal acetabular development.)

Other Options:

A. Pelvic Osteotomy

• Not the immediate next step
• Done in older children (>2–3 years)
• Used when acetabulum is shallow

First you must reduce the hip, then osteotomy may be considered later if needed.

C. Manipulation Under Anesthesia

• Essentially part of closed reduction
• Already attempted in this case

D. Total Hip Replacement

• Completely inappropriate
• Used in older children >10yrs

Quick DDH Management Trick

| Age | Treatment

| --- | ---------

| 0–6 months | CR + Pavlik harness/ Von Rosen splint

| 6–18 months | Closed/open reduction + spica

| 18mon-10yrs | Femoral osteotomy

| >10 years | THR

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy comes with a fever and pain in his right upper limb. He has an expansile lesion in his right radius in the diaphysis. The histopathology of the lesion is shown below. What is the most accurate test among the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. t (11;22)

A painful diaphyseal bone lesion in a child with small round blue cells on histology suggests Ewing sarcoma, which is most accurately confirmed by detecting EWSR1-ETS fusion gene (commonly EWS-FLI1 from t(11;22)). This tumor typically presents with fever, pain, onion-skin periosteal reaction, and shows sheets of uniform small round blue cells on biopsy.

Why not other options:

A. t(15;17): Seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia (PML-RARA), not bone tumors.

B. RB mutation: Associated with retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma, not small round blue cell tumor of diaphysis.

D. t(11;23): Not the classic translocation for Ewing sarcoma.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy presents with symptoms suggestive of osteomyelitis. An MRI is performed and the radiologist notes a finding indicative of acute osteomyelitis. Which of the following findings is considered pathognomic for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bone marrow edema

On MRI, the earliest and most sensitive finding of acute osteomyelitis is bone marrow edema,

Bone marrow edema gives:

• Low signal on T1
• High signal on T2/STIR sequences due to inflammatory exudate within marrow.
• For early detection of osteomyelitis (because marrow edema appears before cortical destruction), MRI is the imaging modality of choice.

Why not other options:

• Penumbra sign: Seen in subacute osteomyelitis (Brodie abscess), not acute stage. It is a characteristic MRI feature of subacute osteomyelitis (specifically Brodie's abscess), showing a thin rim of granulation tissue lining an abscess cavity.
•
• Sequestrum: Dead bone fragment seen in chronic osteomyelitis.
• Involucrum: New bone formation around sequestrum in chronic osteomyelitis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl sustains a knee injury while playing sports. She presents with pain, swelling, and inability to bear weight. Radiograph is shown below. Which of the following statements regarding this injury is most accurate?
options: It has the best prognosis due to preservation of germinal layer
It is an extra-articular fracture with low risk of growth disturbance
It involves both proliferative and hypertrophic zones of physis
It requires precise anatomical reduction to prevent joint incongruity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It requires precise anatomical reduction to prevent joint incongruity

Physeal (growth plate) injuries are classified using the Salter-Harris system, which predicts both anatomical involvement and prognosis.

Key principles to remember:

• Type I: Through physis only

Usually spares germinal layer → good prognosis

• Type II: Physis + metaphysis (most common)

Germinal layer preserved → good prognosis

• Type III: Physis + epiphysis (intra-articular)

Risk of growth disturbance and joint incongruity

• Type IV: Metaphysis + physis + epiphysis

Crosses germinal layer → high risk of growth arrest

Requires precise anatomical reduction

• Type V: Crush injury to physis

Often radiologically occult initially

Worst prognosis due to germinal layer destruction

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 14-year-old male presents with anterior knee pain that has been gradually worsening over the past few weeks. He is actively involved in sports, particularly soccer, and reports increased pain with running and jumping. X-ray is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Osgood-Schlatter disease

What is Osgood–Schlatter disease?

It is traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity caused by repeated pulling of the patellar tendon.

Occurs due to:

• Repetitive quadriceps contraction
• Sports involving jumping/running

Common in:

• Adolescent boys
• Ages 10–15 years

X-ray Findings

Typical features include:

• Fragmentation of tibial tuberosity
• Irregular ossification
• Soft tissue swelling over tibial tubercle

The image shows changes at the tibial tuberosity below the patella, consistent with this condition.

A. Patellofemoral pain syndrome

• Usually normal X-ray
• Pain behind patella, not at tibial tuberosity.

C. Patellar tendonitis

• Occurs at inferior pole of patella
• Seen in adults/athletes, not typical adolescent growth-plate pathology.

D. Meniscus tear

• Causes locking, clicking, joint line tenderness
• Not anterior tibial tubercle pain.

Exam Trick

| Condition | Location of Pain

| --------- | ----------------

| Osgood–Schlatter disease | Tibial tuberosity

| Sinding-Larsen-Johansson | Inferior pole of patella

| Patellofemoral syndrome | Behind patella

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 15-year-old male with pain and swelling in the thigh since last one month. X-ray is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ewing sarcoma

Ewing sarcoma is a highly malignant small round cell tumor seen in children and adolescents, most commonly involving the diaphysis of long bones (femur, tibia) and pelvis.

Characteristic radiographic features:

• Onion-skin (lamellated) periosteal reaction
• Moth-eaten or permeative lytic lesion
• Soft-tissue mass
• Diaphyseal location

Clinical features:

• Pain and swelling
• Fever, leukocytosis may mimic osteomyelitis
• t(11;22) translocation (EWS-FLI1)

Why NOT others:

A. Osteoclastoma (Giant cell tumor): Occurs after epiphyseal closure (20–40 yrs) and is epiphyseal, not diaphyseal.

C. Brodie abscess: Subacute osteomyelitis with well-defined lytic lesion and sclerotic rim; no onion-skin periosteal reaction.

D. Osteosarcoma: Metaphyseal tumor around knee with sunburst pattern/Codman triangle, not diaphyseal onion-skin pattern.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presents with progressively increasing pain and swelling around the knee. X-ray of the distal femur shows an aggressive lesion with mixed lytic and sclerotic areas along with perpendicular spicules of new bone formation radiating from the cortex. Which of the following is the most appropriate explanation for the radiological appearance described?
options: Layered periosteal reaction due to repetitive hemorrhage
Rapid tumor growth causing perpendicular periosteal bone formation
Slow-growing lesion leading to cortical thinning and expansion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rapid tumor growth causing perpendicular periosteal bone formation

The described finding is the “sunburst appearance”, a classic feature of osteosarcoma.

Pathophysiology:

• Rapidly growing malignant osteoid-producing tumor
• Lifts periosteum and stimulates new bone formation
• Bone spicules form perpendicular to cortex → sunburst pattern

Other associated features:

• Codman triangle (periosteal elevation)
• Metaphyseal location (distal femur, proximal tibia)
• Occurs in adolescents

Other Options:

Option A. Describes onion-skin appearance of Ewing sarcoma

Option C. Suggests benign expansile lesions like giant cell tumor

Option D. Not a mechanism for this radiological pattern

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 19-year-old male patient comes to the clinic for follow-up 3 weeks after a traumatic fracture in his right thigh. On examination, he was found to have a hard palpable mass near the fracture site. X-ray of the area shows the findings below. A histological section shows central fibrous tissue and mature bone at the periphery. Which of the following is true about this patient's diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Myositis ossificans

Key clues

• 19-year-old male
• History of trauma with fracture
• 3 weeks later → hard palpable mass near fracture site
• X-ray shows calcification in soft tissue
• Histology: central fibrous tissue with mature bone at the periphery

These findings are classic for Myositis Ossificans.

It is heterotopic bone formation in muscle, usually occurring after trauma.

Common features:

• Occurs weeks after injury
• Painful or firm mass
• Peripheral ossification on imaging

Classic Histology (Zonation phenomenon)

This is the key diagnostic feature:

| Zone | Finding

| ---- | -------

| Center | Immature fibroblasts / fibrous tissue

| Intermediate zone | Osteoid formation

| Periphery | Mature lamellar bone

X-ray shows: Peripheral calcification with central lucency

Other options:

A. Parosteal osteosarcoma

• Malignant tumor
• Shows central ossification

C. Osteochondroma

• Cartilage-capped bony projection
• Arises from metaphysis
• Continuous with cortex and medulla

D. AV fistula

• Vascular abnormality
• No bone formation.

|

| ---

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 19-year-old male presents with localized bone pain in the tibia. Imaging reveals a small radiolucent lesion surrounded by dense reactive sclerosis. The pain improves with NSAIDs. Which of the following is a histological feature of the most likely diagnosis?
options: Trabeculae of woven bone surrounded by fibrovascular stroma
Malignant osteoid production with atypical mitoses
Multinucleated giant cells surrounding hemorrhagic spaces
Fibrous tissue with scattered irregular bony trabeculae
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trabeculae of woven bone surrounded by fibrovascular stroma

Osteoid osteoma presents in adolescents/young adults with:

• Localized bone pain (often nocturnal)

• Pain relieved by NSAIDs (due to high prostaglandin production)

• X-ray: small radiolucent nidus surrounded by dense reactive sclerosis

Histology shows:

• Interlacing trabeculae of woven bone (osteoid)

• Surrounded by highly vascular fibrovascular stroma

• Prominent osteoblasts lining the trabeculae

This distinguishes it from:

• Osteosarcoma → malignant osteoid with atypia

• Giant cell tumor → multinucleated giant cells

• Fibrous dysplasia → fibrous stroma with irregular “Chinese letter” bone trabeculae.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 22-year-old man comes to the physician because of a progressive swelling and pain in his right ring finger for the past 2 days. The pain began while playing football, when his finger got caught in the jersey of another player who forcefully pulled away. Examination shows that the right ring finger is extended. There is pain and swelling at the distal interphalangeal joint. When the patient is asked to make a fist, his right ring finger does not flex at the distal interphalangeal joint. There is no joint laxity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon at its point of insertion
Closed fracture of the distal phalanx
Rupture of the extensor digitorum tendon at its point of insertion
Inflammation of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon sheath
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon at its point of insertion

• Injury while playing football when finger got caught in a jersey and pulled away
• Pain and swelling at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint
• Finger remains extended
• Patient cannot flex the DIP joint when making a fist

This is the classic mechanism of “Jersey Finger.”

✅ Option A: Rupture of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon at its point of insertion

Why this happens

• The flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon inserts at the base of the distal phalanx.
• It is responsible for flexion of the DIP joint.
• When a player grabs another player's jersey and the finger is forcefully extended, the FDP tendon can avulse from its insertion.

Classic Clinical Findings

• Finger held in extended position
• Inability to flex the DIP joint
• Pain and swelling at the distal phalanx/DIP
• Usually affects ring finger most commonly

B. Closed fracture of distal phalanx

→ Would not specifically cause isolated loss of DIP flexion.

C. Rupture of extensor digitorum tendon

→ Causes mallet finger where the patient cannot extend the DIP, not flex it.

D. Inflammation of FDP tendon sheath

→ Seen in tenosynovitis, with pain and swelling but not acute loss of flexion after trauma.

• Jersey finger → cannot FLEX DIP
• Mallet finger → cannot EXTEND DIP

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman comes to the OPD for evaluation of new-onset foot pain. The pain is located at the heel and is most pronounced when she gets up from sitting after a long period of time. She enjoys running every evening for one hour. Direct pressure to the bottom of the heel elicits sharp pain, but mediolateral squeezing of the heel causes no discomfort. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of the patient's foot pain?
options: Entrapment of the posterior tibial nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inflammation of the plantar aponeurosis

Plantar fasciitis is the most common cause of heel pain, characterized by:

• Pain at the plantar heel, worst with first steps after rest (post-static dyskinesia)
• Tenderness on direct pressure at medial calcaneal tubercle
• Common in runners and prolonged standing

It results from inflammation and microtears of the plantar aponeurosis at its calcaneal attachment.

Why not other options:

A. Posterior tibial nerve entrapment: Tarsal tunnel syndrome → burning/tingling, not classic first-step heel pain.

B. Morton neuroma: Pain between 3rd–4th toes, worse with tight shoes; forefoot, not heel.

C. Stress fracture: Pain with mediolateral heel squeeze (positive squeeze test).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 23-year-old male is undergoing a complete anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction surgery in the main orthopedic theater. During the operation, a blood vessel that supplies oxygenated blood to the ACL is ligated to prevent bleeding. The orthopedic surgeon asks his assistant to identify this vessel. Which one of the following vessels should he identify?
options: Perforating branches of the femoral artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Middle genicular artery

Blood supply of ACL

The ACL is supplied primarily by: Middle genicular artery

• Branch of popliteal artery
• Pierces posterior capsule
• Supplies:

• ACL
• PCL
• Synovium
• Cruciate ligaments

A) Perforating branches of femoral artery

• Supply posterior thigh muscles
• Not intra-articular

B) Lateral femoral circumflex artery

• Supplies lateral thigh
• Contributes to hip blood supply

D) Medial femoral circumflex artery

• Main supply to femoral head
• Important in neck of femur fractures

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 24-year-old man presents 6 weeks after a road traffic accident with persistent ankle pain. He had sustained a talar neck fracture that was managed with closed reduction and casting. On follow-up radiograph, a subchondral radiolucent band is seen in the dome of the talus. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of this finding?
options: Early feature of avascular necrosis requiring urgent decompression
Indicator of preserved vascularity of the talus
Suggestive of subchondral collapse of talus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Indicator of preserved vascularity of the talus

• The subchondral radiolucent band in the talar dome seen 6–8 weeks after a talar neck fracture is known as the Hawkins sign.
• Hawkins sign indicates preserved vascularity of the talus, as it represents subchondral bone resorption due to intact blood supply.

• Presence of Hawkins sign → GOOD prognostic sign

• Implies revascularization of talus
• Low risk of avascular necrosis (AVN)

• Absence of Hawkins sign → suspicious for AVN

• Requires closer follow-up and possible further imaging (e.g., MRI)

Why not other options:

A. Early AVN requiring decompression: Hawkins sign actually suggests viable bone, not AVN

C. Subchondral collapse: Collapse is a late feature of AVN, not an early radiolucent band

D. Post-traumatic osteoarthritis: Presents later with joint space narrowing, osteophytes, not this sign

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 25-year-old mason presents with left hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated after a fall. Which statement is false about the likely diagnosis?
options: Femoral head appears smaller than the other side on X-ray
Stimson’s method can be used to reduce it
Femoral head palpable in the groin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Femoral head appears smaller than the other side on X-ray

The clinical picture — hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated — points to an anterior dislocation of the hip.

(Contrast with posterior dislocation: flexed, adducted, internally rotated)

The question asks for the FALSE statement

The correct answer is A — "Femoral head appears smaller than the other side on X-ray"

This is FALSE because in anterior dislocation, the femoral head is displaced toward the X-ray beam (anteriorly/closer to the film), so it actually appears larger than the opposite side, not smaller.

(In posterior dislocation, the head moves away from the beam → appears smaller)

Why the other options are TRUE (and therefore not the answer)

| Option | Why it's TRUE in anterior dislocation

| ------ | -------------------------------------

| B - Femoral vessels may be injured | The femoral neurovascular bundle lies anteriorly — directly in the path of the dislocated head → risk of femoral artery/nerve injury

| C - Stimson's method can reduce it | Stimson's gravity method works for both anterior and posterior dislocations

| D - Femoral head palpable in groin | In anterior dislocation, the head goes forward into the groin/obturator region → palpable in the groin ✓

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman comes to the emergency department after she awkwardly landed on her foot while playing volleyball. An X-ray of the foot is shown. The physician proceeds to immobilize her foot with a cast. Which of the structures is the most commonly injured in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior talofibular ligament

The lateral ligament complex of the ankle has three ligaments:

| Ligament | Injury frequency

| -------- | ----------------

| Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) | Most commonly injured

| Calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) | Second most common

| Posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL) | Rarely injured

So the most common structure injured is: Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL)

Achilles tendon

Achilles rupture presents with:

• Sudden “pop” in the back of ankle
• Cannot plantarflex
• Positive Thompson test

This injury is different from a typical ankle sprain.

Posterior talofibular ligament

This ligament is very strong.

It usually tears only in severe ankle dislocations, not common sports sprains.

Peroneus brevis

This is a muscle/tendon, not the ligament usually injured in ankle sprains.

Though it may be irritated, it is not the most common structure injured.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman visits the doctor with pain and weakness in her right forearm and hand for several months. Two years ago, she had a fracture in her ulnar shaft and a dislocation of her radial head that required surgery. On examination, there is mild tenderness a few centimeters distal to the lateral epicondyle. She has significant weakness when trying to extend her right middle finger and radial deviation on extension of the wrist. Sensation is normal. Which nerve is most likely affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Posterior interosseous nerve

PIN is:

• A branch of radial nerve → Purely motor
• Supplies:

• Finger extensors, Thumb extensors, Extensor carpi ulnaris

Normally wrist extension uses:

• Extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL)
• Extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB)
• Extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU)

In PIN palsy:

• ECU is weak
• ECRL still works (supplied before PIN branches out from radial nerve.

So wrist extends but deviates radially.

A) Anterior interosseous nerve

• Motor branch of median nerve → Affects flexors (FPL, FDP index)
• Difficulty in making OK sign
• No extensor weakness

B) Superficial radial nerve

• Pure sensory nerve → Causes numbness dorsum of hand
• No motor weakness

D) Ulnar nerve

• Affects intrinsic hand muscles → Clawing of 4th and 5th digits
• No extensor weakness

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 26-year-old football player presents with acute knee pain after twisting his right knee while the foot was planted. He reports a “click” followed by intermittent locking of the joint. On examination, there is joint line tenderness and a positive McMurray test. MRI reveals a longitudinal vertical tear in the posterior horn of the medial meniscus extending into the vascular zone. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is/are correct? A. The medial meniscus is more commonly injured due to its firm attachment to the medial collateral ligament B. Tears in the outer one-third of the meniscus have better healing potential C. Bucket-handle tears commonly involve radial fibers of the meniscus D. The lateral meniscus is less mobile than the medial meniscus E. Locking of the knee is most commonly seen with flap tears rather than longitudinal tears
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A and B

• A. True → Medial meniscus is less mobile due to attachment to MCL, making it more prone to injury
• B. True → Outer 1/3rd = red zone (vascular) → better healing → repair preferred
• C. False → Bucket-handle tear = longitudinal vertical tear, not radial
• D. False → Lateral meniscus is more mobile (no firm LCL attachment)
• E. False → Locking is classic for bucket-handle (longitudinal) tears, not flap tears

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 27-year-old man presents with chronic low back pain for 2 years. The pain improves with exercise and worsens with rest. He also reports morning stiffness lasting more than 1 hour. On examination, there is reduced chest expansion and limited lumbar flexion. X-ray pelvis shown below. Which of the following is the earliest pathological site involved in this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Enthesis (site of ligament/tendon insertion)

Ankylosing spondylitis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy characterized by inflammation at the enthesis.

\

• Primary pathology begins at entheses (enthesitis)
• Common sites:

o    Annulus fibrosus attachment

o    Ligament attachments

• Leads to:

o    Erosion followed by new bone formation

o    Syndesmophyte formation

o    “Bamboo spine” appearance in advanced disease

Clinical features:

• Inflammatory back pain (better with activity, worse with rest)
• Morning stiffness
• Reduced chest expansion
• Bilateral sacroiliitis (hallmark)

Other Options:

Option A. Disc is not the primary site

Option B. Endplate involvement is secondary

Option D. Synovitis may occur but is not the initiating pathology

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Four days ago, she injured her right knee while playing basketball. Increased laxity of the right knee joint is noted when the knee is flexed to 30° and an inward pressure is applied at lateral thigh with one hand and outward pressure with medial ankle with the other hand. The examination finding in this patient is most likely caused by damage to which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. F

Key clues:

• Knee flexed to 30°
• Inward pressure at lateral thigh
• Outward pressure at medial ankle

This is the Valgus Stress Test.

Valgus stress test checks the Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL) ---> So the injured structure must be MCL.

Look at the knee diagram:

• A → ACL
• B → Lateral meniscus
• C → LCL
• D → PCL
• E → Medial meniscus
• F → MCL

So MCL = F.

Option A (Lateral meniscus) ❌

Meniscus injury causes:

• Joint line tenderness
• Locking of knee
• Positive McMurray test

Not valgus laxity.

Option C (LCL) ❌

• LCL injury is tested by Varus stress test, not valgus.
• Varus = pressure inside → outward.

Option D (Medial meniscus) ❌

Meniscus injuries cause:

• Clicking
• Locking
• Joint line pain

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Four days ago, she injured her right knee while playing basketball. Increased laxity of the right knee joint is noted when the knee is flexed to 30° and an inward pressure is applied at lateral thigh with one hand and outward pressure with medial ankle with the other hand. The examination finding in this patient is most likely caused by damage to which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Medial collateral ligament

The question says:

• Knee flexed to 30°
• Inward pressure on lateral thigh
• Outward pressure on medial ankle
• Increased laxity

This maneuver describes the Valgus Stress Test.

The valgus stress test evaluates the Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL).

• A valgus force pushes the knee medially (inward).
• This stresses the medial structures of the knee, especially the MCL, which prevents excessive valgus movement.
• If the knee becomes lax (loose) during this test → the MCL is injured.

A. Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)

ACL injuries are tested by:

• Lachman test
• Anterior drawer test

These check forward movement of the tibia, not valgus stress.

B. Lateral meniscus

Meniscus injuries cause mechanical symptoms like:

• Knee locking
• Clicking
• Joint line tenderness

They do not cause valgus instability.

C. Lateral collateral ligament (LCL)

LCL injury is tested using the Varus Stress Test, not valgus.

• Varus stress → LCL
• Valgus stress → MCL

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 28-year-old male patient with short stature, and coarse facies presents to the OPD. X-ray is shown below. The glycosaminoglycan involved in the condition is a prominent component of which among the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cartilage

The features described in the question point to Mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS).

What happens in Mucopolysaccharidosis?

There is defective degradation of glycosaminoglycans, leading to accumulation of:

• Dermatan sulfate
• Heparan sulfate
• Keratan sulfate

GAGs are major components of:

➡ Cartilage extracellular matrix

They provide:

• Resilience
• Shock absorption
• Water retention

This explains the skeletal abnormalities seen in MPS.

❌ A. Cornea

Although GAG accumulation may cause corneal clouding (especially in Hurler syndrome), the question asks where GAGs are major structural components rather than merely deposited.

❌ C. Kidney basement membrane

Contains type IV collagen and laminin, not primarily GAGs.

❌ D. Synovial fluid

Contains hyaluronic acid, but it is not the major structural location responsible for skeletal abnormalities.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 28-year-old man is brought after a high-speed motor vehicle accident. He was wearing a lap seat belt at the time of impact. He complains of severe back pain. CT scan of the lumbar spine is shown, demonstrating a horizontal fracture line (as indicated by arrows). Which of the following is the most likely associated clinical concern in this patient?
options: High risk of cervical spinal cord transection
Associated intra-abdominal visceral injury, especially bowel injury
Isolated posterior ligamentous injury without bony involvement
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Associated intra-abdominal visceral injury, especially bowel injury

The image shows a Chance fracture, which is a flexion-distraction injury of the spine.

• Horizontal fracture extending through:

o    Vertebral body

o    Pedicles

o    Posterior elements

• Classically occurs due to lap seat belt injury
• Most commonly involves thoracolumbar junction (T12–L2)

Mechanism:

• Sudden forward flexion over a fixed fulcrum (seat belt)
• Leads to distraction of posterior elements and splitting of vertebra

Clinical importance:

• Strong association with intra-abdominal injuries:

o    Small bowel injury

o    Mesenteric tears

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Injury is at thoracolumbar region, not cervical spine

C. Osteoporotic fractures are compression-type, not horizontal distraction fractures

D. Chance fracture involves bony structures, not just ligaments

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with a 3-year history of gradually worsening low back pain, bilateral buttock pain, and stiffness. Symptoms are worse in the morning and relieved with stretching and hot showers. He also reports fatigue but denies fever, chills, night sweats, or weight loss. Physical examination reveals a stooped posture and tenderness over the lumbar spine midline and sacroiliac joints. Which of the following pathologic findings is most likely responsible for this patient's symptoms?
options: Areas of bony erosions and new bone formation
Areas of disorganized trabecular and cortical bone thickening
Disc protrusion and thickening of the ligamentum flavum
Plasma cell infiltrate in bone marrow
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Areas of bony erosions and new bone formation

Chronic inflammatory back pain in a young adult (morning stiffness, improvement with exercise, sacroiliac tenderness, stooped posture) is characteristic of ankylosing spondylitis. The underlying pathology involves enthesitis (inflammation at tendon/ligament insertions) leading to:

• Bony erosions
• Subsequent new bone formation (syndesmophytes)
• Progressive spinal fusion (“bamboo spine”)

Thus, the disease is characterized by areas of bony erosions followed by reactive new bone formation, causing stiffness and reduced mobility.

Why not other options:

B. Paget disease: Bone thickening, not inflammatory back pain.

C. Spinal stenosis: Neurogenic claudication, not morning stiffness.

D. Multiple myeloma: Plasma cells, lytic lesions.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30 year old female presents with dysphagia and weight loss over the past 6 months. Her primary physician observed the following findings. What is her possible diagnosis based on the work up?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Scleroderma

Scleroderma (systemic sclerosis) commonly causes soft-tissue calcifications (calcinosis cutis) in the hands, visible on X-ray as multiple dense calcified deposits around fingers.

Key associations:

• CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia
• Dysphagia occurs due to esophageal smooth muscle fibrosis and dysmotility
• Radiology: soft-tissue calcification, acro-osteolysis of distal phalanges

Thus, hand calcinosis with dysphagia strongly suggests systemic sclerosis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old male athlete presents with chronic low back pain aggravated by extension and relieved by rest. He also reports intermittent radicular pain along the posterior thigh. The lateral lumbosacral X-ray provided shown below. Which of the following is the most likely pathogenesis of the lesion indicated by the arrow?
options: Degenerative facet joint arthritis leading to instability at L4–L5
Stress fracture of pars interarticularis resulting in vertebral slippage
Acute compression fracture of L5 vertebral body
Posterior ligamentous complex disruption due to trauma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Stress fracture of pars interarticularis resulting in vertebral slippage

The image shows spondylolisthesis at L5–S1. In a young adult, especially an athlete, the most common cause is isthmic spondylolisthesis.

Pathogenesis:

• Repetitive stress → defect (spondylolysis) in pars interarticularis
• Leads to instability and anterior slippage of vertebral body

Typical features:

• Occurs at L5–S1
• Associated with extension-based activities (gymnastics, sports)
• May produce radiculopathy due to nerve root compression

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Degenerative type occurs in older patients and commonly at L4–L5

C. Compression fracture presents with vertebral height loss, not forward slip

D. Ligamentous injury is usually acute and associated with trauma

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents to the physician with right wrist pain after a fall while jogging. Physical examination shows decreased grip strength and tenderness between the tendons of the extensor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis. X-ray of the right wrist shows no abnormalities. This patient is at increased risk for which of the following complications?
options: Avascular necrosis of the scaphoid bone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Avascular necrosis of the scaphoid bone

Snuffbox tenderness = suspected scaphoid fracture

•

Even if the initial X-ray is normal, a scaphoid fracture can be present (due to the oblique orientation of the bone, it may be missed).

•

The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply-Blood enters distally and travels proximally.

• So if the waist of the scaphoid fractures, the proximal fragment loses blood supply.-->This leads to avascular necrosis (AVN).

A. Hypesthesia of hypothenar eminence

This occurs with ulnar nerve injury.

clinically :

• Numbness of little finger
• Weak grip
• Clawing of hand

B. Contracture of the palmar aponeurosis

Features:

• Progressive finger flexion deformity
• Thickened palmar fascia

D. Collapse of the lunate bone

This refers to Kienböck disease.

Cause: Avascular necrosis of lunate

Usually associated with chronic trauma or negative ulnar variance, not snuffbox tenderness.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of left shoulder pain, numbness, and tingling in his left hand. He mentions that the symptoms worsen when he raises his arm above his head. He works as a construction worker, frequently lifting heavy tools. Physical examination reveals decreased fine touch in the 4th and 5th fingers of the left hand and weakened grip strength on the left side. Palpation of the neck reveals diffuse pain. The patient’s left arm is held in abduction, extension, and external rotation, and he is instructed to turn his head toward it while breathing deeply, causing a decreased radial pulse on the left side. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the patient’s findings?
options: Median nerve compression at the wrist
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anterior scalene muscle hypertrophy

Classic thoracic outlet syndrome

• The question describes Adson's manoeuvre

What does Adson’s test indicate?

• Compression of the subclavian artery + lower brachial plexus between the anterior and middle scalene muscles.
• Deep inspiration tightens the scalene muscles → narrows interscalene triangle → compresses structures.

Anterior scalene muscle hypertrophy

Construction worker lifting heavy tools → repetitive neck/shoulder strain

→ Scalene muscle hypertrophy

→ Compression of:

• Subclavian artery (↓ radial pulse)
• C8–T1 nerve fibers (4th & 5th digit symptoms)

Ruling out other options:

•

A. Median nerve compression at wrist → (Carpal tunnel syndrome) {affects 1st–3rd digits, not 4th–5th }

•

Numbness in thumb, index, middle, and radial half of ring finger (Carpal tunnel does NOT affect 5th digit)

• Worse at night
•

Thenar muscle weakness

•

B. Rotator cuff tendinopathy→ no pulse change, no numbness in fingers

•

Shoulder pain with movement

• Painful arc (60–120° abduction)
• Weakness in abduction or external rotation

•

C. C8 nerve root compression → would not cause decreased radial pulse

•

Numbness in 4th and 5th fingers ✔

• Weak grip ✔
• Neck pain ✔

Pulse reduction = vascular compression → think thoracic outlet.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 32-year-old man presents 3 months after a road traffic accident in which he sustained a fracture on the right side. He now complains of inability to extend his wrist and fingers, and numbness over the dorsal aspect of the hand and first dorsal web space. On examination, triceps power is fully intact. Which of the following best describes the nerve injury?
options: Injury to the radial nerve in the axilla
Injury to the posterior interosseous nerve
Injury to the radial nerve at the spiral groove
Injury to the median nerve at the elbow
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Injury to the radial nerve at the spiral groove

Mid-shaft humerus fracture is the classic cause of radial nerve injury at the spiral groove.

Triceps is spared because its branches arise proximal to the groove.

Wrist drop + finger drop + dorsal hand sensory loss = complete picture.

Why not B (PIN)?

PIN is pure motor — no sensory loss. The presence of dorsal hand numbness definitively excludes PIN.

Why not A (Axilla)?

Axillary injury → triceps paralyzed. Intact elbow extension rules this out.

Why not D (Median nerve)?

Median nerve → weakness of wrist flexion, thumb opposition, thenar wasting + sensory loss over palmar surface — none of which are present here.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 4 hours after being bitten by a venomous snake. Her pulse is 132/min, and her blood pressure is 102/79 mmHg. Examination shows right lower leg swelling, ecchymosis, and blistering. Right ankle dorsiflexion elicits severe pain. A manometer inserted into the lateral compartment of the lower leg reveals an intracompartmental pressure of 68 mmHg. In addition to administration of antivenom, the patient undergoes fasciotomy. Two weeks later, she reports difficulty walking. Neurologic examination reveals a loss of sensation over the lower part of the lateral side of the right leg and the dorsum of the right foot. Right foot eversion is 1/5. There is no weakness in dorsiflexion. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Superficial peroneal nerve

This patient has:

• Loss of sensation over lateral leg & dorsum of foot
• Weak foot eversion
• Normal dorsiflexion (deep peroneal nerve intact)

These findings localize injury to the superficial peroneal nerve

Commonly affected in lateral compartment syndrome of the leg.

🧠 Structures are in the lateral compartment LEG?

• Fibularis (peroneus) longus
• Fibularis brevis
• Superficial peroneal nerve

Function:

• Foot eversion
• Sensation to lateral leg + dorsum of foot

Localisation of lesion:

• Weak eversion → lateral compartment muscle weakness
• Sensory loss over lateral leg + dorsum foot → superficial peroneal nerve
• Normal dorsiflexion → deep peroneal nerve is intact

A) Sural nerve

• Sensory only
• Supplies posterolateral leg and lateral foot
• Does NOT control eversion

B) Deep peroneal nerve

• Supplies anterior compartment
• Controls dorsiflexion
• Sensory between 1st and 2nd toes only

Here dorsiflexion is normal → so deep peroneal intact.

C) Tibial nerve

• Supplies posterior compartment
• Plantarflexion
• Sensation sole of foot

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 35-year-old female came with persistent back ache, not responding to conservative treatment. She has a history of heavy weight lifting 4 months back with progressively increasing pain that worsens on walking and starts radiating down her legs within 100m range of walking, she however feels no pain on climbing up the stairs. Most probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lumbar canal stenosis

Lumbar canal stenosis causes neurogenic claudication due to compression of cauda equina/nerve roots.

Key features:

• Back pain radiating to legs on walking
• Pain occurs after short walking distance
• Relieved by flexion (sitting, bending forward, climbing stairs uphill)
• Worse with extension (walking on flat surface)

Climbing stairs relieves symptoms because spinal flexion increases canal diameter, making lumbar canal stenosis the most likely diagnosis.

Why not other options:

A. Vertebral compression fracture: Acute localized back pain, worse with movement; no neurogenic claudication pattern.

B. PIVD (Disc prolapse): Radicular pain not typically relieved by flexion; pain often worsens with sitting/coughing.

D. Peripheral arterial disease: Vascular claudication → pain on walking and climbing stairs; not posture-dependent relief.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 35-year-old man undergoes open reduction and internal fixation for a tibial shaft fracture. At 4 weeks follow-up, radiographs show minimal external callus formation despite proper alignment. Histology from the fracture site shows direct formation of lamellar bone without a cartilage intermediate. Which of the following best explains this pattern of fracture healing?
options: Secondary bone healing with endochondral ossification
Primary bone healing with haversian remodeling
Delayed union due to impaired vascularity
Non-union due to instability at fracture site
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Primary bone healing with haversian remodeling

Fracture healing occurs via two main mechanisms:

| Feature | Primary (Direct) Healing | Secondary (Indirect) Healing

| ------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------

| Stability required | Absolute stability (rigid fixation) | Relative stability

| Gap at fracture site | Minimal (<1 mm) | Larger gap

| Callus formation | Absent | Present (prominent)

| Mechanism | Haversian remodeling (cutting cones) | Endochondral + intramembranous ossification

| Intermediate tissue | No cartilage intermediate | Soft callus (cartilage) formed

| Bone formed initially | Lamellar bone directly | Woven bone first, then lamellar

| Stages | No distinct stages | Hematoma → soft callus → hard callus → remodeling

| Blood supply | Requires good vascularity | Can occur even with some disruption

| Typical examples | ORIF with compression plating | Casting, intramedullary nailing

| Time taken | Slower initial healing | Faster initial healing

| Radiological feature | No visible callus | Visible callus formation

| Clinical significance | Indicates rigid fixation | Most common mode of healing

In this case:

• Rigid fixation (ORIF)
• Minimal callus
• Direct lamellar bone formation

→ Indicates primary bone healing

Why other options are incorrect:

Option A. Would show callus and cartilage intermediate

Option C. Would show impaired healing, not organized lamellar bone

Option D. Non-union shows fibrous tissue, not bone formation

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 4-month-old female infant, born in breech presentation, is brought with decreased movement of the left lower limb. On examination, there is limitation of abduction of the left hip. Galeazzi sign is positive. Ultrasonography confirms a dislocated hip joint. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Closed reduction and hip spica casting
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pavlik harness application

This infant is 4 months old with confirmed developmental dysplasia of the hip.

Management depends on age:

• 0–6 months:

• First-line treatment is Pavlik harness
• Maintains hip in flexion and abduction
• Allows spontaneous reduction of femoral head

• 6–18 months:

• Closed reduction + hip spica
• Open reduction ± osteotomy

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Open reduction is reserved for late or failed cases

B. Closed reduction is preferred after 6 months of age

D. Osteotomy is used in older children

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 4-year-old child presents with a history of progressive weakness, irritability, and delayed growth. He was started on appropriate treatment at a CHC. A repeat wrist X-ray is performed, as shown. Based on the clinical features and radiographic findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Healing Rickets

Healing rickets is characterized radiologically by dense provisional zone of calcification (white line of healing) at the metaphysis after initiation of vitamin D and calcium therapy.

Features of healing rickets:

• Reappearance of sharp metaphyseal line (white line of Frankel)
• Reduction in metaphyseal cupping and fraying
• Increased mineralization of previously osteopenic bone
• Seen after treatment for nutritional rickets

Thus, in a treated child with prior rickets, appearance of dense metaphyseal lines indicates healing rather than active disease.

Why NOT others:

• A. Non-healing rickets: Would show cupping, fraying, and widening of metaphysis with poor mineralization — not dense white line.
• B. Scurvy: Shows white line of Frankel + scorbutic zone + Pelkan spurs, but clinical features include bleeding gums, petechiae, severe pain — not typical here.
• D. Osteopetrosis: Shows diffuse generalized bone sclerosis (“bone within bone”), not metaphyseal healing lines.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 4-year-old presents with a pink but pulseless arm following an injury. X-ray is shown below. What is the best next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Reduction and pinning

The key clinical picture:

• 4-year-old child
• Pink but pulseless arm after injury
• Supracondylar fracture on X-ray

A pink pulseless hand means:

• No palpable radial pulse
• BUT the hand is still perfused (pink, warm) — likely via collateral circulation
• The management principle:

In a pink pulseless hand with supracondylar fracture → Reduce the fracture FIRST

• Fracture reduction often restores arterial flow.
• If pulse returns → observe.
• If limb becomes pale/cold or pulse not restored after reduction → vascular exploration.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 40-year-old man presents with wrist pain after a fall on an outstretched hand. The X-ray is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Volar Barton’s fracture

A Barton fracture is an intra-articular fracture of the distal radius rim associated with radiocarpal dislocation/subluxation.

X-ray Description

• Fracture involves the rim (lip) of distal radius
• Intra-articular extension into wrist joint
• Associated displacement of carpus with the fractured fragment
• Seen best on lateral wrist X-ray

Types

1. Dorsal Barton fracture

• Fracture of dorsal rim of distal radius
• Dorsal displacement/subluxation of carpus along with distal fragment
• Usually due to fall on extended wrist

2. Volar (reverse) Barton fracture

• Fracture of volar rim of distal radius
• Volar displacement of carpus with fragment
• Often due to fall on flexed wrist

Key differentiating point

• Colles fracture: extra-articular distal radius fracture
• Barton fracture: intra-articular rim fracture with radiocarpal subluxation/dislocation

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 41-year-old woman comes to the doctor because of gradually progressive weakness in her right hand over the past few weeks. She goes to the gym to lift weights 5 times a week. With the dorsum of the right hand on a flat surface, the patient is unable to move her thumb to touch a pen held 2 cm above the interphalangeal joint of the thumb. An MRI of the right arm shows compression of a nerve that passes through the pronater teres muscle. Based on the examination findings, loss of innervation of which of the following muscles is most likely in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Abductor pollicis brevis

• Compression of the median nerve at the level of the pronator teres (pronator teres syndrome) causes weakness of thenar muscles, especially abductor pollicis brevis, leading to impaired thumb abduction (inability to lift thumb perpendicular to palm).
• This helps differentiate median nerve palsy from radial and ulnar nerve injuries based on specific thumb movement deficits.

Why not other options:

A) Adductor pollicis: Innervated by the ulnar nerve → causes weak thumb adduction (Froment sign), not affected in median nerve compression.

C) Extensor pollicis brevis: Innervated by the radial nerve (posterior interosseous nerve) → affects thumb extension, not thumb abduction.

D) Abductor pollicis longus: Also innervated by the radial nerve → abducts thumb at the carpometacarpal joint.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 42-year-old female complains of soft, fluctuating swelling in front of the knee. She reports discomfort and difficulty while moving her knee. MRI is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Housemaid's knee

• Soft, fluctuant swelling anterior to patella
• Pain with knee movement or kneeling
• MRI/USG: fluid collection in prepatellar bursa
• Common in occupations involving frequent kneeling (housemaids, carpet layers)

This is classic for Prepatellar bursitis/ Housemaids knee

Housemaid’s knee = Prepatellar bursitis

• It occurs due to repeated kneeling, which causes inflammation of the prepatellar bursa located between the patella and skin.

A. Clergyman’s knee

❌ This is infrapatellar bursitis

• Swelling below the patella, not in front.

C. Gout

❌ Causes joint inflammation, severe pain, and crystal deposition — not a localized superficial fluctuating swelling.

D. Pes anserinus bursitis

❌ Occurs medial to the knee, below the joint line.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman presents with symmetrical pain and swelling of the small joints of the hands for 8 months. Morning stiffness lasts more than 1 hour. On examination, there is ulnar deviation of fingers and swan-neck deformities as shown below. Laboratory investigations show positive anti-CCP antibodies. Which of the following is the earliest pathological change in the affected joints?
options: Cartilage destruction due to proteolytic enzymes
Formation of pannus leading to joint erosion
Synovial membrane hyperplasia with inflammatory cell infiltration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Synovial membrane hyperplasia with inflammatory cell infiltration

Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune inflammatory arthritis primarily affecting synovium.

Sequence of pathology:

1.    Earliest change:

• Synovial membrane inflammation
• Hyperplasia with infiltration by T cells, B cells, and macrophages

2.    Progression:

• Formation of pannus (granulation tissue)
• Pannus invades cartilage and bone

3.    Late changes:

• Cartilage destruction
• Joint deformities (ulnar deviation, swan neck)
• Fibrosis and ankylosis

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Cartilage destruction is a later event

B. Pannus formation occurs after synovial inflammation

D. Subchondral sclerosis is more typical of osteoarthritis

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 45 year old male patient sustained a tibial fracture was managed conservatively with a plaster cast. A few days later, severe pain was elicited on passive stretching. What is the indication of fasciotomy in this patient?
options: Compartment pressure less than 30 mm Hg
Diastolic blood pressure more than 100 mm Hg
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Differential pressure less than 30 mmHg

Indication for fasciotomy in compartment syndrome:

• Fasciotomy is required when ΔP (diastolic BP − compartment pressure) ≤ 30 mmHg.
• A differential pressure <30 mmHg indicates critically reduced tissue perfusion and risk of ischemic necrosis → urgent decompression is needed.
• Severe pain on passive stretch is the earliest clinical sign of compartment syndrome.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 45-year-old female presents with a painful, pulsatile swelling over the pelvis. X-ray shows an expansile lytic lesion with cortical thinning. MRI shows the presence of fluid-fluid levels. Which primary malignancy most commonly gives pulsatile bone metastasis as listed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma

Pulsatile, expansile lytic bone metastases are characteristic of hypervascular tumors, most commonly clear cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC).

• Highly vascular metastasis → may present as pulsatile swelling
• Expansile lytic bone lesions with cortical thinning
• MRI may show fluid–fluid levels due to hemorrhage
• Common sites: pelvis, vertebrae, long bones

Other hypervascular metastases:

• Thyroid carcinoma
• Hepatocellular carcinoma
• Melanoma

However, the most common primary malignancy causing pulsatile bone metastasis is clear cell RCC.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 45-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to left wrist pain after a fall. The patient was walking in his house when he tripped over a rug and landed on his outstretched hand. Medical history is notable for celiac disease, hypertension, and hypothyroidism for which he takes appropriate daily medications. X-ray of the left wrist is shown below. Which of the following is the most significant risk factor for bone fracture in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Celiac disease

• Celiac disease is a significant risk factor for osteoporosis and fragility fractures due to chronic malabsorption of calcium and vitamin D, leading to decreased bone mineral density.
• Patients with untreated or longstanding celiac disease can develop osteopenia/osteoporosis at a younger age, predisposing them to low-impact fractures such as distal radius (Colles) fractures after minor trauma (eg, fall on outstretched hand).
• Therefore, in relatively young patients presenting with fragility fractures, clinicians should evaluate for secondary causes of osteoporosis, including celiac disease, endocrine disorders, and malabsorption syndromes.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department following a motor vehicle collision. He reports right hip pain and numbness along the right thigh. Physical examination shows decreased sensation to light touch over a small area of the medial thigh. X-rays of the pelvis show a displaced pelvic ring fracture. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?
options: Sensory deficit of the dorsal foot
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Impaired adduction of hip

• Motor vehicle collision
• Displaced pelvic ring fracture
• Decreased sensation over a small area of the medial thigh

That small patch of medial thigh sensation is the giveaway.

Nerve involved

This sensory area is supplied by the obturator nerve.

The obturator nerve:

• Origin: L2–L4
• Motor: Hip adductor muscles
• Sensory: Medial thigh

Pelvic fractures commonly injure this nerve as it runs along the pelvic wall and obturator canal.

Expected finding

If the obturator nerve is injured → hip adduction becomes weak or impaired.

✅ Correct Answer

D. Impaired adduction of hip

❌ A. Sensory deficit of dorsal foot

→ Deep peroneal nerve / common peroneal nerve

❌ B. Impaired hip extension

→ Inferior gluteal nerve (gluteus maximus)

❌ C. Impaired dorsiflexion of foot

→ Deep peroneal nerve

Pelvic fracture + medial thigh numbness

→ Obturator nerve injury

→ Loss of hip adduction

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with difficulty walking, particularly noticing that he frequently trips over his right foot while walking on level ground. He denies any pain but reports a tingling sensation over the dorsum of the right foot for the past 3 weeks, following an episode of prolonged squatting during a plumbing job. His gait is shown in the accompanying video. Based on the gait pattern demonstrated in the video, which of the following is the most likely site of nerve involvement?
options: Tibial nerve at the popliteal fossa
Common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck
Femoral nerve at the inguinal ligament
Sciatic nerve at the greater sciatic notch
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck

High steppage gait results from foot drop due to weakness of ankle dorsiflexors (tibialis anterior) and evertors, most commonly caused by common peroneal (fibular) nerve injury at the fibular neck — a site vulnerable to compression from prolonged squatting, crossing legs, or tight casts, since the nerve winds superficially around the fibular head here.

• The patient lifts the leg higher than normal (excessive hip and knee flexion) to prevent the dropped foot from dragging on the ground, and the foot then slaps down (foot slap) due to loss of controlled dorsiflexion.
• A. Tibial nerve injury causes loss of plantarflexion and inversion, not steppage gait.
• C. Femoral nerve injury causes quadriceps weakness with buckling of the knee, not foot drop.
• D. Sciatic nerve injury can cause foot drop too (since it gives rise to the common peroneal nerve) but would typically also involve hamstring weakness and more extensive sensory loss — the history of squatting strongly localizes to the fibular neck specifically.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient with suspected thoracic outlet syndrome is being examined. Hyperabduction of the arm on the affected side causes a reduction in the radial artery pulsation. X-ray is shown. What is this test known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Wright's test

This is Wright’s test (also called the hyperabduction test).

• In thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS), hyperabduction of the arm compresses the neurovascular bundle (axial/subclaivan artery, brachial plexus) beneath the pectoralis minor tendon.
• If the radial pulse decreases or disappears during hyperabduction, the test is positive.
• That exact mechanism = Wright’s test.

A. Adson’s test → Neck extension + head rotation affected side + deep inspiration: pulse ↓ (scalene compression).

B. Halstead (costoclavicular maneuver) → Shoulder drawn down and back, Downward traction on arm → tests costoclavicular compression.

C. Roos test → Arms abducted + externally rotated + repetitive hand opening/closing

D. Wright’s test → Arm hyperabduction → ↓ radial pulse ✔

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman was taken to a trauma centre after suffering an accident. An X-ray of her pelvis was taken. In this instance, what is the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Closed Reduction + Internal fixation

Looking at the image:

• Fracture line through the neck of femur
• Intracapsular fracture
• Seen in a 45-year-old patient

This is a fracture neck of femur.

Fracture Neck of Femur – Treatment

1. < 65 years → Preserve head

• <3 weeks: Closed reduction + internal fixation (CRIF)
• >3 weeks: Augmented osteotomy

2. > 65 years

• Hemiarthroplasty
• Associated OA: Total hip replacement

Why other options are incorrect?

A. Hemiarthroplasty ❌

This is used in:

• Elderly patients
• Poor bone quality
• High risk of avascular necrosis

Not preferred in younger patients because we try to preserve the native femoral head.

B. Augmentation osteotomy ❌

This is done for:

• Non-union of femoral neck fracture
• Late complications
• Not the initial treatment in acute trauma.

D. Open reduction + internal fixation ❌

Open reduction is done when:

• Closed reduction fails
• Severe displacement

Initial approach is closed reduction first.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 52-year-old diabetic man presents with complaints of pain and swelling over his left middle finger, which appears as below. What is the next line of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Incision and drainage

The image shows a fluctuant, erythematous swelling of the fingertip nail bed consistent with paronychia.

In diabetics, infections can progress rapidly. Once an abscess has formed, definitive treatment is incision and drainage (I&D).

• Warm soaks or topical antibiotics are useful only in early cellulitis.

• Oral antibiotics alone are inadequate once pus is present.

• Delay can lead to osteomyelitis or compartment necrosis of the pulp.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman comes to the office due to right shoulder pain for 4 months. She reports that the pain has improved since its onset, but now she has trouble with activities such as washing her hair or reaching the upper shelves of the kitchen cabinets. Heating pads and ice packs have not helped. She has had no fever, weight loss, or trauma. Medical history includes hypertension treated with lisinopril and hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. On examination, there is mild atrophy of the right deltoid muscle. Active and passive range of motion of the right shoulder is markedly reduced in abduction, flexion, and internal and external rotation compared to the left. Sensation in the upper extremities and strength in the hands and elbows are preserved. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Range-of-motion exercises

This patient has adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder), characterized by progressive shoulder pain followed by marked restriction of both active and passive range of motion. It is commonly associated with diabetes and hypothyroidism.

Management is primarily conservative, with physical therapy and range-of-motion exercises as first-line treatment to restore mobility and prevent permanent stiffness.

Why not other options:

A. Deltoid biopsy: No primary muscle disease; problem is joint capsule stiffness.

B. MRI cervical spine: Would cause radicular pain/neurologic deficits; ROM restriction wouldn’t be both active & passive.

D. Nerve conduction studies: No neuropathy signs; sensation & distal strength normal.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 6-year-old girl is evaluated for early-onset puberty and multiple bone lesions. On examination, she has café-au-lait spots as shown below. Hormonal tests confirm hyperfunction of multiple endocrine glands. What is the shape of the CALMs described as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coast of Maine

McCune–Albright syndrome presents with the triad of:

• Café-au-lait macules (irregular “coast of Maine” borders)
• Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (multiple bone lesions)
• Precocious puberty / multiple endocrine hyperfunction

It is caused by a postzygotic activating mutation of the GNAS gene, leading to constitutive activation of the Gs alpha subunit and increased cAMP signaling. Because the mutation is mosaic, the condition is not inherited and results in patchy involvement of skin, bone, and endocrine tissues.

Why NOT others:

A. Coast of California: Neurofibromatosis type 1 → café-au-lait spots with smooth “coast of California” borders + neurofibromas; no endocrine hyperfunction.

Coast of Maldives and Coast of Bay of Bengal are related to geography, not related to medicine.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 60 year old female underwent hip replacement. After 1 year she developed fever and pain in the joint. Radiograph revealed loosening of prosthesis. The implant had to be removed. The histological image of the tissue adjoining the implant is show below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Metallosis

Metallosis is a complication of joint prostheses caused by metal particle debris from implant wear. These particles accumulate in surrounding tissues, leading to chronic inflammation, macrophage reaction, and prosthesis loosening.

Histology shows black granular metallic pigment within macrophages and giant cells in periprosthetic tissue. Patients present with pain, implant loosening, and sometimes systemic metal toxicity, often requiring removal or revision of the prosthesis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 65-year-old patient suffers with extracapsular femoral neck fracture. What would be the most appropriate management option for her management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intramedullary nailing

For extracapsular fractures, common fixation methods are:

• Dynamic hip screw (DHS)
• Intramedullary nail

Among the options given, intramedullary nailing fits best.

| Type of fracture | Treatment

| ---------------- | ---------

| Intracapsular neck of femur fracture | Hemiarthroplasty(elderly)/ CR-IF (young)

| Extracapsular fracture | Internal fixation

A. Russell’s traction ❌

Russell’s traction is temporary management used for:

• Femoral shaft fractures
• Pre-operative stabilization

Not the definitive treatment.

B. Bar and boot plaster ❌

This is an old conservative treatment.

Modern management prefers surgical fixation.

D. Hemiarthroplasty ❌

This is done for intracapsular neck of femur fractures because:

• Blood supply to femoral head is compromised
• Risk of avascular necrosis

But here the fracture is extracapsular, where blood supply is preserved. So replacement is unnecessary.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 66-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination after a below-knee amputation of the right lower leg. Three weeks ago, he had an acute arterial embolism that could not be revascularized in time to save the leg. He now reports episodic hot, shooting, and tingling pain in the right lower leg that began shortly after the amputation. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the past 30 years. His current medications are metformin and prophylactic subcutaneous heparin. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 135/88 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a slightly erythematous stump with clean sutures. The skin overlying the stump is warm and well-perfused. Muscle strength and sensation are normal throughout the remaining extremity and the left lower extremity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phantom limb pain

Phantom limb pain is neuropathic pain perceived in an amputated limb due to maladaptive cortical reorganization and persistent activation of peripheral and central pain pathways. It typically presents as burning, shooting, or tingling pain in the missing limb shortly after amputation, despite normal healing of the stump and no signs of infection or ischemia.

Thus, episodic neuropathic pain in the absent limb after amputation is most consistent with phantom limb pain.

Why not other options:

B. Foreign body reaction: Would show local inflammation, discharge, poor wound healing.

C. Reinfarction: Would cause ischemic signs in stump (cold, pale, poorly perfused).

D. Osteomyelitis: Fever, severe pain, purulent discharge, raised inflammatory markers.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 67-year-old man comes to the OPD due to 2 days of back pain. He was moving boxes in his garage when the pain started. The pain is not relieved by lying down and increases in intensity when straining and coughing. He cannot sleep at night due to pain and has taken acetaminophen several times without relief. He has never had such pain before. Physical examination shows 2+ symmetrical knee and ankle jerk reflexes. Straight leg raising test is negative. There is point tenderness to palpation and percussion along the midline at the fourth lumbar vertebra. Which of the following is the most likely underlying etiology of this patient's current condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Loss of bone mineral density

In elderly patients, acute onset focal back pain with point vertebral tenderness after minimal strain suggests a vertebral compression fracture, most commonly due to osteoporosis (loss of bone mineral density).

• Age >65 years
• Pain after minor activity (lifting, bending)
• Midline vertebral tenderness
• Pain worsens with coughing/straining
• Normal neurologic exam (unless severe collapse)

Why not other options:

A. Facet arthritis: Chronic back pain, not acute; paraspinal pain, not midline vertebral tenderness.

B. Nerve root demyelination: Radicular pain, neuro deficits, positive SLR expected — absent here.

C. Ligament sprain: Diffuse muscle tenderness, improves with rest; no focal vertebral tenderness.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 68-year-old man presents to the clinic due to progressively worsening pain in his lower limbs for the past 6 months. He reports the pain is deep and aching and worsens with activity. There is no history of trauma or fever. On examination, the legs are bowed with palpable warmth over the shins, and imaging shows trabecular thickening and cortical bone expansion in both tibiae and fibulae. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely seen in this patient?
options: High calcium, Low phosphorus, High ALP
Normal calcium, Normal phosphorus, Normal ALP
High calcium, high phosphorus, High ALP
Normal calcium, Normal phosphorus, High ALP
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Normal calcium, Normal phosphorus, High ALP

This patient has features of Paget disease of bone (bone pain, bowing of legs, warmth, cortical thickening and trabecular enlargement).

Paget disease involves increased osteoclastic and osteoblastic activity leading to high bone turnover. Typical laboratory findings:

• Normal serum calcium
• Normal serum phosphorus
• Elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) due to increased bone formation

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presents with painless swelling of the right ring finger for 3 months. There is gradual enlargement without significant redness or acute tenderness. The X-ray of the hand is shown. It reveals an expanded phalanx with cortical thinning and a cystic, ballooned appearance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Spina ventosa due to tuberculous dactylitis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Spina ventosa due to tuberculous dactylitis

The image shows a ballooned expansion of a phalanx with cortical thinning, which is characteristic of spina ventosa.

• Occurs in children
• Involves short tubular bones of hands/feet
• Caused by skeletal tuberculosis (tuberculous dactylitis)
• Bone appears expanded like a “wind-filled sail” (hence the name spina ventosa)
• Minimal pain and chronic course

Pathogenesis:

• Hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis
• Granulomatous inflammation → bone expansion and destruction

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Enchondroma is usually asymptomatic and shows well-defined lytic lesion without marked ballooning

C. Pyogenic osteomyelitis presents acutely with pain, fever, and periosteal reaction

D. Ewing sarcoma shows aggressive features like onion-skin periosteal reaction

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 75-year-old woman presents to the clinic after a fall. She complains of right hip and thigh pain. Examination reveals that her right leg is shorter than her left and externally rotated. Which of the following pathological changes is most likely to be present in this patient?
options: Cortical bone overgrowth and sclerosis due to defective osteoclasts
Impaired mineralization of osteoid and hyperactive osteoblasts
Decreased cortical and trabecular bone mass with normal bone mineralization
Woven and lamellar bone mosaic pattern due to increased osteoclast and osteoblast activity resulting in bone of low quality
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decreased cortical and trabecular bone mass with normal bone mineralization

An elderly woman with a fall followed by a shortened, externally rotated leg most likely has a fragility fracture of the femoral neck due to osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is characterized by:

• Decreased cortical and trabecular bone mass
• Normal bone mineralization
• Increased fracture risk, especially hip, vertebrae, and wrist

Thus, osteoporosis involves quantitative bone loss with normal mineralization, leading to fragile bones.

Why not other options:

A. Defective osteoclasts → Osteopetrosis → dense but brittle bones; not typical in elderly.

B. Impaired mineralization → Osteomalacia → defective mineralization, bone pain; not classic fragility fracture pattern.

D. Mosaic bone pattern → Paget disease → disorganized bone remodeling.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young female patient complains of low back pain radiating to the right hip, back of the thigh, leg, and ankle after an intense workout of lifting some heavy weights. MRI shows the following finding. Which function will be weak here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. EHL

Posterolateral L4–L5 disc herniation most commonly compresses the traversing L5 nerve root, causing radicular pain along the lateral leg and dorsum of foot.

Clinical Clue First

The patient has pain radiating to:

• Right hip
