• Back of thigh
• Leg
• Ankle

After lifting heavy weights → suggests lumbar disc herniation.

On the sagittal MRI shown, the disc protrusion is at L4–L5 level.

Root Affected in L4–L5 Disc Herniation

In lumbar disc herniation:

• Disc level L4–L5 → compresses L5 nerve root

Key Function of L5 Root

L5 mainly controls:

• Great toe extension
• Dorsiflexion of foot

Most specific muscle: Extensor Hallucis Longus (EHL)

Weakness will cause:

• Difficulty extending the great toe
• Trouble heel walking

Other Options:

A. Hip flexion

Controlled mainly by:

• Iliopsoas
• L1–L3 roots

B. Ankle dorsiflexion

• Although L5 contributes, dorsiflexion is also supplied by L4.
• Therefore less specific than EHL.

D. Ankle plantar flexion

Controlled mainly by:

• S1 root
• Gastrocnemius & soleus

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young marathon runner is participating in a marathon competition. After running for 100 m, he develops pain at the anteromedial aspect of tibia which was mild to start with, but increased on further running. X-ray was normal. The doctor ordered a bone scan. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Shin splint

Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) present with exercise-induced pain along the anteromedial tibial border.

• Occurs especially in runners and military recruits.
• Gradual onset pain that worsens with running
• Tenderness along medial tibial shaft
• Early X-ray is normal
• Bone scan/MRI shows periosteal stress reaction
• Caused by repetitive traction and stress on tibial periosteum
• Represents early stress injury
• May progress to stress fracture if activity continues.
• Management includes rest, activity modification, proper footwear, and physiotherapy.

A. Lisfranc fracture ❌

• Lisfranc injury involves the tarsometatarsal joints of the foot, not the tibia.
• Pain is typically located in the midfoot, especially over the dorsum of the foot.
• It usually occurs due to trauma such as twisting of the foot or fall, not repetitive running.
• X-ray often shows displacement of metatarsals or widening between 1st and 2nd metatarsals.
• The question clearly states pain in the tibia, so this does not fit.
•

B. Jones fracture ❌

• Jones fracture occurs at the base of the 5th metatarsal.
• Pain is located on the lateral side of the foot, not the tibia.
• It is usually caused by acute inversion injury of the foot, not gradual running pain.
• Local tenderness is at the 5th metatarsal base, not along the shin.

D. Nutcracker fracture ❌

• Nutcracker fracture is a compression fracture of the cuboid bone in the foot.
• It occurs when the forefoot is forcibly abducted, compressing the cuboid between calcaneus and metatarsals.
• Pain is present in the lateral midfoot region, not along the tibia.
• It is usually traumatic, not a repetitive stress injury from running.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: All are true about treatment of femoral shaft fracture in different pediatric age groups, except:
options: Pavlik harness is used for infants under 6 months
Spica cast is preferred for ages 6 months to 5 years
Flexible nails are used in adolescents >10 years
Gallows traction is useful in children under 2 years and <12 kg
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Flexible nails are used in adolescents >10 years

Age-wise Management of Pediatric Femoral Shaft Fractures

Infants (< 6 months): Pavlik harness

• Keeps hips flexed and abducted
• Simple and effective because infants remodel well

Children (6 months – 5 years): Hip spica cast

• Standard treatment
• Excellent remodeling potential

Children (5 – 10 years): Flexible intramedullary nails (Titanium elastic nails)

Adolescents (>10–12 years): Rigid/ Locked intramedullary nails

Because:

• Weight is higher
• Flexible nails are not strong enough

So Option C is FALSE.

Small children (< 2 years and <12 kg)

Gallows traction

• Both legs suspended vertically
• Uses body weight for traction

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: All are true about types of nerve injuries, except:
options: Neuropraxia involves segmental demyelination without axonal damage
Axonotmesis involves axonal interruption with intact neural tubes
Neurotmesis results from temporary ischemia with full recovery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neurotmesis results from temporary ischemia with full recovery

Peripheral nerve injuries are classified by Seddon classification:

• Neuropraxia: Mildest injury; segmental demyelination without axonal damage → complete recovery
• Axonotmesis: Axonal disruption with intact endoneurium/neural sheath → recovery possible via regeneration
• Neurotmesis: Most severe; complete nerve transection with destruction of endoneurial tubes → requires surgical repair and recovery often incomplete

Temporary ischemia with full recovery describes neuropraxia, not neurotmesis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: All of the following are part of the Denis column theory for vertebral fractures, except:
options: Anterior column includes anterior longitudinal ligament and anterior 2/3 of vertebral body
Middle column includes posterior part of disc and posterior longitudinal ligament
Posterior column contains spinous process and PLL
Involvement of middle column with another column is considered unstable
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Posterior column contains spinous process and PLL

DENNIS THREE COLUMNS:

| Column | Structures Included

| ------ | -------------------

| Anterior column | Anterior longitudinal ligament (ALL), anterior 2/3 of vertebral body, anterior part of annulus fibrosus

| Middle column | Posterior 1/3 of vertebral body, posterior part of annulus fibrosus, posterior longitudinal ligament (PLL)

| Posterior column | Pedicles, lamina, facet joints, spinous processes, ligamentum flavum, interspinous ligament, supraspinous ligament

| Rule | Meaning

| ---- | -------

| One column injury | Usually stable

| Two column injury | Potentially unstable

| Middle column involvement with another column | Unstable fracture

| Option | Statement | True / False | Reason

| ------ | --------- | ------------ | ------

| A | Anterior column includes ALL and anterior 2/3 of vertebral body | ✅ True | Correct definition

| B | Middle column includes posterior disc and PLL | ✅ True | Correct

| C | Posterior column contains spinous process and PLL | ❌ False | PLL belongs to middle column, not posterior

| D | Middle column involvement with another column → unstable | ✅ True | Key rule

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: All of the following are true regarding congenital torticollis, except:
options: Head is tilted toward the affected side with chin rotated away
It is due to fibrosis of the sternocleidomastoid muscle
Birth injury during breech delivery may be a cause
It is more common in children with cerebral palsy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It is more common in children with cerebral palsy

🧠 Congenital Muscular Torticollis (CMT)

This condition occurs due to fibrosis/shortening of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle, usually related to birth trauma.

Typical posture:

·         Head tilted toward the affected side

·         Chin rotated to the opposite side

✔ Why A, B, C are TRUE

A. Head is tilted toward the affected side with chin rotated away

✔ Classic posture of torticollis.

Example:

If right SCM is affected →

• Head tilts right
• Chin rotates left

B. It is due to fibrosis of the sternocleidomastoid muscle

✔ Correct.

This fibrosis may occur due to:

• Birth trauma
• Intrauterine malposition
• SCM hematoma → fibrosis

C. Birth injury during breech delivery may be a cause

✔ Correct.

Difficult delivery (especially breech) can injure SCM → hematoma → fibrosis → torticollis.

D. It is more common in children with cerebral palsy

❌ Incorrect.

• Congenital torticollis is unrelated to cerebral palsy.
• CP may cause spastic torticollis, but that is a different neurological condition, not congenital muscular torticollis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: All of the following classification systems are correctly matched to their indication, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mayo classification – Shoulder instability

Orthopedic classification systems are used for specific injuries:

• Neer classification: Proximal humerus fractures
• Gartland classification: Supracondylar fracture of humerus (children)
• AO–Magerl classification: Thoracolumbar spine fractures
• Mayo classification: Used for olecranon fractures, not shoulder instability

The Mayo classification is used for olecranon fractures, not for shoulder instability.

Shoulder instability classifications include Bankart, Hill-Sachs, Rockwood (AC joint)

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: All of the following elbow conditions are correctly described, except:
options: Baseball pitcher’s elbow – Osteoarthritis and joint incongruity
Little leaguer’s elbow – Partial avulsion of medial epicondyle
Pulled elbow – Downward dislocation of radial head
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Javelin thrower’s elbow – Olecranon bursitis

| Option | Condition | Actual Pathology | Statement Given | Correct / Incorrect

| ------ | --------- | ---------------- | --------------- | -------------------

| A | Baseball pitcher’s elbow | Valgus overload → osteochondritis/degeneration of capitellum and joint incongruity | Osteoarthritis and joint incongruity | ✅ Correct

| B | Little leaguer’s elbow | Traction injury → medial epicondyle apophysitis / partial avulsion | Partial avulsion of medial epicondyle | ✅ Correct

| C | Javelin thrower’s elbow | Valgus extension overload → medial ligament strain, posteromedial impingement, osteophytes | Olecranon bursitis | ❌ Incorrect

| D | Pulled elbow (Nursemaid’s elbow) | Radial head subluxation due to annular ligament slip | Downward displacement/subluxation of radial head | ✅ Correct

Javelin thrower’s elbow occurs due to repeated valgus stress during throwing, leading to:

• Ulnar collateral ligament strain
• Posteromedial impingement
• Olecranon osteophytes

It is NOT olecranon bursitis (which is usually due to trauma or prolonged pressure).

Thus, associating javelin thrower’s elbow with olecranon bursitis is incorrect.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An 11-month-old boy with CTEV has not responded to POP casting over 6 months. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Turco’s procedure

Management of congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV/clubfoot) follows a stepwise approach:

• Initial treatment: Serial manipulation and POP casting (Ponseti method)
• If resistant to casting by 6–12 months of age, surgical correction is required
• Turco’s posteromedial soft-tissue release is the standard procedure for resistant CTEV in infants

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An old lady fell in the bathroom with an outstretched hand. She was managed conservatively. Later, she developed the deformity as shown in the figure. Most likely fracture sustained was:
options: Intra-articular fracture distal end of radius
Extra-articular fracture distal end of radius
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Extra-articular fracture distal end of radius

An elderly woman who falls on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) most commonly sustains a Colles' fracture, which is an extra-articular fracture of the distal radius.

If treated conservatively, malunion may occur, leading to the characteristic "dinner fork" (silver fork) deformity shown in the image.

Features of Colles' fracture

• Mechanism: Fall on an outstretched hand with the wrist in extension
• Fracture site: Distal radius, approximately 2–3 cm proximal to the articular surface
• Type: Extra-articular
• Displacement: Distal fragment is displaced dorsally, radially, and proximally, with dorsal angulation and supination
• Common patient: Elderly postmenopausal women with osteoporosis

Why the other options are incorrect?

A. Intra-articular fracture of the distal end of the radius

• Refers to Barton's fracture or other intra-articular distal radius fractures.
• These involve the radiocarpal joint and do not typically produce the classic dinner fork deformity.

C. Scaphoid fracture

• Usually occurs in young adults after FOOSH.
• Presents with anatomical snuffbox tenderness.
• Does not cause a dinner fork deformity.

D. Dislocation of the wrist

• Rare due to strong ligamentous support.
• Produces gross wrist deformity but not the characteristic appearance of a healed Colles' fracture.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Arrange the following external fixators used for treatment of fracture of tibia in order of increasing stability: I.Ilizarov II.Uniplanar frame with one rod III.Biplanar frame IV.Uniplanar frame with two rods
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. II, IV, III, I

External fixator stability depends on number of rods, planes, and ring fixation.

Stability increases as construct complexity increases:

• Uniplanar single rod → least stable
• Uniplanar two rods → more stable
• Biplanar frame → increased multiplanar stability
• Ilizarov circular fixator → most stable due to tensioned wires and circular ring construct

Thus, stability (increasing order):

• Uniplanar one rod < Uniplanar two rods < Biplanar frame < Ilizarov.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Choose the incorrect statement regarding the given image:
options: There is no restriction of movement
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Squatting is not possible

The image shows a Jaipur Foot prosthesis (used in below-knee amputees).

Key Features of Jaipur Foot

• Cosmetically resembles a normal barefoot
• Made of rubber → flexible
• Allows:

• Squatting
• Sitting cross-legged
• Barefoot walking

• Designed for Indian lifestyle (uneven terrain, barefoot habits)
• Contrast: SACH foot → rigid, no squatting

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: During a Forensic Medicine Conference, a detailed discussion is held on the mechanisms of death in cases of judicial hanging. One of the topics focuses on the anatomical structures involved in the upper cervical spine and their role in the cause of death when subjected to the forces involved in hanging. A case is presented where an individual subjected to judicial hanging was found to have significant cervical spine injuries during the autopsy. Based on the anatomical and forensic analysis, which of the following structures is most likely to be involved in causing death due to rupture in cases of judicial hanging?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Transverse Ligament of Dens

In judicial hanging, the drop is designed to produce sudden hyperextension and distraction of the upper cervical spine, particularly at the C1–C2 level (atlanto-axial joint).

This leads to:

• Fracture of the dens (odontoid process)
• Rupture of stabilizing ligaments
• Displacement of C1 over C2
• Compression or transection of the upper spinal cord/medulla

This injury pattern is historically called: Hangman’s fracture

But ligament rupture, especially of the transverse ligament, plays a crucial role in allowing the dens to move backward and damage the spinal cord.

The transverse ligament of the atlas:

• Prevents posterior displacement of dens
• Maintains stability of atlanto-axial joint
• Protects the spinal cord

In Judicial Hanging

When the transverse ligament ruptures:

• The dens moves backward
• It compresses the spinal cord or medulla
• Leads to instant death due to brainstem injury

So rupture of this ligament allows fatal displacement of the dens.

A. Upper band of cruciate ligament-Incorrect

The cruciate ligament complex has:

• Transverse ligament
• Superior longitudinal band
• Inferior longitudinal band

The upper band only connects dens to occiput and does not play the primary stabilizing role.

The transverse part is the key stabilizer.

B. Apical ligament of dens-Incorrect

The apical ligament:

• Connects tip of dens → basion of occipital bone
• Very thin and weak
• Often absent or rudimentary

D. Membrana tectoria- Incorrect

Membrana tectoria is:

• Continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament
• Covers the dens and cruciate ligament posteriorly

It provides secondary stability, but it does not hold the dens in position like the transverse ligament.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Earliest way to detect development of compartment syndrome in a patient with cast is:
options: Check radial pulse by displacing the cast
Weakness in movement of the limb
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decreased response to analgesia

• The earliest sign of compartment syndrome is severe pain out of proportion to injury, especially pain not relieved by analgesics and pain on passive stretch of muscles.
• Other signs (pallor, pulselessness, paralysis, paresthesia) are late findings indicating advanced ischemia.
• Thus, decreased response to analgesia is the earliest indicator of developing compartment syndrome.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Evaluate the following statements with respect to intertrochanteric fracture: a) More common in males than females. b) 1 year mortality rate is 20-30%. c) It is more commonly associated with nonunion than fracture neck of femur. d) 1 year mortality can be reduced by operating within 48 hours.
options: a, b, c, d are correct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. b and d are correct

INTERTROCHANTERIC FRACTURE FEMUR

• Intertrochanteric fractures are extracapsular fractures of the proximal femur that occur between the greater and lesser trochanter.
• This metaphyseal region has a more abundant blood supply, contributing to a higher union rate and less osteonecrosis compared to femoral neck fractures.

INTERTROCHANTERIC FRACTURE VS NECK OF FEMUR FRACTURE

| FEATURE | INTRACAPSULAR NECK FRACTURE | INTERTROCHANTERIC FRACTURE

| ------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------

| Patient profile | - | Patients are more likely to be older, in poorer health and have comorbid conditions (in comparison to neck femur).

| Age | Common after 50 years (but most common in 7th decade) | Common after 60 years (but most common in 8th decade)

| Sex | Both fractures are more common in elderly females but males are relatively more prone to develop fracture intertrochanteric femur

| Velocity of trauma | Trivial (usually) | Significant (as compared to neck femur)

| Pain | Mild | Severe

| Swelling and Ecchymosis | Nil | Severe

| Tenderness | In Scarpa’s triangle | Over greater trochanter

| External rotation deformity | <45 degrees | > 45 degrees (lateral border of foot touching couch)

| Shortening | <1 inch | >1 inch

| Broadening of greater trochanter | Absent | Present

| Straight leg raising and Ability
to walk | May be present in impacted fractures | Absent (Not possible)

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Following clubfoot surgery, which of the following is the commonest residual deformity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Forefoot adduction.

In clubfoot (CTEV) the deformity components are remembered by CAVE:

• C → Cavus
• A → Adduction (forefoot)
• V → Varus (hindfoot)
• E → Equinus

After clubfoot surgery (posteromedial release / Turco procedure) some deformities may persist or recur.

Most Common Residual Deformity

The most common residual deformity after clubfoot correction is:

➡ Forefoot adduction

Reason:

• Medial soft tissues remain tight
• Incomplete correction of midfoot adduction

❌B. Internal tibial torsion

• May be associated with clubfoot
• But not the most common residual deformity

❌C. Forefoot supination

• Can occur due to tibialis anterior overpull
• But still less common than adduction

❌D. Equinus

• Usually well corrected surgically by Achilles tendon lengthening

So persistent equinus is less common.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the classification used and grade of the shown injury in a child:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gartland’s classification Type III

• It is a lateral elbow X-ray of a child showing supracondylar fracture of the humerus

This fracture in children is classified using Gartland classification.

| Type of garland fracture | Description

| ------------------------ | -----------

| Type I | Undisplaced fracture

| Type II | Displaced but posterior cortex intact

| Type III | Completely displaced fracture

| Type IV | Multidirectional instability

• The distal fragment is completely displaced
• There is no cortical contact
• Classic posterior displacement

This fits Gartland Type III.

While the typical supracondylar fracture is not a Salter-Harris (SH) fracture, very young children (under age 2) can suffer a SH type II equivalent. Because their distal humeral chondro-epiphysis is mostly cartilage, it can be easily misdiagnosed.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the correct statements with respect to CTEV. 1. 50% cases are bilateral with male predominance 2. Forefoot is adducted and supinated 3. Ponsetti technique is preferred for correction 4. Adduction should be corrected first
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3

Congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV/clubfoot) is characterized by:

• Male predominance with \~50% bilateral cases
• Deformity components: forefoot adduction, hindfoot varus, equinus, and cavus (forefoot is adducted & supinated)
• Ponsetti method (serial casting ± Achilles tenotomy) is the treatment of choice

Correction sequence in Ponsetti:

• Cavus → Adduction → Varus → Equinus (CAVE)

So, cavus is corrected first, not adduction.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the type of Salter-Harris injury:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type 2

A Salter–Harris Type II fracture is the most common physeal injury. It involves:

• Fracture through the physis (growth plate)
• Extension into the metaphysis
• Characteristic Thurston–Holland metaphyseal fragment

Mnemonic: SALTER

• I – Straight (physis)
• II – Above (physis + metaphysis)
• III – Lower (physis + epiphysis)
• IV – Through (metaphysis, physis, epiphysis)
• V – Rammed (crush injury)

Thus, physeal fracture with metaphyseal involvement indicates Type II.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: In a patient with Colles fracture, rupture of which tendon is most commonly seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Extensor pollicis longus

Classic complication of Colles fracture:

Correct Answer

✅ Extensor pollicis longus (EPL)

Why EPL ruptures in Colles fracture?

A Colles fracture involves the distal radius with dorsal displacement.

The extensor pollicis longus tendon runs:

• Along the dorsal surface of the distal radius
• Through the 3rd dorsal compartment
• Around Lister’s tubercle

After a Colles fracture:

The fracture fragment or callus can rub against the tendon

Blood supply to the tendon may be compromised

This leads to delayed tendon rupture, usually weeks after injury (2-6 weeks post fracture)

Clinical clue

Patient suddenly cannot extend the thumb at the IP joint.

B. Extensor carpi ulnaris ❌

• Runs on the ulnar side of the wrist
• Not affected by distal radius fracture.

C. Abductor pollicis longus ❌

• Located in the 1st dorsal compartment
• Involved in De Quervain’s tenosynovitis, not Colles fracture rupture.

D. Extensor pollicis brevis ❌

Also in the 1st dorsal compartment

Less vulnerable compared to EPL.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Indications for surgery in a patient with Potts spine are all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Only clinico-radiological diagnosis of TB

Surgical intervention in Pott’s spine (spinal tuberculosis) is indicated for complications or diagnostic uncertainty. Indications for surgery:

• Neurological deficit (e.g., urinary incontinence, evolving cauda equina)
• Spinal instability or deformity
• Failure of medical therapy
• Need for tissue diagnosis or to confirm drug-resistant TB

Not an indication:

• Only clinico-radiological diagnosis without neurological deficit or instability. Thus, uncomplicated spinal TB is managed primarily with antitubercular therapy, not surgery.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Injury to which nerve can lead to the following appearance while making a fist?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Median nerve

Median nerve injury results in the “hand of benediction” when attempting to make a fist due to paralysis of the lateral forearm flexors (FDS, FDP to index/middle, FPL).

Features:

• Inability to flex thumb, index, and middle fingers
• Only ring and little fingers flex → characteristic appearance when making a fist
• Seen in proximal median nerve lesions (eg, supracondylar humerus fracture)

This differs from:

A. Ulnar nerve injury: clawing of ring & little finger at rest

B. Radial nerve injury: wrist drop (loss of extension)

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Match the following fracture descriptions with their most appropriate classification systems:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-B, 2-C, 3-D, 4-E, 5-F, 6-A

Educational objective:

Correct pairing of fracture types with their standard classification systems is essential:

• Open fractures → Gustilo-Anderson
• Physeal injuries → Salter-Harris
• Neck of femur → Garden
• Long bone fractures → AO/OTA
• Pelvic fractures → Young-Burgess
• Spine fractures → Denis classification

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Match the following osteochondritis disorders with their site.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-B, 2-A, 3-C, 4-D, 5-E

Osteochondritis disorders are osteochondroses involving avascular necrosis of epiphyses/apophyses in growing children, and are best remembered by site-specific associations:

• Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease → Head of femur (hip)
• Osgood–Schlatter disease → Tibial tuberosity (traction apophysitis)
• Köhler disease → Navicular bone (foot)
• Panner disease → Capitulum of humerus (elbow)
• Freiberg disease → Head of 2nd metatarsal

Patterns to recognize:

• Occur in children/adolescents due to repetitive stress + vascular insufficiency
• Present with pain, swelling, and activity limitation

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Most dangerous type of odontoid fracture as per Anderson and D' Alonzo classification and its respective management is:
options: Type I- immobilization in rigid collar
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type II-screw fixation

According to Anderson and D’Alonzo classification, Type II odontoid fracture (through the base of dens) is the most dangerous due to high risk of nonunion and instability from poor blood supply.

Anderson & D’Alonzo Classification

Type I

• Tip of dens
• Rare, usually stable
• Managed with rigid collar

Type II : MOST IMPORTANT

• Fracture at base of dens-Between dens and body of C2
• Poor blood supply
• Highest risk of:

o   Nonunion

o   Instability

o   Neurological injury

his is considered the most dangerous type

Type III

• Extends into body of C2
• Good healing potential
• Often treated conservatively (halo vest)

Management of Type II

Young patient:

• Anterior odontoid screw fixation

Elderly:

• Posterior C1–C2 fusion

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Patient had difficulty in walking upstairs. When he was made to bear weight on right lower limb, the left-sided pelvis dropped down but when he was standing on the left lower limb, the right-sided pelvis moved up. Which of the following is the likely lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right superior gluteal nerve palsy

•

The superior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus medius and minimus, which stabilize the pelvis during single-leg stance.

•

In Trendelenburg sign, when standing on the affected limb, the pelvis drops on the opposite side due to weak hip abductors.

•

Here, standing on the right leg causes left pelvis drop, indicating weakness of right gluteus medius/minimus → right superior gluteal nerve palsy.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The biopsy of the following lesion will yield which of the following?
options: Lobules of atypical cartilage cells with high cellularity
Pleomorphic cells producing primitive woven bone and osteoid
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Primitive small, round blue cells

•

Ewing sarcoma typically presents in children/adolescents with a diaphyseal bone lesion and onion-skin periosteal reaction on X-ray. Biopsy shows primitive small round blue cells (high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio), often associated with t(11;22) EWS-FLI1 translocation.

•

It is a malignant small round cell tumor of bone requiring multimodal therapy (chemotherapy + surgery ± radiotherapy).

Why not other options:

A. Lobules of atypical cartilage cells: Seen in chondrosarcoma → malignant cartilage tumor in older adults, not small round blue cell tumor of children.

B. Pleomorphic cells producing woven bone & osteoid: Seen in osteosarcoma → malignant osteoid production with pleomorphic cells and sunburst/Codman triangle.

D. Mononuclear tumor cells & giant cells: Seen in giant cell tumor (osteoclastoma) → epiphyseal lesion in young adults, not diaphyseal pediatric tumor.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The following condition develops due to which vessel?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Medial circumflex femoral artery

The MRI demonstrates avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head, characterized by:

• Hip pain aggravated by weight-bearing
• Subchondral collapse (crescent sign in later stages)
• Patchy/serpiginous marrow signal abnormalities on MRI
• MRI is the most sensitive investigation for early AVN

The principal blood supply to the adult femoral head is from the: ✅ Medial circumflex femoral artery (MCFA)

Its retinacular (ascending cervical) branches run along the femoral neck beneath the capsule and supply most of the femoral head. Interruption of these vessels leads to osteonecrosis.

High-yield Blood Supply of the Femoral Head

| Vessel | Contribution

| ------ | ------------

| Medial circumflex femoral artery | Major blood supply to the adult femoral head ✅

| Lateral circumflex femoral artery | Minor contribution

| Artery of ligamentum teres (from obturator artery) | Important in children; minimal in adults

Common Causes of Avascular Necrosis

• Trauma (femoral neck fracture, hip dislocation)
• Corticosteroid therapy
• Alcohol abuse
• Sickle cell disease
• Systemic lupus erythematosus
• Decompression sickness
• Gaucher disease

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The following finding is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acromegaly

Acromegaly causes characteristic hand X-ray changes due to excess growth hormone and IGF-1 leading to periosteal bone growth and soft-tissue thickening.

Radiographic features:

• Spade-like enlargement of distal phalanges
• Tufting and widening of terminal phalanges
• Increased soft tissue thickness
• Joint space widening

These findings help differentiate acromegaly from:

A. Hyperparathyroidism → subperiosteal bone resorption

C. Psoriatic arthritis → pencil-in-cup deformity

D. Rheumatoid arthritis → marginal erosions and joint space narrowing

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The following pelvic X-ray was seen in a patient. All the following signs will be present except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gaenslen sign

The X-ray shows:

• DDH of hip with shallow acetabulum and displaced femoral head.
• DDH presents with:

o   Ortolani sign: palpable “clunk” on reduction of dislocated hip

o   Barlow sign: hip can be dislocated with adduction and posterior pressure

o   Narath sign: increased distance between greater trochanter and pubic symphysis (proximal migration of femur)

Gaenslen sign is not associated with DDH; it is used to detect sacroiliac joint pathology (eg, sacroiliitis).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The index shown in the image below is useful for planning management of which condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Scoliosis

• The image depicts: Risser sign, which assesses ossification of the iliac apophysis (grades I–V)
• Used to determine skeletal maturity.

The Risser index helps:

• Predict remaining spinal growth
• Risk of curve progression in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.

📌 Why It Matters in Scoliosis

Management decisions depend on curve severity + skeletal maturity.

Example:

• Small curve + low Risser stage → High risk of progression → brace
• Large curve + low Risser stage → surgery may be required
• High Risser stage → Curve progression less likely

Thus, it guides decisions regarding observation, bracing, or surgery in scoliosis.

❌ B. DDH

Evaluated using Acetabular Index and Hilgenreiner line, not Risser.

❌ C. Ankylosing spondylitis

Assessed using sacroiliac joint changes and spinal imaging.

❌ D. AVN

Evaluated using Ficat and Arlet staging on MRI.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the correct classification for the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Schatzker classification grade 4

The image shows corresponds to a Schatzker type IV pattern.

Schatzker Type IV: fracture of the medial tibial plateau, often associated with high-energy trauma and knee instability;

• May cause ligament/vascular injury.
• Type IV injuries require urgent evaluation for neurovascular damage and usually surgical fixation.

• Type I–III → lateral plateau
• Type IV → medial plateau (worst prognosis among unicondylar)
• Type V → bicondylar
• Type VI → metaphyseal-diaphyseal dissociation

❌A. Neer classification: Used for proximal humerus fractures.

❌B. Ideberg classification: Used for glenoid (scapular) fracture.

❌C. Sanders classification: Used for calcaneal fractures based on CT findings.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the likely defect in the following condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Enchondral ossification

🧠 The X-ray shows features typical of Achondroplasia:

Key findings:

• Rhizomelic limb shortening (proximal limb segments shortened)
• Short femur
• Relatively normal trunk
• Widened metaphysis
• Bowed legs

These are classic radiologic features of Achondroplasia, the most common cause of disproportionate dwarfism.

⭐ Genetic Mutation in Achondroplasia

• Achondroplasia is caused by mutation in the FGFR3 gene.
• Achondroplasia is the most common cause of disproportionate short stature

FGFR3 = Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor 3

Mutation causes:

• Inhibition of chondrocyte proliferation
• Impaired endochondral ossification
• Result → short long bones

📌 Important exam point

It is a gain-of-function mutation.

A. Fibrillin-2

Associated with Congenital contractural arachnodactyly (Beals syndrome).

Features:

• Long limbs
• Arachnodactyly

👉 Opposite of short-limb dwarfism.

B. FGFR2

Associated with craniosynostosis syndromes, such as:

• Apert syndrome
• Crouzon syndrome

Not dwarfism.

D. Iduronate Sulfatase

Deficiency causes Hunter syndrome (MPS II).

Features:

• Coarse facies
• Organomegaly
• Developmental delay

Not achondroplasia.

🧠 Quick revision

| Disease | Gene Mutation

| ------- | -------------

| Achondroplasia | FGFR3

| Marfan syndrome | Fibrillin-1

| Apert / Crouzon | FGFR2

| Hunter syndrome | Iduronate sulfatase

• Rhizomelic limb shortening (proximal limbs)
• Normal trunk length
• Large head with frontal bossing
• Narrow interpedicular distance in lumbar spine
• Trident hand appearance

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis based on the given X-ray?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fibrous dysplasia

The “Rind sign” on X-ray refers to a thick sclerotic margin surrounding a radiolucent lesion,

• Classically seen in fibrous dysplasia, especially in the proximal femur.

Fibrous dysplasia shows:

• Ground-glass appearance
• Endosteal scalloping
• Sclerotic rim (rind sign)
• Possible shepherd’s crook deformity in femur

Thus, a well-defined lesion with a sclerotic rind suggests fibrous dysplasia.

Pathophysiology:

• Replacement of normal bone with fibrous tissue + immature woven bone
• The body tries to stabilize the weak bone
• So it lays down reactive sclerosis at the periphery

That reactive sclerosis forms the thick white border = rind sign.

So it’s basically:

• Weak abnormal bone inside
• Strong defensive bone outside

❌ A. ABC (Aneurysmal Bone Cyst)

• Expansile/pulsatile
• Soap-bubble appearance
• Fluid–fluid levels on MRI
• No thick sclerotic rim

❌ B. SBC (Simple Bone Cyst)

• Central lucent lesion
• Thin cortex
• Fallen fragment sign possible
• No thick rind

❌ D. Enchondroma

• Cartilage tumor
• Stippled calcifications
• More common in small bones of hands

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis based on the images shown?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mafucci disease

Maffucci syndrome is characterized by multiple enchondromas (cartilage tumors within bone) associated with soft-tissue hemangiomas.

• Multiple enchondromas → bone deformities, fractures, limb shortening
• Soft-tissue vascular lesions (hemangiomas) → calcified phleboliths on X-ray
• Asymmetric involvement of extremities
• Increased risk of malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma and other malignancies

Differentiation:

• Ollier disease: multiple enchondromas without hemangiomas
• Maffucci syndrome: enchondromas + hemangiomas (hallmark)

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis of the image shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Coxa vara

Coxa vara is defined as a decreased femoral neck–shaft angle (<120°).

Leads to:

• Shortened limb, Limp
• Increased stress on femoral neck
• Reduced hip abduction

On X-ray, the femoral neck appears more horizontal with reduced neck–shaft angle.

Thus, decreased neck–shaft angle indicates coxa vara.

Normal neck–shaft angle- 125°–135°

If angle:

•

< 120° → Coxa vara

•

> 135° → Coxa valga

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the most appropriate treatment for the following fracture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Internal fixation using compression plate

Galeazzi fracture: X-ray findings:

• Fracture of the distal 1/3rd shaft of radius
• Dislocation/subluxation of ulnar head at wrist (DRUJ disruption)
• Look at the wrist → abnormal distal radius–ulna relationship

Mechanism: Fall on outstretched hand with forearm pronation

Management of Galeazzi fracture

Treatment of choice = ORIF

Steps:

1. Open reduction and internal fixation of radius

• Compression plate fixation (DCP/LCP)

2.

After radius fixation → assess DRUJ stability

3.

Stable DRUJ → immobilize in above-elbow cast in supination

4. Unstable DRUJ →

• Repair TFCC/DRUJ stabilizers if needed
• Temporary K-wire fixation of DRUJ

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the most common area affected, in the given image, in case of tuberculosis of hip?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2

In tuberculosis of the hip, the most common initial site of involvement is the superolateral part of the acetabulum (weight-bearing area).

TB reaches the hip via hematogenous spread and typically involves:

• Acetabular roof (most common)
• Then femoral head/neck
• Leads to gradual joint destruction and deformity

Early involvement of the weight-bearing acetabular region results in pain, limp, and progressive joint space narrowing in hip tuberculosis.

Identification (labeled parts):

1. Greater trochanter
2. Superolateral acetabulum (weight-bearing dome) → most common site in hip TB
3. Femoral head
4. Lesser trochanter / femoral neck region

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the sequence of performing a Thomas test? I. Passive flexion of affected hip II. Active flexion of normal hip III. Measure the flexion angle IV. Checking for lumbar lordosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. IV, II, I, III

What is Thomas Test actually checking?

• It checks for hip flexion contracture (tight iliopsoas).
• If the hip cannot fully extend, it means there’s a fixed flexion deformity.

Why is the sequence important?

First check for lumbar lordosis (IV)

• Because the pelvis naturally has lumbar lordosis.
• If you don’t first flatten the lumbar spine, you’ll get a false reading. So the test is done in a very specific order.

Active flexion of the normal hip (II)

• Patient flexes the normal hip toward the chest.
• This flattens lumbar lordosis.
• Pelvis is stabilized.

Passive flexion of the affected hip (I)

• Now the affected hip is assessed.
• If it cannot lie flat on the table → flexion contracture present.

Measure the flexion angle (III)

• If the thigh remains elevated,
• Measure the angle between thigh and table.
• That angle = degree of deformity.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What other finding would be expected in this 25-year-old male with abnormal pelvis MRI?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute painful red eye

MRI pelvis showing bilateral sacroiliitis in a young male suggests ankylosing spondylitis (seronegative spondyloarthropathy).

Common extra-articular manifestations include:

• Acute anterior uveitis → presents as painful red eye with photophobia
• Enthesitis
• Aortic regurgitation

Thus, a patient with ankylosing spondylitis is likely to have episodes of acute painful red eye due to anterior uveitis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following findings is least likely to be seen in a patient with a radial nerve injury at the elbow?
options: Loss of extension of the metacarpophalangeal joints of the hand
Weakness of thumb extension and retroposition
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Loss of wrist extension

This question describes a lesion of the radial nerve at the elbow, typically involving the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN).

The extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL) receives its motor supply proximal to the division of the radial nerve, so it remains functional.

As a result:

• Wrist extension is preserved, although it is weak.
• Since extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU) is weakened, wrist extension occurs mainly through ECRL, producing radial deviation.

Therefore, complete loss of wrist extension is unlikely.

Why the other options are correct?

A. Loss of extension of the metacarpophalangeal joints ✔️

• The posterior interosseous nerve supplies the finger extensors.
• Patients cannot actively extend the MCP joints.

B. Weakness of thumb extension and retroposition ✔️

• Extensor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, and abductor pollicis longus are supplied by the PIN.
• Thumb extension and retroposition are impaired.

D. Radial deviation of the wrist ✔️

• ECRL remains intact.
• ECU is paralyzed.
• Wrist extends with radial deviation, a classic feature of PIN palsy.

questions.text: Which of the following is not true about intracapsular fracture of femur neck?
options: Displacement is less common than extracapsular fractures
Contour of greater trochanter is normal
Tenderness is mainly present over the anterior joint line

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which part of 2nd metatarsal is involved in the march fracture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neck

March Fracture

• March fracture = stress fracture of metatarsal bones
• Occurs due to repetitive stress
•

Common in:

o   Soldiers marching long distances

o   Marathon runners

o   Athletes

•

Most commonly affects the 2nd metatarsal

Typical Site

• Neck of the 2nd metatarsal ✅
• This region experiences maximum bending stress during walking or marching
• Repetitive loading → fatigue fracture

A. Head ❌

• Located at metatarsophalangeal joint
• Experiences mainly compressive forces
• Not a common site for stress fractures

C. Shaft ❌

• Stress fractures can occur, but
• Classical march fracture site is the neck, not the shaft
• Shaft fractures are less typical for march fractures

D. Base ❌

• Located near tarsometatarsal joints
•

Commonly involved in:

o   Lisfranc injuries

o   Traumatic fractures

•

Not typical for march fractures

• March fracture → Neck of 2nd metatarsal
• Jones fracture → Base of 5th metatarsal
• Lisfranc injury → Tarsometatarsal joint

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A child with a history of recurrent respiratory infections presented with complaints of pain around the knee and a high fever. X-ray shows lytic and sclerotic bone. His peripheral blood smear is shown in the image below. Aspirate from the joint will most likely show:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Salmonella

Sickle-shaped RBCs:

• Reduce immunity → predispose to infection

Infection develops

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: According to WHO guidelines, which investigation is specifically recommended for confirming the diagnosis of TB spine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CBNAAT

Cartridge Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test

• Detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA
• Identifies Rifampicin resistance

Back pain + constitutional symptoms

Suspect TB spine

↓

MRI → Best imaging (extent, abscess)

↓

Obtain sample (biopsy/aspirate)

Start ATT

Pathophysiology

• Hematogenous spread from lungs
• Affects vertebral bodies (anterior part)
• Leads to:

• Vertebral collapse
• Kyphosis (gibbus deformity)
• Paravertebral abscess

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An adolescent presents with mild localized pain over the lower limb. X-ray shows a well-defined lytic lesion with sclerotic margins located in the metaphysis of the tibia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Brodie's abscess

Brodie's abscess presents as a well-defined metaphyseal lytic lesion with thick sclerotic margins in adolescents, representing subacute osteomyelitis typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

Key Features:

• Oval/round lytic lesion
• Thick sclerotic border
• Located in metaphysis (especially tibia)
• Minimal periosteal reaction

| Option | Verdict | Why

| ------ | ------- | ---

| A. Simple bone cyst | ❌ | Central, metaphyseal but no sclerotic rim, fluid-filled

| B. Aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) | ❌ | Expansile, “blow-out” lesion, septations, no thick sclerosis

| C. Chondroblastoma | ❌ | Epiphyseal lesion, not metaphyseal

| D. Brodie’s abscess | ✅ | Metaphyseal + lytic + sclerotic rim + mild symptoms

| Feature | Brodie’s Abscess | Simple Bone Cyst | ABC | Chondroblastoma

| ------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | --- | ---------------

| Age | Adolescents | Children | <20 yrs | Adolescents

| Site | Metaphysis | Metaphysis | Metaphysis | Epiphysis

| Margin | Sclerotic rim | Thin | None | Variable

| Nature | Infection | Fluid cyst | Blood-filled | Tumor

| Symptoms | Mild pain | Often asymptomatic | Pain/swelling | Joint pain

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the likely diagnosis based on the given CT scan?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chronic osteomyelitis

Chronic osteomyelitis is characterized by periosteal thickening, sclerosis, and central lucency within the bone, which are key diagnostic features visible on imaging.

Hallmark Triad (MUST KNOW):

• Sequestrum → dead bone fragment (dense)
• Involucrum → new bone formation around it
• Cloaca → opening for pus drainage

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy presents with a two-month history of pain and swelling in his lower leg. Radiography demonstrates an onion-skin periosteal reaction, and biopsy shows PAS-positive small round blue cells. Which of the following chromosomal translocations is most commonly associated with this tumor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. t(11;22)

Ewing sarcoma is a highly malignant small round blue cell tumor that typically affects children and adolescents. It commonly arises in the diaphysis of long bones and is characterized by an “onion-skin” periosteal reaction on X-ray. Histologically, the tumor consists of PAS-positive small round blue cells due to abundant intracellular glycogen. The hallmark genetic abnormality is the t(11;22)(q24;q12) translocation, which produces the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion gene, an abnormal transcription factor that drives tumorigenesis.

Why not the other options?

• A. t(8;14): Seen in Burkitt lymphoma, involving c-MYC activation.
• B. t(15;17): Seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), producing the PML-RARA fusion gene.
• D. t(9;22): The Philadelphia chromosome, seen in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and some cases of ALL, producing the BCR-ABL fusion gene.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy presents with pain and swelling over the right humerus for 2 months. He also has a fever and raised ESR. Blood tests show leucocytosis with neutrophilia. An X-ray of the humerus is shown below. Which of the following is the next?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MRI of the affected limb

Here, the main differential diagnoses are Ewing sarcoma and chronic osteomyelitis, both of which can present with pain, fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and destructive bone lesions with periosteal reaction on X-ray.

MRI is usually performed first because it:

• Defines the local extent of the lesion
• Assesses bone marrow involvement
• Detects soft tissue extension
• Helps identify abscess formation, sequestrum, sinus tracts, favoring osteomyelitis
• Evaluates relation to neurovascular structures
• Helps plan the optimal biopsy site

MRI is highly sensitive for both infection and malignant bone tumors, although findings may overlap.

Important Clinical Principle: “MRI first, biopsy later”

In suspected primary bone tumors, the standard approach is:

1. Initial X-ray
2. MRI of the entire involved bone
3. Tissue diagnosis (biopsy)

This sequence is important because an improperly planned biopsy can:

• contaminate tissue planes,
• complicate limb-salvage surgery,
• and interfere with definitive oncologic management.

Why biopsy is still essential

Despite MRI findings, definitive differentiation between Ewing sarcoma and chronic osteomyelitis often remains difficult radiologically, because both can show:

• marrow edema,
• cortical destruction,
• periosteal reaction,
• soft tissue mass,
• contrast enhancement.

Therefore, histopathological confirmation is ultimately required.

Why the approach remains controversial

The controversy arises because:

• MRI findings can strongly suggest one diagnosis but are not always definitive.
• Some clinicians advocate early biopsy when imaging is equivocal.
• Others emphasize MRI before biopsy to avoid poor biopsy tract placement and to better characterize lesion extent.

In modern orthopedic oncology practice, the accepted approach is generally:

MRI for characterization and surgical planning, followed by image-guided biopsy for confirmation.

Other options

• Bone marrow biopsy → used mainly in hematologic malignancies (e.g., leukemia, lymphoma), not primary evaluation of focal bone lesions.
• PET scan → useful for staging/metastatic evaluation after diagnosis, not the initial next step.
• CT-guided biopsy → diagnostic/confirmatory procedure, usually performed after MRI planning.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 19-year-old man presents with persistent night pain localized to the distal femur. An X-ray of the femur is provided. What is the most likely radiologic diagnosis suggested by this finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Codman's triangle

Codman’s triangle is a type of aggressive periosteal reaction produced when a rapidly growing bone lesion lifts the periosteum away from the cortex, forming a triangular area of new subperiosteal bone. It is classically associated with osteosarcoma, especially in adolescents involving the metaphysis of long bones (most commonly around the knee).

Why not the other options?

• A. Sun-ray appearance: Another periosteal reaction seen in osteosarcoma, characterized by spiculated bone radiating perpendicular to the cortex.
• C. Onion peel appearance: Lamellated periosteal reaction classically seen in Ewing sarcoma.
• D. Osteochondroma: A benign exostosis showing cortical and medullary continuity with the parent bone, not an aggressive periosteal reaction.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman reports mild, dull aching pain in her left hand after accidentally striking a finger against a door frame. Examination shows minimal tenderness with preserved range of motion. An X-ray of the hand is provided. Based on the history, examination and imaging, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Enchondroma

Enchondroma is a benign intramedullary cartilaginous tumor that most commonly arises in the small bones of the hands and feet. It is often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally or after a pathological fracture following trivial trauma. X-ray typically shows a well-defined, expansile lytic lesion with chondroid (“rings and arcs”) calcification.

Why not the other options?

• A. Giant Cell Tumor (GCT): Typically occurs in the epiphysis of long bones in skeletally mature adults, not the phalanges.
• C. Brown Tumor: Seen in hyperparathyroidism and is associated with other features such as subperiosteal bone resorption and elevated PTH.
• D. Aneurysmal Bone Cyst (ABC): An expansile, blood-filled metaphyseal lesion affecting younger patients; MRI shows characteristic fluid-fluid levels.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 9-year-old child presents with pain and swelling over the mid-shaft of the tibia, along with low-grade fever and an elevated ESR. An X-ray of the tibia is shown below. Based on the clinical features and radiographic findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ewing Sarcoma

Ewing sarcoma is a highly malignant small round blue cell tumor that commonly affects children and adolescents (5–20 years). It typically arises in the diaphysis of long bones and presents with pain, swelling, fever, elevated ESR, and leukocytosis, often mimicking osteomyelitis. The characteristic X-ray finding is an “onion-skin” (lamellated) periosteal reaction.

Why not the other options?

• A. Osteosarcoma: Usually arises in the metaphysis around the knee and shows sunburst appearance and Codman’s triangle.
• C. Non-ossifying fibroma: A benign, asymptomatic metaphyseal fibrous lesion discovered incidentally.
• D. Osteoid osteoma: Causes night pain relieved by NSAIDs and shows a small radiolucent nidus with surrounding sclerosis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presented with multiple swelling in hand & wrist. Finger X-ray is given. Identify:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Multiple enchondromatosis

Enchondromas are benign medullary cartilage tumors, common in hand bones.

• Presence of multiple enchondromas
• Benign cartilage tumors inside bone

| Location | Medullary cavity

| Bone shape | Expansion, deformity

Important Clinical Points

• Painless swelling
• Bone deformity
• Risk of pathological fracture
• Risk of malignant transformation → chondrosarcoma

enchondromas = Ollier’s disease; with hemangiomas = Maffucci syndrome. Brown tumors occur in hyperparathyroidism, osteophytes in osteoarthritis.

| Feature | Enchondromatosis | Brown Tumor | Osteophytes

questions.text: Following is the x-ray of an 18-year-old boy who complains of fever, pain in the lower limb, local rise of temperature, and tenderness in the area shown. On investigation, he has increased ESR. What can be the likely diagnosis?

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which bone tumor is classically associated with the formation of a Codman's triangle and a sunburst appearance on radiographic imaging?

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which thyroid malignancy is most likely associated with the skull finding shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Follicular carcinoma

Follicular carcinoma spreads hematogenously, commonly to bone, producing lytic skull lesions.

Radiologic Signature:

• Lytic, expansile lesion in calvarium
• Often hypervascular
• Can produce a “blow-out” / ballooned appearance
•

•

• Expansile
• Highly vascular

questions.text: Which type of translocation is seen in diaphyseal tumor with small blue round cells?

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| Age | Children/teens

| Location | Diaphysis of long bones

| X-ray | Onion-skin periosteal reaction

| Histology | Small round blue cells

| Symptoms | Pain + swelling + fever

A diaphyseal tumor composed of small round blue cells strongly suggests Ewing sarcoma, which is defined by the t(11;22)(q24;q12) translocation creating the EWSR1–FLI1 fusion gene. This fusion drives oncogenesis and is the key molecular hallmark used for confirmation.

| Translocation | Disease

| ------------- | -------

| t(11;22) | Ewing sarcoma ✅

| t(15;17) | APL

| t(2;13) | Rhabdomyosarcoma

| t(9;22) | CML

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: 3-point bony relationship is maintained in which fracture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Supracondylar humerus fracture

The elbow has a beautiful geometric signature:

Three bony points in elbow:

• Olecranon
• Medial epicondyle
• Lateral epicondyle

Positions:

• Extension → straight line
• Flexion (90°) → triangle

Fracture vs Dislocation

• Fracture is above the condyles
• Joint alignment remains intact
• So the triangle is preserved

| Feature | Supracondylar Fracture | Elbow Dislocation

| ------- | ---------------------- | -----------------

| 3-point relation | Maintained | Lost

| Site | Above condyles | Joint

| Common in | Children | Adults

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man falls from a height and lands on his feet. He develops pain along the medial side of the knee, difficulty walking, and pain that worsens during knee flexion. Which of the following structures is most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Medial meniscus

The medial meniscus is the most commonly injured meniscus because it is firmly attached to the medial collateral ligament (MCL) and the joint capsule, making it less mobile than the lateral meniscus. Meniscal injuries typically occur following twisting or rotational forces on a flexed, weight-bearing knee and present with medial joint line pain, pain during knee flexion, locking, clicking, and difficulty walking.

Why not the other options?

• B. Lateral meniscus: More mobile and therefore less commonly injured; pain is localized to the lateral joint line.
• C. Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL): Presents with a non-contact twisting injury, audible “pop,” immediate hemarthrosis, and anterior knee instability (positive Lachman test).
• D. Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL): Usually injured by a dashboard injury or fall on a flexed knee, causing posterior tibial sag and a positive posterior drawer test.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 38-year-old man falls directly onto the front of his knee while descending stairs. He presents with acute knee pain and swelling and is unable to perform an active straight-leg raise or actively extend the knee. Which of the following injuries is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Patellar tendon rupture

A patellar tendon rupture disrupts the extensor mechanism of the knee, preventing force transmission from the quadriceps muscle to the tibia. As a result, the patient is unable to actively extend the knee or perform a straight-leg raise, which is the key clinical finding.

Patients typically present with:

• Sudden pain after a fall or forceful quadriceps contraction
• Inability to actively extend the knee
• Inability to perform a straight-leg raise
• Patella alta (high-riding patella) on lateral knee X-ray due to loss of distal patellar attachment
• Palpable defect below the patella

Why not the other options?

• A. Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear: Presents with a twisting injury, immediate hemarthrosis, instability ("giving way"), and a positive Lachman or anterior drawer test. Active knee extension is preserved.
• C. Meniscal tear: Causes joint-line tenderness, locking, clicking, and pain with twisting movements, but patients can usually extend the knee unless mechanical locking occurs.
• D. Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tear: Commonly results from a dashboard injury or fall onto a flexed knee, causing posterior knee instability and a positive posterior drawer test. The extensor mechanism remains intact.

High-yield pearl

• Loss of active knee extension = Injury to the extensor mechanism.
• Think of:

• Quadriceps tendon rupture → Usually older patients (>40 years); patella baja (low-riding patella).
• Patellar tendon rupture → Usually younger patients (<40 years); patella alta (high-riding patella).

Exam tip:

• A patient who cannot perform a straight-leg raise almost always has a disruption of the quadriceps tendon, patella, or patellar tendon rather than an isolated ligament or meniscal injury.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A football player had a twisting injury of the knee with no clinical bony injury. Which test is being performed here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lachman’s test

Key clue in question:

• Football player
• Twisting injury
• No bony injury :  Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) injury

And the best test for ACL: Lachman’s test

Knee flexed \~20–30°

↓

Stabilize femur

↓

Pull tibia anteriorly

↓

Excess movement → ACL tear

| Test | Structure Tested | Position | Key Feature

| ---- | ---------------- | -------- | -----------

| Lachman | ACL | 20–30° flexion | Most sensitive

| Anterior drawer | ACL | 90° flexion | Less reliable

| Posterior drawer | PCL | 90° flexion | Posterior shift

| McMurray | Meniscus | Flexion + rotation | Click

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with ankle pain. MRI demonstrates an Achilles tendon rupture. Based on the MRI findings, which of the following is the most appropriate statement?
options: Plastering and immobilization is the treatment of choice
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thompson test is positive

Achilles tendon rupture typically presents with sudden posterior ankle pain, often accompanied by a sensation of a “pop,” difficulty walking, and inability to perform plantar flexion. The diagnosis is primarily clinical, with a positive Thompson (Simmonds–Thompson) test, and can be confirmed by ultrasound or MRI.

• When the calf muscle is squeezed, the foot fails to plantarflex, indicating a disrupted Achilles tendon.

Why not the other options?

• A. Goutallier classification is used: Incorrect. Goutallier classification grades fatty degeneration of rotator cuff muscles, not Achilles tendon injuries.
• C. Plastering and immobilization is the treatment of choice: Not universally true. Management depends on patient age, activity level, and type of rupture. Many active patients benefit from surgical repair, while selected patients may be managed non-operatively with functional bracing.
• D. Steroid injection is indicated: Incorrect. Corticosteroid injections into or around the Achilles tendon are contraindicated because they increase the risk of tendon rupture.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Finkelstein’s sign/test is done to diagnose which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. de Quervain’s tenosynovitis

Finkelstein’s test is used to diagnose de Quervain’s tenosynovitis, which involves inflammation of the first dorsal compartment tendons:

• Abductor pollicis longus (APL)
• Extensor pollicis brevis (EPB)

A positive test produces pain over the radial styloid when the thumb is flexed into the palm and the wrist is deviated ulnarly.

Why not other options?

• A. Adhesive capsulitis: Diagnosed by restriction of both active and passive shoulder movements.
• B. Golfer’s elbow: Medial epicondylitis; pain with resisted wrist flexion/pronation.
• C. Trochanteric bursitis: Causes lateral hip pain and tenderness over the greater trochanter.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The test shown below is performed to assess the integrity or function of which anatomical structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anterior cruciate ligament

Sudden deceleration / pivot injury

↓

Twisting of knee

↓

ACL tear

↓

Anterior instability of tibia

The anterior draw test, performed with the knee at 90 degrees flexion, specifically tests the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) by assessing anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur. The Lachman test at 20 degrees flexion is more sensitive for ACL injuries.

Function of ACL

• Prevents anterior displacement of tibia
• Prevents hyperextension
• Provides rotational stability

| Ligament | Test | Movement Checked

| -------- | ---- | ----------------

| ACL | Anterior drawer, Lachman | Anterior tibia

| PCL | Posterior drawer | Posterior tibia

| MCL | Valgus stress | Medial opening

| LCL | Varus stress | Lateral opening

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which muscle on the other supporting side is problematic when standing on one leg?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gluteus Medius

When a person stands on one leg: The opposite side of the pelvis tends to drop due to gravity

To prevent that: The gluteus medius of the stance leg contracts

Trendelenburg Mechanism

• Standing on right leg
• Right gluteus medius contracts
• Keeps pelvis level on left side

If weak: Pelvis drops on opposite side → Trendelenburg sign

Clinical Importance

Weak gluteus medius →

• Trendelenburg sign (positive)
• Waddling gait

Causes:

• Superior gluteal nerve injury
• Hip joint pathology
• Muscle weakness

| Muscle | Function | Clinical Role

| ------ | -------- | -------------

| Gluteus medius | Abduction | Pelvic stabilization (Trendelenburg)

| Gluteus maximus | Extension | Rising, climbing

| Iliacus | Flexion | Hip flexion

| Quadratus lumborum | Pelvic tilt | Accessory stabilization

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old female developed a tumor at the knee joint. Biopsy-image is given below and shows multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells.What is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Giant cell tumour

The biopsy image shows characteristic multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells, with nuclei having a similar appearance to the surrounding mononuclear cells, suggestive of giant cell tumour.

Giant cell tumours are benign but locally aggressive tumours of bone and consist of a proliferation of mononuclear cells with scattered macrophages. They are most commonly seen between 20-45 years of age. GCTs can occasionally be associated with Paget’s disease of bone and focal dermal hypoplasia (Goltz syndrome).

They typically affect the metaphyses of long bones, more commonly the distal femur, proximal tibia, distal radius and proximal humerus. Patients present with pain and a mass.

A GCT is typically seen on X-ray as an eccentric, lobulated, lytic lesion with non-sclerotic borders, giving a soap bubble appearance. They usually have little or no matrix calcification, new bone formation or periosteal reaction. Tumours that extend into the soft tissues are seen as soft-tissue masses which may be covered by a thin layer of sclerosis. They are usually within the metaphysis but may involve the physis and subchondral plate. If malignant, the tumour appears as a lytic lesion with a sclerosing destructive tumour adjacent to it.
