questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 35-year-old pregnant woman woman develops back pain radiating to the posterolateral aspect of the leg after lifting a heavy suitcase from the ground. There is sensory loss over the anterolateral aspect of the leg, dorsum of the foot, and great toe. Medial Hamstring reflex is diminished. Other deep tendon reflexes are normal.MRI picture is shown below. The most probable diagnosis is ____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. L4-L5 disc prolapse

The MRI which shows a disc extrusion at the L4-L5 level, along with the clinical scenario is diagnostic of L4-L5 disc prolapse.

Neurological features:

* Weakness of extensor hallucis longus and dorsiflexors of the foot.

* Sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the lower thigh, anterolateral aspect of knee and leg, dorsum of the foot, and the great toe and one or more adjacent toes (i.e., 1st web space) but never the little toe.

* Knee jerk and ankle jerk are normal.

Treatment:

* Continuous bed rest and traction for 2 weeks will reduce the herniation in over 90% of cases.

* Operative removal of the disc by unilateral laminectomy is indicated in

* Cauda equina compression syndrome that does not clear up within 6 hours of starting bed rest and traction

* Neurological deterioration under conservative treatment

* Persistent pain and signs of sciatic tension after 3 weeks

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A child is unable to carry supination and pronation movements but is able to flex his elbow, since his childhood. His xray was taken and is as shown below.What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Proximal radioulnar synostosis

The clinical vignette along with the x-ray gives the diagnosis of proximal radioulnar synostosis.

Radioulnar synostosis

* a rare condition where there is an abnormal connection between the radius and ulna bones of the forearm.

* can be congenital, when it is a result of a failure of the bones to form separately, or following an injury (post-traumatic).

* causes loss of rotation, but the elbow flexion is retained.

* rotational osteotomy can give a more suitable angle of pronation–supination but rarely succeeds.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A mother with history of breech during her pregnancy brings her newborn baby to the OPD. On examination, the doctor notices asymmetric thigh folds in her child, with limited abduction of thigh and gets a click sound on doing so. A brace as shown in the picture is prescribed by the doctor. What can be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Congenital dysplasia of hip (DDH)

Pavlik harness is the immediate management in this newborn, with history and examination suggestive of congenital dysplasia of hip (DDH).

In a child of age less than 6 months with DDH, closed reduction with Pavlik harness or Von rosen spllint is done.

Pearl PF1193: Age wise management of DDH

AGE OF THE PATIENT
MANAGEMENT

Less than 6 months
Closed reduction with Pavlik harness or von Rosen splint

6-18 months
Closed or open reduction followed by hip spica after reduction

18-36 months
Open reduction with femoral osteotomy and pelvic osteotomy (Salter's osteotomy, Pemberton osteotomy, Steel osteotomy)

3-8 year
Open reduction with femoral shortening and pelvic osteotomy

8-18 year

Open procedure with femoral shortening with pelvic osteotomy or total hip replacement

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient who had a history of fracture of his right leg came for a follow-up appointment where his cast was removed for assessment. The doctor found that the area was deformable but not displaceable and thus he re-applied the cast. What stage of fracture healing is the patient likely to be in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Soft callus

In this case, the inflammation stage is over however the area has not completely healed as the fracture was deformable, thus the most likely stage is the soft callus stage.

Endochondral ossification occurs in the later stages (not in the early stages).

Stage of induction: Osteogenic potential cells are activated via BMP (bone morphogenic protein), hypoxia, and bioelectric effects.

Stage of inflammation: There is hemorrhage, cellular proliferation, and vascular ingrowths.

Stage of soft callus: The hematoma is organized with fibrous tissue, cartilage, and woven bone.

Stage of hard callus: If immobilization is complete, the bone heals by membranous ossification. If not, it heals by endochondral ossification.

Stage of remodeling: the lamellar bone will be deposited, but there will be no remodeling of rotational malalignment.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young girl had thigh swelling with discharging sinus from which a bony fragment came out. The parents were concerned about what it was and asked the doctor. What is the term used for it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sequestrum

A piece of dead bone is called sequestrum.

Sequestrum acts as the nidus of infection in chronic osteomyelitis.

Sequestrum is a piece of dead bone. It is formed when a fragment of bone gets separated from the healthy bone due to necrosis. It varies in size from a spicule to a large fragment. This sequestrum acts as a nidus for infection. It is the most common cause of non-healing in chronic osteomyelitis.

The involucrum is the dense new sclerotic bone surrounding the sequestrum. It is formed from deep layers of stripped periosteum.

Cloacae are the perforations in the involucrum. Pus and tiny spicules of bone may be discharged through them.

Sinus tract is formed when the abscess from the infected bone drains out through the skin.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young male patient sustained a right tibial shaft fracture following a road traffic accident. The patient's right leg was immobilized with a plaster cast. This patient now presents to the emergency with severe pain in the leg. On examination, the distal pulses are absent, on passive stretching the pain increases, and on opening the plaster, the right leg appears edematous and numerous blisters are seen. Considering the suspected diagnosis, what would be the most appropriate management in this case?
options: Opening of the plaster is sufficient
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fasciotomy

In the above given clinical scenario of a patient with tibial fracture following an RTA, now presenting with severe leg pain, absent distal pulses, increase pain on passive stretch and leg looking edematous, suggests acute compartment syndrome, and it is treated immediately with fasciotomy.

Compartment syndrome is a condition characterized by elevated pressure within the osteofascial compartment resulting in impaired local circulation.

The classic features of ischemia in acute compartment syndrome include the 5 Ps:

* Pain: Pain is the first symptom of acute compartment syndrome. Ischemic muscle is highly sensitive to touch. On the passive stretching of the muscles, severe pain can be elicited.

* Paresthesia: Paresthesia and hypoesthesia may be noted due to compression of nerves traversing the affected compartment. They are the first signs of nerve ischemia.

* Pallor: Pallor of the skin may not always be seen. The skin outside the compartment may be normally perfused, as only the intra-compartmental perfusion may be affected.

* Paralysis: Paralysis of muscle groups affected in that compartment is a late sign.

* Pulselessness: Usually, the peripheral pulses and capillary return are intact in the early stages, unless there is a major arterial injury. If pulses are absent, arteriography is indicated.

The diagnosis can be confirmed by measuring the intra-compartmental pressure using a split catheter introduced into the compartment. The difference between diastolic and compartment pressure is known as the differential pressure (ΔP). A differential pressure (ΔP) of less than 30 mm Hg (4.00 kilopascals) is an indication for immediate compartment decompression.

Treatment: The threatened compartment must be promptly decompressed, merely splitting the plaster is utterly useless and the limb must be nursed flat. Elevating the limb causes a further decrease in end capillary pressure and aggravates muscle ischemia. In the case of compartment syndrome in the leg, Fasciotomy means opening all four compartments (anterior, lateral, deep posterior and superficial compartments). Wounds to be left open and inspected 2 days later, if tissues are healthy, the wounds can be sutured. If there is muscle necrosis, debridement is to be carried out.

The image below shows a fasciotomy.

Pearl PF1498: Acute compartment and Crush syndrome

1. Acute Compartment Syndrome

Acute compartment syndrome is an elevation of the intracompartmental pressure (ICP) which increases the risk for tissue ischemia and necrosis.

Causes: Fractures (70%) and severe soft tissue injuries (30%). Common fractures causing compartment syndrome include tibial diaphyseal (most common), distal radius, and forearm fractures.

Pathology: Increased pressure in one of the osseofascial compartments due to bleeding, oedema or inflammation. A vicious cycle of ischemia → edema→ ischemia leading to necrosis of the muscles and nerves within the compartment in 6 hours or less.

Clinical features: Five Ps: Pain, Paraesthesia, Pallor, Paralysis and Pulselessness.

Management: Fasciotomy to decompress the threatened compartment if the differential pressure (ΔP) goes < 30 mmHg.

2. Crush syndrome

Crush syndrome is the systemic manifestation of muscle necrosis. It is commonly caused due to prolonged external compression of an extremity.

Causes: Crush injuries sustained during motor vehicle accidents, earthquakes, mining and other occupational accidents.

Pathology: Underperfusion of muscle causes myonecrosis. When the limb is freed, there is a release of toxic metabolites causing reperfusion injury. Reactive oxygen metabolites create further tissue injury. Free myoglobin can get precipitated in the renal glomeruli.

Clinical features: The affected limb is pulseless, red, swollen and blistered. Sensation and muscle power may be lost. There can be signs of impaired renal function, metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia and hypocalcaemia.

Management: Encouraging high urine output, alkalization of the urine, hemofiltration, radical excision of dead muscles, fasciotomy if there is compartment syndrome.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the xray finding seen in a patient with flurosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteosclerosis

Osteosclerosis is seen in a patient with fluorosis.

The characteristic pathology involves sub-periosteal new bone formation, osteosclerosis(Most commonly seen vertebrae, ribs, and pelvis), and hyperostosis at the bony attachments of ligaments, tendons, and fascia.

Fluorosis is a disease where excessive deposition of calcium occurs in bone and soft tissues.

Fluorine stimulates osteoblastic activity and fluorapatite crystals are laid down in bone which is resistant to osteoclastic resorption.

This leads to calcium retention, impaired mineralization, and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about the condition?
options: May be caused due to pin prick injury
Most common causative organism is Klebsiella
May be treated initially by antibiotics
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Most common causative organism is Klebsiella

The condition depicted above is known as a felon and the false statement is "most common causative organism is Klebsiella" as the most common organism causing felon is Staphylococcus aureus.

* A felon  (a.k.a whitlow) is an abscess in the subcutaneous tissues of the distal pulp of a finger or thumb (thumb is more common).

* Infection can be caused by a penetrating injury from a foreign body or from “finger sticks” for medical reasons (e.g., hematocrit and blood glucose determinations).

* S. aureus is the organism most commonly isolated from fingertip infections.

* Abscesses beginning deep, especially if untreated, penetrate the periosteum and cause osteomyelitis; the more superficial ones cause skin necrosis.

* Treatment consists of antibiotics and an incision for drainage. The vertical incision is preferred and all septa are to be broken during drainage.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: With respect to tuberculosis of hip, which of the marked areas are affected commonly?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1

The most common area affected is acetabulum which is marked as 1 in the figure.

Multiple cavitations occurs in femoral head and the acetabulum. Eventually, the head or the acetabulum gets partially absorbed. By the constant pull of the muscles acting on the hip, the remaining head of femur may dislocate from the acetabulum onto the ilium,giving rise to the so called wandering acetabulum.

Early stages of tb hip are characterised by synovial hypertrophy and effusion. The pannus of the hypertrophied synovium extends fully around the articular cartilage destroying it. The joint is filled with pus and granulation tissue.

The sequential destruction is:

* Dislocation of femoral head

* Destruction of articular cartilage

* Synovial hypertrophy

* Multiple cavitations

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presented to the emergency department with pain and swelling of the right knee. Radiograph shows the following finding. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Patellar fracture

The radiograph shows the displaced patellar fracture.

A patellar fracture can either occur via a direct injury to the knee or because of a violent contraction of the quadriceps.

The fracture may be undisplaced either because of the pre-patellar expansion of the quadriceps tendon which holds the fragments together or because of the patellar retinaculae on the sides.

Patellar fracture results in the disruption of the extensor apparatus (not the flexor apparatus).

Due to the disruption of the extensor apparatus, the patient will not be able to lift his leg with the knee in full extension; it remains in a position short of full extension (extensor lag). Clinically, it can be tested using the Active Straight leg raising (SLR) test, which the patient will not be able to perform.

The extensor apparatus of the knee includes the Quadriceps femoris muscle with its tendon, the patella bone and, the ligamentum patellae with its insertion into the tibial tuberosity.

An un-displaced fracture of the patella is treated with a plaster cast extending from the groin to just above the malleoli, with the knee in full extension. This is called as a cylinder cast and is usually left in place for a period of at least 3 weeks.

A two part fracture (Displaced transverse fracture) of the patella must be reduced, and the fragments are fixed with tension band wiring using K wires and the extensor retinaculae is repaired

Other treatment options which are available for patellar fracture are:

* Undisplaced patellar fractures with minimal joint incongruity and intact extensor retinaculum can be treated by cylinder cast.

* Displaced patellar fractures are usually treated by tension band wiring.

* Severely comminuted fractures where the reduction of the fragments is difficult are treated by patellectomy.

Pearl PF1177: Tension band wiring

A tension band wire is a form of internal fixation used to convert distraction forces into compression forces, promoting bone healing.

It is used in:

* Fracture patella

* Fracture olecranon

* Fracture lateral malleolus

* Fracture greater trochanter

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old male comes to the casualty with a history of a road traffic accident and left hip pain. On examination, the leg is in flexion, abduction, and external rotation deformity, with lengthening of the limb. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterior dislocation of hip

In the clinical scenario of a patient with a road traffic accident who developed left hip pain with flexion, abduction, and external rotation deformity, along with lengthening of the same limb, this is very characteristic of anterior dislocation of the hip.

Anterior dislocation of the hip is less common than posterior hip dislocations and accounts for about 10-20% of all hip dislocations. This injury is usually sustained following a high-energy accident.

Clinical features: On physical examination, the affected limb will be abducted and externally rotated. It is also slightly flexed. Additionally, a prominent anterior bulge will be present either in the pubic region or in the groin region.

According to the position assumed by the femoral head, anterior dislocation of the hip can further be classified as

* Type I - Superior or pubic

* Type II - Inferior or obturator

Radiological findings:

* The displaced femoral head will appear larger than the normal side

* As the thigh is externally rotated lesser trochanter is more prominent.

* A lateral view X-ray will be confirmatory.

Treatment of anterior dislocation includes a closed reduction under sedation or general anesthesia. If closed reduction fails, an open procedure may be planned.

Patient with an externally rotated, abducted, and slightly flexed left leg due to anterior dislocation of the hip-

Other options:

Option A: Posterior hip dislocation - It is commonly seen following dashboard injuries, and in this condition, the patient presents with flexion, adduction, and internal rotation deformity. Radiological findings seen in posterior hip dislocation are:

* The femoral head is displaced superiorly and laterally

* The femoral head appears smaller than normal

* The lesser trochanter is not visualized

* The femoral head and posterior acetabular wall fractures may also be seen

Option C: Intertrochanteric fracture of the femur - This is usually sustained following a fall or RTA, and the leg is short and externally rotated. Clinical findings are more marked than the neck of femur fractures.

Option D: Fracture neck of the femur - Here, there can be shortening and external rotation of the limb. Radiological findings seen are:

* Fracture in the neck of the femur

* External rotation of the femur, with the lesser trochanter appearing more prominent

* Break in the trabecular stream

* Break in the Shenton's line

Pearl PF1181: Common clinical features of anterior and posterior dislocations of the hip

Anterior dislocation
Posterior dislocation

Prevalence
Less common
Most common

Type of injury
Deceleration injury/ Fall from height
Dashboard injury

Attitude of the limb
Flexion, abduction, external rotation (FABER)
Flexion, adduction, internal rotation (FADIR)

Length of the limb
Lengthened
Shortened

Radiological findings

• Femoral head may be seen inferior to the acetabulum
• Femoral head appears larger than normal
• Lesser trochanter is prominent

• Femoral head is displaced superiorly and laterally
• Femoral head appears smaller than normal
• Lesser trochanter is not visualised

Nerve injured
Femoral nerve
Sciatic nerve

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 45-year-old male patient presents to the OPD with complaints of increasing pain in his right hand over the past few months. On examination, there is a palpable lump, and an x-ray was done which is given below. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chondrosarcoma

The clinical presentation at this age and the radiograph showing popcorn calcification are suggestive of chondrosarcoma.

Chondrosarcoma is the second most common nonhematological primary malignancy of the bone(Osteosarcoma is the commonest). It can be primary or secondary. Secondary chondrosarcomas develop at the site of a previously existing benign cartilage lesion.

Primary chondrosarcomas are commonly seen at 40-60 years of age whereas the age group for secondary chondrosarcoma is 25-45 years.

Clinical features:

* Pelvis, proximal femur, and proximal humerus are the common locations.

* The hand is a rare location. However, it is the most common primary bone malignancy in the hand.

* Primary chondrosarcoma usually presents with increasing pain and a palpable lump.

* Asymptomatic radiological abnormality is a common presentation in enchondromas but is not seen in chondrosarcomas.

Radiological findings:

* It arises from the medullary cavity and shows irregular matrix calcification.

* Characteristic calcification pattern is described as "popcorn", "punctate", or "comma-shaped"

* Bone destruction, cortical erosion, and periosteal reaction may be seen.

* CT or MRI is used to identify the presence of secondary chondrosarcomas.

* Secondary chondrosarcoma is suspected of the cartilage cap of the lesion is more than 2 cm in a skeletally mature patient.

Treatment:

* Extended curettage with intraoperative adjuvant treatments is considered for low-grade lesions confined to the medullary canal.

* Low-grade lesions with soft tissue extensions should be treated as high-grade lesions.

* High-grade lesions are managed with wide or radical resection or amputation.

* Chemotherapy is not indicated for conventional chondrosarcoma but is used for mesenchymal or dedifferentiated variants.

* Radiotherapy is only used as a palliative measure for surgically inaccessible tumors.

Other options:

Option A: Osteosarcoma is the most common non-hematologic primary malignancy of bone. It occurs most commonly in the second decade of life. It is typically metaphyseal. The distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus are the common sites.

Radiographic findings: The periosteal reaction is the typical finding and it may take the form of a "Codman's triangle" or it may have a "sunburst (sunray) appearance" on X-ray.

Option B: Ewing's sarcoma is a primary malignant tumor of the bone commonly involving the age group of 4-25 years. It commonly involves the diaphysis of the long bones like the femur, tibia, fibula, and humerus.

Radiographic findings: Onion-peel appearance due to deposition of periosteal reaction in layers is the typical finding.

Option C: Osteoclastoma or Giant cell tumor: The commonly affected age group is 20-40 years with a slight female preponderance. The distal end of the femur is the most common location followed by the proximal tibia and distal radius.

Radiographic findings:

* Eccentrically located solitary lytic lesion in the epiphysis

* Soap bubble appearance

* Periosteal new bone formation is absent.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the hospital with complaints of pain and limping. The symptoms started 6 months back and gradually worsened. The child appears to be healthy with normal height and weight. On examination, there is mild wasting on the right side, abduction ( especially in flexion ), and internal rotation is limited due to pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perthes disease

A young male patient with normal height and weight and complaints of pain and limping gradually progressing over 6 months and examination findings of limited abduction and internal rotation is likely to have Perthes's disease. The image shows a mushroom-shaped femoral head that is laterally displaced in a dysplastic acetabular socket.

Between 4 and 7 years of age, the femoral head may depend on the lateral epiphyseal vessels for its blood supply and venous drainage almost entirely. These vessels situated in the retinacula make them susceptible to stretching and to pressure from an effusion.

The disease is characterized by the disruption of blood flow to the head of the femur. Due to which the bone goes for osteonecrosis and stops growing. Over time, healing occurs by new blood vessels infiltrating the dead bone and removing the necrotic bone which leads to a loss of bone mass and a weakening of the femoral head.

Clinical features include a boy of 4-8 years complaining of pain and limping. Symptoms continue for weeks on end or recur intermittently. The hip looks deceptively normal. Although initially, all movements are painful; with time, abduction with internal rotation is always limited.

Xray findings depend on the stages

* Necrotic phase: Radiographically dense areas which indicate new bone formation is soon followed by bone necrosis.

* Fragmentation phase: Alternating patches of density and lucency. Sometimes a crescentic subarticular fracture is often seen in lateral view

* Re-ossification phase: Epiphyseal density increases in this phase

* Healing phase: Normal femoral head or mushroom-shaped femoral head which is laterally displaced in a dysplastic acetabular socket.

Guidelines to treatment are derived from the review by Herring,

Children under 6 years - symptomatic treatment including activity modification is appropriate

Children aged 6-8 years - Bonge age and Catterall Staging determines the modality of treatment. Options include abduction brace or osteotomy.

For children aged 9 and above - operative containment is the choice.

Note:Salter's extrusion angle helps to assess the femoral head extrusion. Normal is 50 degrees or more.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the diagnosis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Klippel Feil syndrome

The image shows a low posterior hairline and a short webbed neck which is suggestive of Klippel Feil syndrome.

Klippel Feil syndrome is a disorder of development in which there is a bilateral failure of scapular descent associated with marked anomalies of the cervical spine and failure of fusion of the occipital bones.

Triad seen in Klippel Feil syndrome:

* Low posterior hairline

* Short webbed neck

* Restriction of neck movements

Scoliosis, Short stature, and Sprengel's deformity are important associations of Klippel-Feil syndrome.

Other options:

Option A: Ankylosing spondylitis: It is a chronic progressive inflammatory condition affecting the sacroiliac joints and the axial skeleton. It is commonly seen in young male adults and they typically present with an insidious onset back pain that improves with exercise. The earliest radiological finding is erosion and fuzziness of the sacroiliac joints and the characteristic late sign is the bamboo-spine appearance.

Option B: Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy:-

* Autosomal dominant disorder.

* Earlier and most severe weakness is in the facial and shoulder muscles (scapular winging).

* Flattening or concavity of deltoid contour, with wasted biceps and triceps.

* Calf hypertrophy is not a feature, foot drop may be seen.

* Lumbar lordosis and kyphoscoliosis are common complications.

Option D: Sprengel deformity:

* The deformity is the main symptom and is noticed at birth and occasionally bilateral.

* The shoulder on the affected side is elevated, and the scapula feels abnormally high, smaller, and prominent.

* The neck appears shorter than usual and there may be kyphosis or scoliosis of the upper thoracic spine.

* Shoulder movements are painless but abduction and elevation may be limited by the fixation of the scapula.

* X-rays will show the elevated scapula and associated vertebral anomalies; as a bony bridge between the scapula and the cervical spine (the omovertebral bar).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The brace shown in the given image is of a _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Taylor brace

The image shows a Taylor brace.

Taylor brace is designed to control the upper and lower regions of the spinal column and support your spine whilst standing, sitting, and walking after spinal surgery.

Braces are used to prevent progression and avoid surgery in scoliotic curves between 20 and 30 degrees. A variety of braces are available, some are created as cast and some are prefabricated. They usually extend from the thoracic and lumbar spine to the pelvis and have pads to push the spine into correct alignment.

Other options:

Option A: Boston brace is a type of thoraco-lumbosacral-orthosis (TLSO brace). It has a hard polypropylene outer shell with a soft foam lining inside. It is used in patients whose scoliosis curve apex is at T7 or lower.

Option B: Milwaukee brace also known as cervical-thoracic-lumbosacral orthosis or CTLSO is a back brace used in the treatment of spinal curvatures (such as scoliosis or kyphosis) in children. It is less commonly used nowadays due to the convenience of modern braces. It is still used for scoliosis with high thoracic and cervical spine curves.

Option D: Anterior spinal hyperextension (ASHE) brace is an anterior spinal hyperextension brace used in dorsolumbar spinal injury. A hyperextension brace will take the pressure off the weak vertebrae and limit forward bending.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The fracture seen in the Xray given below is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Galeazzi's fracture

The X-ray reveals an oblique fracture in the lower third of radius with dislocation of the distal radio-ulnar joint, which is suggestive of Galeazzi's fracture.

In Galeazzi's fracture, there is a radial bone fracture at the middle and distal third junction and associated distal radio-ulnar joint subluxation or dislocation. It may be possible to demonstrate the instability of the radioulnar joint by ‘ballotting’ the distal end of the ulna (‘piano-key sign’).

Galeazzi's fracture is the fracture of the lower third of the radius and the subluxation or dislocation of the distal radioulnar joint. This injury usually happens when one falls on an outstretched hand. The most common clinical feature is tenderness over the distal end of the forearm.

The aim of treatment for this fracture is to preserve supination and pronation of the forearm. In children, closed reduction is usually enough to achieve perfect reduction. However, in adults, open reduction using a k-wire fixation or compression plating is usually required. It is also important to look for ulnar nerve damage.

Galeazzi's fracture can cause complications such as malunion due to displacement of the fragment. This often results in deformity and limitation in supination and pronation.

Other Options:

Option B: Monteggia fracture: It is the fracture of shaft of ulna with dislocation of proximal radio-ulnar joint

Option C: Smith's fracture: It is also known as "Reverse Colle's fracture". It is the fracture of the distal radius with palmar angulation of the distal bone fragment.

Option D: Colle's fracture: It is the fracture of the distal radius with dorsal angulation of the distal bone fragment.

Pearl PF0377: Named fractures of the upper limb

Colle's fracture: Fracture of the distal radius with dorsal angulation of the distal bone fragment.

Smith's fracture: Reverse Colles' fracture. Fracture of the distal one-third of the radius with palmar displacement.

Galeazzi fracture-dislocation: Fracture of the lower third of the radius and subluxation of the distal radio-ulnar joint.

Monteggia fracture-dislocation: Fracture of the shaft of the ulna with dislocation of a proximal radio-ulnar joint.

Barton’s fracture: Intra-articular fracture of the distal radius.

Rolando's fracture: Intra-articular comminuted fracture of the base of the first metacarpal with a T or Y configuration.

Chauffeur's fracture or the Hutchinson fracture: Fracture of the radial styloid.

Essex–Lopresti lesion: Fracture of the radial head with disruption of the interosseous membrane and distal radial ulnar joint ligaments.

Nightstick fracture: Isolated fracture of the ulnar bone.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following is the most radiosensitive tumour?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ewing's sarcoma

The radiosensitive tumor among the following is Ewing's sarcoma. All others are radioresistant tumors.

Ewing sarcoma is a malignant bone tumor characterized by primitive round cells without obvious differentiation. It accounts for 6% to 10% of primary malignant bone tumors.

Ewing sarcoma follows osteosarcoma as the second most common group of bone sarcomas in children. Approximately 80% of affected patients are younger than 20 years. Boys are affected slightly more frequently than girls. Usually, the tumor arises in the diaphysis of long tubular bones, especially the femur and the flat bones of the pelvis. Fever, elevated sedimentation rate, anemia, and leukocytosis may be seen.

Plain radiographs show a destructive lytic tumor with permeative margins that extend into the surrounding soft tissues. Multiple layers of reactive bone are formed by the periosteal response, giving the bone an onion skin-like appearance.

Ewing's sarcoma is managed with a combination of radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and surgery. This sarcoma is highly sensitive to radiotherapy and in certain cases, tumors affecting important bones can be treated with radiotherapy or a combination of radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

Pearl PF1484: Radiosensitive and Radioresistant Tumors

Highly radiosensitive tumors are

* Lymphoma

* Seminoma

* Myeloma

* Ewing’s sarcoma

* Wilm’s tumour

Highly radioresistant tumors are

* Melanoma

* Osteosarcoma

* Pancreatic carcinoma

* Hepatic carcinoma

* Renal cell carcinoma

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old male patient presented with complaints of a gradually progressive swelling around his wrist joint for 3 months. Given below is the image of the swelling and the X-ray film. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteoclastoma

The clinical presentation and the X-ray showing an eccentric expansile lesion with a soap bubble appearance are suggestive of osteoclastoma or giant cell tumor(GCT).

Osteoclastoma usually affects young adults in the age group of 20-40 years. The most common location of the tumor is the distal femur followed by the proximal tibia. Involvement of the distal end of the radius is also seen and the tumor is more aggressive in this location.

Radiographic findings in GCT:

* A solitary, possibly loculated, lytic lesion in the epiphysis

* Eccentric location, most often subchondral

* Expansion of the overlying cortex

* Soap bubble appearance - The tumor is homogeneously lytic with trabeculae of the remnants of bone traversing it, giving it a loculated appearance called soap bubble appearance

* No calcification within the tumor

* No or minimal reactive sclerosis around the tumor.

Treatment :

* Extended curettage and bone grafting.

* En-bloc wide resection and reconstruction are done for advanced stages, local recurrence, and tumors not responding to other methods.

* Resection without reconstruction is done for lesions in expandable bones like distal ulna, clavicle, etc.

* Irradiation and/or embolization are used for inoperable lesions in the spine and pelvis.

* Bisphosphonates have been shown to reduce the proliferation of osteoclasts and hence have been shown to stabilize local and metastatic disease.

* Denosumab is approved for use in unresectable tumors in skeletally mature patients.

Other options:

Ewing's sarcoma:

It is a primary malignant tumor of the bone commonly involving the age group of 4-25 years. It commonly involves the diaphysis of the long bones like the femur, tibia, fibula, and humerus.

Radiographic findings: Onion-peel appearance due to deposition of periosteal reaction in layers is the typical finding.

Osteosarcoma:

It is the most common non-hematologic primary malignancy of bone. It occurs most commonly in the second decade of life. It is typically metaphyseal. The distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus are the common sites.

Radiographic findings: The periosteal reaction is the typical finding and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have a sunburst (sunray) appearance on X-ray.

Osteochondroma:

Osteochondromas are common benign bone tumors. The lesions consist of a bony mass, often in the form of a stalk, produced by endochondral ossification of a growing cartilaginous cap. The common sites of involvement are the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 74-year-old man presented with low back pain that was radiating to his legs. On examination of the spine, a palpable step was felt in the lumbosacral region. The X-ray of the spine is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Spondylolisthesis

In the above clinical scenario, the patient most likely has spondylolisthesis. A palpable step in the lumbosacral spine, called a step sign is a classic clinical feature of this condition. Moreover, in the X-ray given, there is a break in the pars interarticularlis of the L4 vertebra, which appears like a beheaded Scottish terrier. Hence, it is known as the beheaded Scottish terrier sign and it is diagnostic of spondylolisthesis.

Spondylolisthesis is the anterior displacement of one segment of the spine upon another. It is caused as an end result of spondylolysis.

Normally, the spinous processes of the adjacent vertebrae are aligned with each other. They can be palpated on the back in a smooth way.

In spondylolisthesis, one vertebra has moved over the other. Therefore, a step-off or step sign can be felt over the spinous process at the affected level.

Note: The step-off sign is also used to describe the radiographic appearance of Lisfranc injury of the foot. There is a dorsal displacement of the tarsal bones with respect to the metatarsal bones.

A diagram showing spondylolisthesis and spondylosis is given below:

Spondylolysis refers to defects or stress fractures in the pars interarticularis of the vertebral arch. The most common site for spondylolysis is L5.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the hospital with complaints of pain and limping. The symptoms started 6 months back and gradually worsened. The child appears to be healthy with normal height and weight. On examination, there is mild wasting on the right side. Abduction (especially in flexion) and internal rotation are limited due to pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perthes disease

A young male patient with normal height and weight and complaints of pain and limping gradually progressing over 6 months and examination findings of limited abduction and internal rotation is likely to have Perthes's disease. The image shows a mushroom-shaped femoral head that is laterally displaced in a dysplastic acetabular socket.

Between 4 and 7 years of age, the femoral head may depend on the lateral epiphyseal vessels for its blood supply and venous drainage almost entirely. These vessels situated in the retinacula make them susceptible to stretching and to pressure from an effusion.

Over time, healing occurs by new blood vessels infiltrating the dead bone and removing the necrotic bone which leads to a loss of bone mass and a weakening of the femoral head. Although initially, all movements are painful; with time, abduction with internal rotation is always limited.

* Necrotic phase: Radiographically dense areas which indicate new bone formation is soon followed by bone necrosis.

* Fragmentation phase: Alternating patches of density and lucency. Sometimes a crescentic subarticular fracture is often seen in lateral view

* Re-ossification phase: Epiphyseal density increases in this phase

* Healing phase: Normal femoral head or mushroom-shaped femoral head which is laterally displaced in a dysplastic acetabular socket.

There are different 'head at risk signs' described by Catrell which include:

* lateral subluxation of the femoral head

* speckled calcification in the lateral epiphysis

* Epiphysis being horizontal

* Gage's sign: V-shaped osteoporotic segment in the lateral epiphysis and adjacent metaphysis.

Guidelines to treatment are derived from the review by Herring,

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient sustained a fracture as depicted in the image, following a fall from height. What is this fracture known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Open book fracture

The fracture shown in the image is known as Open book fracture.

Open book fractures are associated with pubic diastasis and/or a fracture of the pubic rami with a posterior pelvic disruption of the sacro-iliac joint.

Other options:

Malgaigne's fracture(image shown below)  involves the pubic rami anteriorly and the sacroiliac joint (SI joint) or ilium near the SI joint on the same side posteriorly.

Bucket handle fracture refers to a vertically orientated fracture through ipsilateral superior and inferior pubic rami with contralateral sacroiliac joint disruption.

Chauffeur's fracture refers to fracture of the radial styloid process in the forearm.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient was diagnosed with supraspinatus tendinitis. What degree of movement of the shoulder would be painful for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 60°-120°

Supraspinatus tendinitis seen in shoulder impingement syndrome is due to repeated rubbing of the tendon (mainly supraspinatus) under the coraco-acromial arc. The patient complaints of increased pain when the arm traverses an arc between 60 and 120 degrees when greater tuberosity negotiates the subacromial space.

Shoulder impingement syndrome:

It is also called supraspinatus syndrome, painful arc syndrome, and swimmer's shoulder and occurs when the tendons of the rotator cuff muscles become irritated and inflamed as they pass through the subacromial space. This can result in pain, weakness, and loss of movement at the shoulder.

Causes of impingement syndrome:

* Supraspinatus tendinitis (Common)

* Complete or partial rupture of the rotator cuff

* Osteoarthritis of the acromioclavicular joint

Clinical features:

* Subacute tendinitis or painful arc syndrome: Anterior shoulder pain after vigorous activity. Treatment is with avoidance of initiating activity, NSAIDs, and physiotherapy.

* Chronic tendinitis: Recurrent attacks of subacute tendinitis and pain is worse at night.

* Cuff disruption: There is progressive fibrosis and disruption of the cuff leading to a partial or full-thickness tear. Treatment includes acromioplasty and repair of rotator cuff.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young male who had a road traffic accident is brought to the emergency department. His left leg is shortened, internally rotated, and adducted. On examination, femoral artery pulsation is not felt. A plain radiograph of his hip was taken which is shown below. What is your diagnosis?
options: Fracture neck of femur with injury to femoral vessels
Anterior dislocation of hip with femoral artery injury
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Posterior dislocation of hip

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of posterior hip dislocation. In this condition, the leg will be in flexion, adduction, and internal rotation.

This injury is seen in patients as a result of a motor vehicle accident. In a patient that is sitting in a car, the hip is flexed and the knee is pushed posteriorly by an impact on the dashboard.

Radiographically, in a patient with a posterior dislocation, the femoral head is displaced, posterior, superior, and slightly lateral to the acetabulum.

The femoral artery pulsation is usually felt against the neck of the femur. Due to the posterior dislocation of the hip joint, the femoral vessels fall backward and the pulsation of the femoral artery cannot be felt. This is called the vascular sign of Narath.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the diagnosis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Syndactyly

The image shows the middle two toes being fused together which is a condition called 'Syndactyly'.

Syndactyly is the fusion of digits that can involve either the fingers or toes. It is a congenital malformation and can be of various degrees based on the extent of fusion of the tissues involved:

* Simple-only soft tissue

* Complex- skin and bone fused

* Incomplete- only part of the web

* Complete- entire web is affected

Pathophysiology: due to lack of apoptosis during development of the digits.

Treatment: Mild or incomplete syndactyly of central digits need no treatment.

If it disrupts the function of the handthen surgical separation of the conjoined structures and reconstruction is needed.

Note:

Syndactyly of border digits can cause progressive deformity with growth and thus this needs early surgical correction.

Care is taken not to injure the digital arteries when multiple digits are involved by separating only one side of a digit at a time.

Other options:

Symphalangism: congenital stiffness of the proximal interphalangeal joints of the fingers.

Polydactyly: extra digits are present in fingers or toes.

Brachydactyly: undergrowth of a digit seen in syndromes like Turner's syndrome.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the type of splint shown in the image called as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cock-up splint

The image shows a cock up splint which is used for radial nerve palsy.

Other options:

Wrist splint -

The wrist splint is used in the management of carpal tunnel syndrome. it can be worn at night to prevent bending of the wrist which typically happens when patients sleep and leads to increased symptoms.

Knuckle bender splint -

In cases of ulnar claw hand where ulnar nerve recovery is anticipated the knuckle bender splint can be used to correct and prevent MCP(metacarpophalangeal) hyperextension.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: While examining a patient with a right forearm fracture, you ask him to make a fist. The following finding is noted during this procedure. What is the sign called as ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pointing index sign

The given image shows the pointing index sign and is associated with median nerve injury at the forearm or elbow.

The pointing index sign is seen in supracondylar fractures of the humerus.

This finding occurs as a result of injury to the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. It results in the loss of function of both flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) and flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS). Hence, the index finger sticks out when the patient is asked to clasp their hand.

Other options:

Option A:  In Froment's sign, due to the weakness of the adductor pollicis muscle, the adduction of the thumb is lost. When asked to hold an object, the patient tries to hold the object by using the flexor pollicis longus muscle. This produces flexion at the interphalangeal joint while holding the book.

Option C:  Paralysis of flexor pollicis brevis can occur in median nerve injury at the arm and elbow. Benediction hand sign (attempt to make a fist gives pointed index and middle finger) and Ochsner's clasping test (attempt to clasp both hands show pointing index finger) are used to test such injuries.

Option D:  Policeman tip deformity, also known as waiter's tip hand or porter's tip hand, is a finding of Erb's palsy due to injury of the upper trunk of the brachial plexus involving C5 and C6. The hand is adducted, medially rotated, and hangs by the side with the elbow extended and pronated.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 17-year-old boy presents to the clinic with complaints of a painless lump on the lateral aspect of his left knee. The radiograph of the patient is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteochondroma

The given radiograph and clinical vignette suggests the diagnosis of osteochondroma.

Osteochondromas are benign bone tumors that present commonly in the adolescent age group. They usually present as painless masses in long bones like the femur or humerus. They are seen as well-defined bony protuberances which may be pedunculated or sessile. Pedunculated osteochondromas point away from the joint, towards the diaphysis. The cortex and cancellous bone of osteochondroma blend with that of the host bone. MRI shows a classical cartilaginous cap.

Osteochondromas usually grow with skeletal maturity and stop once growth stops. They rarely undergo malignant transformation.

Treatment is not indicated if the lesion does not produce symptoms. Excision can be done for large lesions with local pressure effects.

Other options:

Option A: Enchondroma is an intramedullary tumor of hyaline cartilage. They are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally. They are usually seen in individuals aged 20 to 50 years, in the tubular bones of the hands and feet. Radiographically, it appears as a central lesion with well-defined, rounded, edges and a thin rind of reactive sclerosis.

Option B: Chondroblastoma is a benign tumor and presents as a painful mass that causes effusion or stiffness. On x-ray, they are seen as round or oval lytic lesions in the epiphysis. The bony cortex is not breached but can appear expanded. The common sites are the ends of long bones. Microscopically, chondroblastoma consists of a sheet of chondroblasts embedded in the chondroid matrix. The calcification is often present and surrounds individual cells giving the appearance of ‘chicken wire.’

Option D:  Giant cell tumor, also known as osteoclastoma, is a benign bone tumor. However, it exhibits locally aggressive behaviour despite its benign nature. It usually affects young adults with a peak incidence in the age group of 20–45 years. It presents as a painful mass. A plain radiograph reveals an eccentric, expansile, lobulated lytic lesion (soap bubble appearance) in the epiphysis. There is minimal calcification within the tumor. Biopsy reveals osteoclast-like giant cells scattered among round or spindle-shaped mononuclear cells.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 20-year-old patient presents with painful swelling in the middle finger around the proximal phalanx. An X-ray was done and it is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Enchondroma

The above clinical vignette and X-ray findings point toward the diagnosis of enchondroma.

Enchondromas are benign tumors consisting of a lobulated mass of cartilage encapsulated by fibrous tissue. It is more commonly seen in 20 to 30 years of age. Small bones of hands and feet are commonly involved followed by the femur and humerus.

The patient usually presents with long-standing swelling from one or more phalanges or metacarpals, without much pain. Diagnosis can be done by X-ray, which can show expanding lytic lesions, occasionally, a biopsy will be required if the diagnosis is unclear. Enchondromas of long bones may undergo malignant transformation into chondrosarcoma.

Treatment is removal by curettage and it is indicated if there is pain or pathological fracture.

Other options:

Option A: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignancy of bone that produces osteoid matrix or mineralized bone.  X-ray shows periosteal reaction and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have a sunburst (sunray) appearance as shown below.

Option B: Ewing's sarcoma is the second most common primary malignancy of bone after osteosarcoma. Onion-peel appearance due to deposition of periosteal reaction in layers is seen on radiology (as shown below) and Homer-Wright rosettes, which are round groupings of cells with a central fibrillary core may be seen histologically.

Option C: Osteoclastoma is also called a giant cell tumour because multinucleated osteoclast-type giant cells are present on histology. The image below shows an X-ray of a giant cell tumor showing an eccentrically located solitary lytic lesion in the epiphysis and the typical soap bubble appearance

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 60-year-old female patient presents with complaints of pain and swelling in the left wrist following a fall on an outstretched hand. On examination, dinner fork deformity can be noticed. What is the most likely displacement seen in this patient?
options: Proximal and ventral displacement of radius
Proximal and dorsal displacement of radius
Proximal and dorsal displacement of ulna
Proximal and ventral displacement of ulna
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Proximal and dorsal displacement of radius

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Colles’ fracture in which proximal and dorsal displacement of the radius is most likely seen.

Colle's fracture is common in postmenopausal after a fall on an outstretched hand.

Clinical presentation -
The patient presents with pain, swelling, and deformity of the wrist. Tenderness may be present. The 'dinner fork deformity ' is the prominence on the back of the wrist and depression in the front. It is due to the dorsal angulation of the distal fracture fragment. The radial styloid process comes to lie at the same level or a little higher than the ulnar styloid process.

Displacements(radius) that may be seen in Colles' fracture:

* Dorsal tilt

* Dorsal shift

* Lateral tilt (Radial tilt)

* Lateral shift (Radial shift)

* Supination

* Impaction of fragment

* Proximal shift

Diagnosis -
Diagnosis is by X-ray.  X-rays show there is a transverse fracture of the radius at the cortico-cancellous junction. A dorsal tilt is the most common.

Management -

* Undisplaced fracture - immobilization in a below-elbow plaster cast for six weeks

* Displaced fractures - manipulative reduction followed by immobilization in Colles' cast in palmar flexion, pronation, and ulnar deviation.

* Comminuted fractures -  transfixed percutaneously using two K-wires

Pearl PF1909: Named fractures of the upper limb

Colle's fracture: Extra-articular fracture of the distal radius with dorsal angulation of the distal bone fragment.

Galeazzi fracture-dislocation: Fracture of the lower third of the radius and subluxation of the distal radio-ulnar joint.

Monteggia fracture-dislocation: Fracture of the shaft of the ulna with dislocation of a proximal radio-ulnar joint.

Barton’s fracture: Intra-articular fracture of the distal radius.

Rolando's fracture: Intra-articular comminuted fracture of the base of the first metacarpal with a T or Y configuration.

Smith's fracture: Reverse Colles' fracture. Extra-articular fracture of the distal one-third of the radius with palmar or ventral displacement (Image below).

Chauffeur's fracture or the Hutchinson fracture: Fracture of the radial styloid.

Essex–Lopresti lesion: Fracture of the radial head with disruption of the interosseous membrane and distal radial ulnar joint ligaments.

Nightstick fracture: Isolated fracture of radial or ulnar bone.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient was brought to the OPD with the following deformity. Identify the condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Genu valgum

The given X-ray of a child with abnormally approximated knees, divergent ankles, and increased intermalleolar distances depicts genu valgum.

A normal knee has 5-7 degrees of physiological outward deviation (valgum). Any increase in angle can result in Genu valgum or knock knee where knees are abnormally approximated and the ankles are divergent.

Intermalleolar distance has been used to assess the degree of genu valgum. It is the distance between the medial malleoli in a standing patient with touching medial femoral condyles. Intermalleolar distances greater than 8 cm are considered pathologic.

Children start developing physiologic genu valgum by age 2, and it becomes most prominent between ages 3 to 4. After that, it typically decreases to a stable, slightly valgus position by age 7 years. Other causes include

* Bilateral Genu Valgum: Physiologic genu valgum, skeletal dysplasia, metabolic bone diseases, osteoarthritis, and rheumatoid arthritis.

* Unilateral Genu Valgum: Trauma, tumors, and infection.

Knee deformities are:

* Genu valgus (valgum) or knock knee - Knees are abnormally approximated and the ankles are divergent.

* Genu varus (varum) or bow knee - Knees are abnormally divergent and the ankles are approximated.

* Windswept deformity - Abnormal valgus deformity of one knee with varus of the other.

* Genu recurvatum - Hyperextension at the knee joint with backward bending.

Pearl PF0382: Important Clinical Features of Rickets

Pearl PF1660: Radiological features of rickets

Radiological features of rickets:

* Loss of provisional zone of calcification: earliest radiological finding of rickets.

* Delayed appearance of the epiphysis

* Widening of growth plate: normal width of growth is 2-4mm. It is increased in cases of rickets due to excessive accumulation of uncalcified osteoid at the growth plate.

* Cupping of metaphysis: normally metaphysis meets epiphysis as a smooth line of sclerosis. But in rickets the line is absent and the metaphyseal ends appear irregular and the cartilage accumulating in the growth plate creates a depression in the metaphysis causing cupping.

* Fraying: indistinct margins of the metaphysis

* Bowing of diaphysis, with thinning of cortices

* In healing rickets, zone of calcification becomes denser.

The above features are prominent at the growth plates where growth is greatest:

* Knee: distal femur, proximal tibia

* Wrist: especially the ulna

* Anterior rib ends: rachitic rosary

The below image shows bowing of legs in rickets.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An 80-year-old female patient was brought to the casualty with a history of slip and fall in the bathroom. She is having pain in the left hip and is unable to walk. She has no history of osteoarthritis. On examination, the left lower limb is shortened and externally rotated. X-ray findings are shown below. How will you manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hemiarthroplasty

The above clinical vignette along with with the X-ray is suggestive of a fracture of the neck of the femur and hemiarthroplasty is the best way to manage this patient.

Clinical features of a fracture of the neck of the femur:

* Painful movements of the hip joint

* Shortening and external rotation of the affected limb

* Tenderness in the hip

* Active straight leg raising is not possible

A plain radiograph of a fracture of the neck of the femur may show the following features:

* Fracture line in the neck of the femur

* External rotation of the femur with the lesser trochanter appearing more prominent

* Displacement of the greater trochanter

* Break in the trabecular stream

* Break in Shenton's line

Management:

* If the age is <65 years and if the patient presents within 3 weeks, then closed reduction with internal fixation with cancellous screws(Option A) is done.

* If a patient <65 years of age presents after 3 weeks, the vascular supply of the femur head is assessed by bone scanning or MRI. If it is vascular, the hip should be reconstructed by either osteotomy (McMurray's or Pauwel's)(Option D), or reconstruction procedures such as Meyers' operation(option B). If the head is not vascular, and the patient is young, the bipolar prosthesis(Hemiarthroplasty) is preferred.

* If the age of the patient is >65 years, then hemiarthroplasty(bipolar prosthesis) is preferred only if the acetabulum is normal(no osteoarthritis), otherwise, total hip replacement is done.

Pearl PF1182: Treatment of fracture neck of femur

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presented to the OPD with the findings. He had suffered a fall on an outstretched hand one year back. What is the diagnosis?
options: An undisplaced supracondylar fracture of humerus
Malunion of a supracondylar fracture of humerus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Malunion of a supracondylar fracture of humerus

The history of falling on an outstretched hand along with the gunstock deformity as seen in the image below are suggestive of malunion of a supracondylar fracture of the humerus.

Cubitus varus deformity or gun stock deformity is a complication of supracondylar humerus fracture that occurs due to malunion. When the distal fragment unites with an excessive backward tilt, there is hyperextension at the elbow.

Supracondylar fractures are the most common fractures in children younger than the age of 7 years. It typically occurs due to a fall on an outstretched arm. They can be of various types as listed below:

* Posterior displacement of distal fracture fragment occurs commonly and is an extension type of fracture.

* Anterior displacement of distal fracture fragment is less common and occurs due to a direct blow on a flexed elbow and is often unstable

* Lateral condylar fractures are due to a varus force on an extended elbow and may extend through the unossified portion of the capitellum into the joint space.

Other options:

Option A: An undisplaced fracture may show a triangular lucency like the sail of a yacht (sail sign), also called a fat pad sign. This is due to the fat pad around the elbow being pushed forward by the hematoma. Also, it would not present with the gun stock deformity.

Option C: The dislocated radial head would present with a discontinuity in the line drawn along the shaft of the proximal radius (the line should normally pass through the capitellum).

The image below shows an anterior dislocated radial head with calcification of the annular ligament:

Option D: Proximal humerus fractures are uncommon in children and will be pathological fractures (due to reasons such as the presence of a bone cyst)

The image below shows a radiograph showing a proximal humerus fracture with the involvement of a greater tubercle:

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with elbow deformity and forearm shortening after a fall. An X-ray was done and given below. What is the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Elbow dislocation

The given clinical history and X-ray are suggestive of elbow dislocation. X-ray shows posterior dislocation of the elbow joint.

Elbow dislocation is the most common dislocation in the pediatric age group and the second most common dislocation after the shoulder in adults.

Posterior dislocation is the commonest type of elbow dislocation. It frequently occurs due to a fall on the outstretched hands with the elbow slightly flexed. Other dislocations are postero-medial, postero-lateral, and divergent.

Anterior dislocation occurs when the elbow is flexed and there is a direct blow on the posterior aspect of the elbow joint.

Clinical features:

* The forearm appears shortened.

* Crepitus is absent.

* The three-point bony relationship is disrupted.

* Olecranon is above the intercondylar line

Elbow dislocation is an emergency and has to be reduced immediately. Closed reduction under general anaesthesia(GA) is attempted first. An above elbow POP slab is applied with 90º elbow flexion and mid-pronation for a period of 3 weeks after closed reduction under GA.

Stimson’s 2 step principles for closed reduction

* Step 1 - traction along the long axis of the humerus to counteract the contraction of biceps, triceps and brachialis

* Step 2 - traction along the long axis of the forearm to bring radius and ulna back into position
2 techniques in closed reduction

Prone technique - Grab the wrist of the injured arm. Apply traction and slight supination to the forearm. Using the other hand, apply pressure to the posterior aspect of the olecranon while the arm is pronated.

Supine technique - a helper stabilizes the humerus against the stretcher with both hands. Grasp the wrist, and apply slow, steady, inline traction, keeping the elbow slightly flexed and the wrist supinated

Complications:

* Early complications include neurovascular injury. Vascular injuries are rare and involve the brachial artery in open fractures associated with elbow dislocation.

* Late complications include myositis ossificans, recurrent dislocations, proximal radioulnar translocation, and ectopic calcifications

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young male who had a road traffic accident is brought to the emergency department. His left leg is shortened, internally rotated, and adducted. On examination, femoral artery pulsation is not felt. A plain radiograph of his hip was taken which is shown below. What is your diagnosis?
options: Fracture neck of femur with injury to femoral vessels
Anterior dislocation of hip with femoral artery injury
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Posterior dislocation of hip

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of posterior hip dislocation. In this condition, the leg will be in flexion, adduction, and internal rotation.

Posterior hip dislocation is the commonest type of hip dislocation accounting for about 80%  of the cases. It is commonly seen following dashboard injuries. The patient presents with flexion, adduction, and an internal rotation deformity.

Radiological findings include femoral head lying above and behind the acetabulum, femoral head appearing smaller than normal, lesser trochanter not visualized as the thigh is internally rotated and the femoral head and posterior acetabular wall fractures may also be seen

Sciatic nerve injury is seen in 10-20 % of cases with posterior hip dislocation. It is usually a neuropraxia type of injury and resolves spontaneously. The femoral artery pulsation is usually felt against the neck of the femur. Due to the posterior dislocation of the hip joint, the femoral vessels fall backwards and the pulsation of the femoral artery cannot be felt. This is called the vascular sign of Narath.

Anterior hip dislocation is less common than posterior hip dislocations and accounts for about 10-20% of all hip dislocations. This injury is usually sustained following a high-energy accident. The affected limb in this condition will be abducted, externally rotated, and slightly flexed.

Note: Although, vascular injuries are seen in posterior dislocations as well, they are most likely with anterior dislocation. This is because of the femoral artery lying anterior to the head

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The below image is of a femur bone. Which of the following muscles is attached to "A"?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iliopsoas

The image shows the posterior surface of the right femur and the structure marked "A" is the lesser trochanter where the iliopsoas muscle is attached.

The Iliopsoas comprises of Psoas major and Iliacus. They arise from the lumbar spine and the inner surface of the ilium bone respectively, and insert on the lesser trochanter. The iliopsoas cause flexion of the hip.

The femur can be divided into the proximal femur, shaft, and distal femur.

* The proximal femur consists of the head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters. The intertrochanteric line is present on the anterior surface at the junction of the neck and shaft of the femur while the intertrochanteric crest is present on the posterior surface. The lesser trochanter is the posteromedial projection of the femur arising posteroinferiorly from the neck-shaft junction.

* The shaft of the femur consists of linea aspera (bony crest present on the posterior surface), gluteal tuberosity, and pectineal line.

* The distal femur consists of the medial condyle, lateral condyle, intercondylar fossa, and patellar surface.

The image below shows attachments of various muscles over the posterior surface of the right femur.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following is not seen in the terrible triad of the elbow?
options: Fracture of the coronoid process of ulna
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fracture of the olecranon

The terrible triad of the elbow consists of three concurrent injuries: elbow dislocation, fracture of the radial head, and fracture of the coronoid process. Fracture of the olecranon is not part of the classic presentation of the terrible triad.

The terrible triad of elbow (also known as Hotchkiss triad) includes

* Posterior dislocation of the elbow

* Radial head fracture

* Fracture coronoid process of ulna

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency room following a bike accident. Examination reveals the right upper limb in abduction and external rotation. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anterior Dislocation of the Shoulder

The upper limb in abduction and external rotation and radiograph are both suggestive of anterior dislocation of the shoulder.

The AP view radiograph shows the disturbed articulation between the humeral head and glenoid fossa. The humeral head is seen below and medial to the glenoid socket. This suggests anterior dislocation of the shoulder joint. In young adults, the common cause for anterior dislocation is athletic injuries, while in older adults, falls are a more common cause.

Anterior dislocation is the most common among shoulder dislocations. It occurs due to a fall on the hands. The head of the humerus is driven forwards and tears the capsule resulting in an avulsion in the glenoid labrum (Bankart lesion). Sometimes, the posterolateral part of the head of the humerus is crushed resulting in the Hill-Sachs lesion.

The clinical features include severe pain and the patient usually supports his dislocated arm with the opposite arm. On examination, the arm is usually abducted, externally rotated and the lateral outline of the shoulder may be straightened and sometimes a prominent acromion process or a bulge below the clavicle may be appreciated.

The anteroposterior radiograph shows the humeral head lying below and medial to the glenoid socket. It may also show the Bankart lesion and the Hill-Sachs lesion.

Other Options:

Option A: Luxatio erecta is also known as inferior dislocation of shoulder. This is caused due to severe hyperabduction. The radiograph shows that the head of the humerus is present below the glenoid and the shaft is in an abducted position.

Option B:  Light bulb sign is seen on AP radiographs in the posterior dislocation shoulder. In posterior dislocation of the shoulder, the humerus rotates internally. This causes changes to the normal radiographic contour of the head of the humerus. The humerus appears similar to a lightbulb in AP views.

Pearl PF2105: Tests for anterior shoulder dislocation

Bryant’s test: Anterior axillary fold is at a lower level on the dislocated side.

Dugas test: The patient is made to place the hand on the opposite shoulder. The examiner then applies gentle pressure on the flexed elbow to make it touch the chest. In shoulder dislocation, the elbow cannot be made to touch the chest.

Hamilton ruler test: In a normal shoulder, a ruler (scale) placed on the lateral side of the arm will not touch the lateral condyle of the humerus and the acromion at the same time.

In anterior shoulder dislocation, the ruler will simultaneously touch the lateral condyle of the humerus and the acromion.

Callway Test: The vertical circumference of the axilla is increased on the dislocated side as compared to the normal side.

Pearl PF1173: Methods of reduction of shoulder dislocation

Kocher's technique - TEAM (Traction → External Rotation → Adduction → Medial Rotation)

Hippocratic method- Surgeon applies a firm and steady pull on the semi-abducted arm by keeping his foot on the axilla against the chest wall. The foot is used as the fulcrum.

Stimson's gravity technique: Patient is left prone and weight is attached to the elbow or wrist on the affected side. Gravity stretches the muscle and reduction occurs in 15-20 minutes.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A carpenter presents with bilateral knee pain and fluctuating swelling in the front of the knee. There is inflammation and tenderness over his knee. MRI of knee is given. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Housemaid Bursitis

The fluctuating swelling in the front of the knee as well as the image, both suggest Housemaid Bursitis.

Housemaid's knee is nothing but prepatellar bursitis and is seen in the lower half of patella and upper half of ligamentum patella. Suprapatellar bursa always communicates with the knee joint.

Lower limb major bursitis:

* Prepatellar Bursitis (Housemaid's Knee)

* Infrapatellar bursitis (Clergyman's knee) (option C)

* Trochanteric Bursitis (Above hip abductor)
The image shows a sagittal section through the left knee joint (lateral aspect) with bursae.

Other options:

Option A: Olecranon bursitis, also known as draughtsman's elbow (or student's elbow or miner's elbow). Olecranon bursitis is a chronic inflammation of the olecranon bursa, as a result of repetitive minor injuries. It is seen in people who tend to keep their elbow rubbed against the desk. The constant friction against the olecranon bursa can lead to the development of bursitis.

Option D: Gout is characterized by an inflammatory reaction that results in the formation of gouty tophi and arthropathy when monosodium urate (MSU) crystals are deposited in the soft tissue and joints. A definitive diagnosis necessitates the microscopic identification of MSU crystals through joint fluid aspiration.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with backache, night sweats, an evening increase in temperature, and unintentional weight loss. Laboratory tests reveal an increase in CRP and ESR levels. An MRI is provided below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pott's spine

The given spine MRI shows a patient with Pott's spine. The image depicts sagittal T1W (A) and T2W (B) images in a patient with spinal tuberculosis showing a well-defined, round lesion (arrow) with T1 hypointensity and T2 iso-hypointensity.

* Pott's disease, also known as tuberculous spondylitis, refers to the vertebral body and intervertebral disc involvement in tuberculosis (TB).

* The spine is the most frequent location of musculoskeletal TB, and commonly related symptoms are back pain and lower limb weakness/paraplegia.

* The spine is involved due to hematogenous spread via the venous plexus of Batson.

* There is usually a slow collapse of one or usually more vertebral bodies, which spreads underneath the longitudinal ligaments.

* This results in an acute kyphotic or "gibbus" deformity.

* This angulation, coupled with epidural granulation tissue and bony fragments, can lead to cord compression.

Radiographic Features:

Features include irregularity of both the endplate and anterior aspect of the vertebral bodies, with bone marrow edema and enhancement seen on MRI:

* T1: hypointense marrow in adjacent vertebrae

* T2: hyperintense marrow, disc, soft tissue infection

* T1 C+ (Gd): marrow, subligamentous, discal, dural enhancement

The paraspinal collections are typically well-circumscribed, with fluid centres and well-defined enhancing margins.

Other options:

Option A: Ankylosing spondylitis: shows Squaring and bridging of the vertebral body, leading to a bamboo spine appearance.

Option B: Multiple myeloma is the malignant production of plasma cells that results in bone pain or fractures, renal failure, increased susceptibility to infections, anemia, hypercalcemia, and manifestations of hyperviscosity. Radiography shows multiple well-defined, punched-out lytic lesions of various sizes scattered throughout the skull, giving the raindrop skull appearance.

Option C: Pyogenic spondylitis denotes infections impacting different components of the spine, including the vertebrae, intervertebral discs, paraspinal soft tissue, or epidural space. This umbrella term covers conditions such as vertebral osteomyelitis, spondylodiscitis, and epidural abscess.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A person presents with complaints of clawing of the 4th and 5th fingers. Along with it, there is sensory loss at tips of these fingers. What structure is most likely to be damaged?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ulnar nerve

The given description is of a clawing of 4th and 5th finger with loss of sensation in the tips of these fingers are classically seen in case of an ulnar nerve injury.

The ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals, adductor pollicis, interossei, and hypothenar muscles in the hand. The lumbricals are primarily responsible for the extension at the interphalangeal joints. Therefore, in ulnar nerve palsy, there is clawing of the medial two fingers.

In ulnar nerve palsy, only the medial two fingers develop clawing, while in a combined median and ulnar nerve palsy, all four fingers develop clawing.

The following tests are done to test the integrity of the ulnar nerve:

* Egawa's test - In a positive test, due to the weakness of the dorsal interossei, side-to-side movements of the middle finger is weak.

* Book test or Froment's sign - The patient is asked to hold a book between the thumb and index finger while the examiner attempt to pull it forcefully. In case of an ulnar nerve injury, the adductor pollicis is paralyzed and the patient attempts to hold the book with the flexor pollicis longus muscle supplied by the median nerve.

* Card test - In the case of weak palmar interossei, the examiner can pull out the card with ease.

Other options

Option B - In radial nerve palsy, the patient presents with a wrist drop due to paralyzed wrist extensors. In high lesions, there is sensory loss on the dorsum of the hand over the anatomical stuff box.

Option C - In median nerve injury, paralysis of opponens pollicis muscle leads to ape thumb deformity. A pointing finger deformity can also be seen due to paralyzed flexors of the fingers.

Option D - The anterior interosseous nerve supplies the flexor digitorum profundus muscle of the index finger and damage to the nerve prevents flexion of the index finger.
