Pearl PF1196: Seddon's classification of nerve injuries

Seddon's classification includes 3 groups

1. Neurapraxia
2. Axonotmesis
3. Neurotmesis

Neurapraxia:

Reversible physiologic conduction block. Occurs due to mechanical pressure causing segmental demyelination.

E.g.,Saturday night palsy, torniquet, and crutch palsy

Axonotmesis:

Axonal interruption. Conduction is lost but the nerve is in continuity and neural tubes are intact.

E.g.,Closed fractures and dislocations

Neurotmesis:

Division of the nerve trunk. Endoneurial tube destruction also occurs.

E.g., Complete section of nerve in open fractures

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A person presents with complaints of numbness, tingling and paresthesias of the thumb, index finger and middle finger. There is numbness at the dorsum of the base of the thumb as well. What structure is most likely to be damaged?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Median nerve

Patient presents with pain and paresthesia over the lateral 3 and a half digits and numbness at the dorsum of the base of the thumb, both of which are indicative of a median nerve injury.

There may be weakness of thumb opposition. In chronic cases, the thenar eminence is wasted. Carpal tunnel syndrome is a common cause and can be associated with rheumatoid arthritis, pregnancy, chronic renal failure, acromegaly, hypothyroidism and gout. The diagnosis is usually made on clinical grounds but nerve conduction studies can confirm the diagnosis.

Median nerve injuries:

Distal injury: Thus an injury to the distal median nerve affects the 1st and 2nd lumbricals sparing the flexor digitorum profundus. This causes hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints, involving the index and middle fingers. This attitude of the hand known as the median claw hand may be seen at rest and is more pronounced on attempting to extend the fingers (attitude is similar to proximal ulnar injury).

Proximal injury: Since the opposing flexor digitorum profundus of the 2nd and 3rd digit that causes the clawing is also affected, the clawing of the hand is less pronounced in distal injuries of the ulnar nerve. The deficits present during voluntary flexion of the digits. Thus, on attempting to make a fist, the flexion of the 2nd and 3rd digits is affected while the 4th and 5th digits are normal giving the Benediction hand sign.

In both cases of median nerve palsy, there is loss of sensations on lateral 3½ digits including the nail beds and distal phalanges on the dorsum of the hand.

Tinel's sign is positive where percussing over the median nerve reproduces symptoms. Phalen's test is positive where the symptoms are reproduced by holding the wrists in full flexion with the dorsum of the hands pressed together.

Other Options:

Option A: Injury to the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. It results in the loss of function of both flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) and flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS). Hence, the index finger sticks out when the patient is asked to clasp their hand.

Option B: In ulnar nerve palsy, only the medial two fingers develop clawing, while in a combined median and ulnar nerve palsy, all four fingers develop clawing.

Option C:  In radial nerve palsy, the patient presents with 'wrist drop' in case of paralyzed wrist extensors, and 'finger drop' when extensor digitorum is paralyzed. When there is compression in the axilla, radial nerve palsy is called Saturday night palsy. There is paralysis of the triceps, and weakness of the wrist and hand. In high lesions, there is sensory loss on the dorsum of the hand over the anatomical stuff box.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the type of epiphysis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pressure Epiphysis

The image depicts the distal end of the tibia which is an example of a pressure epiphysis.

The distal tibial epiphysis, near the ankle joint, is a pressure epiphysis because it primarily bears weight and compressive forces rather than muscular forces.

Pressure epiphysis is articular in nature and takes part in the transmission of weight. Examples are the head of the femur, the lower end of radius, etc.

Other options:

Options A: Tubercles of humerus and trochanters of femur are examples of traction epiphysis because these are the site of major muscle attachments.

Option C: An avulsion epiphysis is a small, separate ossification center that develops at sites where major tendons or ligaments attach to bone, forming due to the pulling forces (traction) of these attachments - common examples include the lesser trochanter of the femur (where psoas major attaches), greater trochanter (gluteal muscles attachment), and tibial tuberosity (patellar tendon attachment).

Option D: An aberrant epiphysis is an accessory ossification center that appears near a main epiphysis but remains separate and typically doesn't contribute to longitudinal growth - examples include the os trigonum behind the talus, os subfibulare near the lateral malleolus, and os tibiale externum at the navicular tuberosity; the key distinction is that avulsion epiphyses form due to mechanical forces at attachment sites.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the type of splint.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bohler Braun splint

The given image shows Bohler Braun splint used for unilateral leg traction.

* The proximal pulley is used to prevent foot drop.

* The 2nd pulley is used for traction in line with the hip.

* The 3rd pulley is used for traction in line with foot.

Other options:

Option A: Thomas splint is used for tibial fractures.

Parts of Thomas splint

* Outer bar

* Inner bar

* Ring

The outer bar has a curvature near its junction to ring to accommodate greater trochanter.

Option B: The image shows a foot abduction orthosis called Dennin Browne splint which is used for correction of CTEV and club foot.

Option D: Cock up splint is a wrist hand orthosis used for radial nerve palsy.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient presenting with a bone tumor showing a sunburst appearance on imaging?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteosarcoma

A bone tumor with a sunburst appearance on imaging is most likely osteosarcoma.

Osteosarcoma is the most common non-hematologic primary malignancy of bone. It occurs most commonly in the second decade of life. It is typically metaphyseal. The distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus are the commonly involved sites.

In osteosarcoma, the tumor lifts the periosteum and incites an intense periosteal reaction. The periosteal reaction is irregular and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have a sunburst (sunray) appearance on X-ray.

Other options:

Option A: Osteoclastoma or Giant cell tumor is commonly seen in the age group of 20-40 years with a slight female preponderance. The distal end of the femur is the most common location followed by the proximal tibia and distal radius.

Radiographic findings:

* Eccentrically located solitary lytic lesion in the epiphysis

* Soap bubble appearance

* Periosteal new bone formation is absent.

Option B: Osteoid Osteoma

The image shows presence of metadiaphyseal cortical osteoid osteoma involving the upper end of the femur with radiolucent nidus surrounded by cortical sclerosis.

Nidus of osteoid osteoma is present in the cortex and hence CT scan will be the best investigation to diagnose osteoid osteoma.

Image:

* Black arrow - Nidus

* White arrow - Cortical sclerosis

Option D: Ewing's sarcoma is a primary malignant tumor of the bone commonly involving the age group of 4-25 years involving the diaphysis of the long bones like the femur, tibia, fibula, and humerus.

X-ray shows onion-peel appearance due to deposition of periosteal reaction in layers is the typical finding.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 17-year-old boy presents to the clinic with complaints of a painless lump on the lateral aspect of his left knee. The radiograph of the patient is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteochondroma

The given radiograph and clinical vignette suggest the diagnosis of osteochondroma.

Osteochondromas are benign bone tumors that present commonly in the adolescent age group. They usually present as painless masses in long bones like the femur or humerus. They are seen as well-defined bony protuberances which may be pedunculated or sessile. Pedunculated osteochondromas point away from the joint, towards the diaphysis. The cortex and cancellous bone of osteochondroma blend with that of the host bone. MRI shows a classical cartilaginous cap.

Osteochondromas usually grow with skeletal maturity and stop once growth stops. They rarely undergo malignant transformation.

Treatment is not indicated if the lesion does not produce symptoms. Excision can be done for large lesions with local pressure effects.

Other options:

Option A: Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia with the proliferation of plasma cells derived from a single clone. It is associated with increased osteoclast activity with suppression of osteoblast activity, causing punched-out lytic lesions in the bone and hypercalcemia.

Option B: Chondroblastoma is a benign tumor and presents as a painful mass that causes effusion or stiffness. On x-ray, they are seen as round or oval lytic lesions in the epiphysis. The bony cortex is not breached but can appear expanded. The common sites are the ends of long bones. Microscopically, chondroblastoma consists of a sheet of chondroblasts embedded in the chondroid matrix. The calcification is often present and surrounds individual cells giving the appearance of ‘chicken wire.’

Option D: Osteoid osteoma is a benign tumor formed of osteoid and woven bone. It is common in men and most commonly occurs in the diaphysis of the femur. It is characterized by night pains relieved by medication. Nidus of osteoid osteoma is seen in the cortex and hence CT is the investigation of choice

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy presents to the OPD with the following findings. On examination, there is high-riding scapula with medial rotation on the left. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sprengel deformity

The image shows an upward elevation of the left scapula relative to the thoracic cage. This is characteristically seen in Sprengel deformity.

Sprengel deformity is a congenital upward elevation of the scapula. It is due to the failure of the scapula to descend completely in embryonic life.

The affected scapula is smaller, shaped differently, abnormally high, and somewhat prominent. Shoulder movements are usually painless. Abduction and elevation of shoulders may be limited due to fixation of the scapula.

The Cavendish classification is used to grade the severity of Sprengel deformity.

If the deformity is mild, no treatment is required. In severe deformity, surgery may be indicated. These procedures include:

* Green procedure

* Woodward procedure

* Mears procedure

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after sustaining a fall onto an outstretched hand. The following cast was applied to the patient. What fracture did the patient suffer from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scaphoid fracture

The cast applied to a patient in the glass-holding position is known as the scaphoid cast/glass-holding cast. It is used to treat scaphoid fractures.

To apply a scaphoid cast, the wrist is held in slight dorsiflexion and the thumb is in abduction and slight flexion, as if a glass is being held between the index finger and thumb. It extends from just below the elbow to just proximal to the metacarpal necks of the digits. On the thumb, the cast extends to just proximal to the interphalangeal joint.

Scaphoid fracture presents with pain and swelling over the radial aspect of the wrist. A fall on an outstretched hand could result in such a fracture. The fracture can be confirmed (when an x-ray does not show a fracture) if there is pain elicited in the anatomical snuff box on the radial border of the wrist.

An oblique x-ray of the wrist should be able to show a scaphoid fracture.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A six-year-old child presented with the given deformity. Identify the deformity.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cubitus valgus

The image shows the cubitus valgus deformity of left elbow most probably arising as a complication of lateral condyle fracture humerus which the patient had 3 years back.

Treatment of cubitus valgus is Medial closed wedge osteotomy or lateral open wedge osteotomy.

Option A: Cubitus varus deformity is also called gunstock deformity. It happens due to the malunion of supracondylar fracture in childhood. Injury to the brachial artery is an important complication.

Option C: Coxa vara is a hip deformity characterized by a reduced angle (less than 120 degrees) between the femoral neck and the femoral shaft.

OptionD : Coxa valga is a hip condition where the angle between the femoral neck and the femoral shaft exceeds 135 degrees.

A combination of coxa vara in one leg and coxa valga in the other (Wind-swept deformity) is seen in rickets

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which test is being performed to detect fixed flexion deformity at hip?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thomas test

Thomas test is used to detect fixed flexion deformity of the hip.

Flexion deformity is seen in the initial stages of the disease. The patient keeps the hip in flexion as this is the position of ease and maximum joint capacity. Soft tissue contractures convert this into a fixed flexion deformity, making locomotion impossible.

In an effort to bring the limb on the ground and to make locomotion possible, the lumbar spine undergoes exaggerated lordosis and thus conceals the fixed flexion deformity. This is revealed by the Thomas test. The easy passage of the examiner's hand between the bed and the back of the patient is considered as a positive test as normally this is not possible.

Other options:

* Trendelenburg test is used to assess the weakness or paralysis of gluteus medius muscle.

* Telescopy test: To asses the stability of the hip joint. Positive telescopy test indicates hip dislocations or fracture neck of femur.

* Ober's test is used in physical examination to identify the tightness of the iliotibial band.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 17-year-old male patient presents with dull aching pain over the back of his ankle. There is tenderness on firm palpation of the swelling. The following findings are seen on X-ray. What is the likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Exostosis

According to the clinical scenario and given X-ray, Exostosis of the bone is the most likely diagnosis.

Exostoses can cause chronic pain ranging from mild to debilitatingly severe, depending on the shape, size, and location of the lesion. It is most commonly found in places like the ribs, where small bone growths form, but sometimes larger growths can grow on places like the ankles, knees, shoulders, elbows and hips. Very rarely are they on the skull. Exostoses can be seen in different types: calcaneal spurs, osteomyelitis, Charcot foot, osteochondroma, and hereditary multiple exostoses.

In osteochondroma, the tumour stops enlarging in size once there is a cessation of growth at the epiphyseal plate. It appears as a small bony protrusion at metaphysis on X-ray. They are benign and rarely transform into chondrosarcomas. They are commonly seen around the knee joint (distal femur) or foot.

Option A: Chondrosarcoma are the second most common primary malignant tumors that occurs in any site of the bone. It presents in 3rd to 7th decade of life and is slow growing, with deep pain and/or shows an enlarging mass. Most commonly involves proximal femur, pelvis and proximal humerus.

X-ray features: Large, intraosseous and osteolytic tumors. Irregular and granular calcifications present which shows a characteristic “honeycomb” or “popcorn”appearance.

Option B: Osteoclastoma has a soap bubble appearance on X-ray and typically affects individuals 20-40 years of age. Axial skeleton involvement is not common

Option D: X-ray features of osteosarcoma: Ill-defined, bone forming lesion showing characteristic Codman’s triangle due to periosteal reaction . Sunburst appearance when the periosteum does not have enough time to lay down a new layer.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 19-year-old man presented with progressive swelling of the lower end of the femur. X-ray of this patient shows a Codman triangle. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteosarcoma

The given clinical scenario of a young patient with a tumour in the distal femur with a Codmnan's triangle on X-ray suggests a probable diagnosis of osteosarcoma.

Osteosarcoma is the most common non-hematologic primary malignancy of bone. It occurs most commonly in the second decade of life. It is typically metaphyseal. The distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus are common sites.

In osteosarcoma, the tumour lifts the periosteum and incites an intense periosteal reaction. The periosteal reaction is irregular and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have a sunburst (sunray) appearance on x-ray.

The x-ray would show the following features.

* Irregular destruction in the metaphysis is overshadowed by the formation of new bone

* Lifting of the periosteum due to the formation of new bone inciting a periosteal reaction

* Bone formation along the blood vessels within the tumour centrifugally gives rise to a sunburst (sunray) appearance on the radiograph.

Treatment: Osteosarcoma is treated by neoadjuvant chemotherapy, wide excision or radical surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. Since here safe margins are difficult to achieve limb ablation is done.

The goal of neoadjuvant and adjuvant chemotherapy is to treat micrometastasis.

T-10 protocol of chemotherapy is used in the management of osteosarcoma. It involves:

* High-dose methotrexate and Citrovorum factor rescue

* Adriamycin

* BCD (bleomycin, cyclophosphamide, dactinomycin/doxorubicin)

Option A: Aneurysmal bone cysts are blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septae. X-ray shows expansile lytic lesions in the metaphyses of the upper tibia.

Option B: Ewing Sarcoma- lesion with poorly marginated edges in the diaphysis of the bone. The lamellated periosteal reaction in diaphysis is suggestive of Ewing’s sarcoma which is a highly radiosensitive tumour.

Option D: Osteoid osteoma is a benign tumour which occurs in the diaphyses of the femur. Classically, the pain is relieved after using NSAID. Codman's triangle is not seen.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 24-year old male stated that he had fallen with his thumb extended and presented with a painful, swollen thumb. The X-ray image is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bennett fracture

The X-ray shows an intra-articular, two-part fracture of the base of the first metacarpal bone known as Bennett fracture.

Option A: Rolando fracture is an intraarticular comminuted fracture of the base of the first metacarpal bone, with a ‘T’ or ‘Y’ configuration.

Option B: Avulsion fracture of the ulnar base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb is known as Gamekeeper’s fracture.

A gamekeeper thumb, also known as a skier’s thumb is an injury to the ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) of the first metacarpophalangeal joint. The UCL may get ruptured or avulsed from its site of insertion on the base of the proximal phalanx. Injury is usually caused by a fall on an outstretched hand with radial and palmar abduction. Patients present with pain, swelling, and ecchymosis around the first metacarpophalangeal joint.

Option D: Epibasal fracture of thumb, also known as pseudo Bennett’s fracture is a two-part extra-articular fracture of the proximal first metacarpal bone. These fractures are stable and do not usually require surgical correction.

Pearl PF1179: Important injuries of the hand

Gamekeeper's thumb: It is an injury of the thumb leading to avulsion, rupture or damage of the Ulnar collateral ligament. It is commonly seen in gamekeepers and also following a fall on an outstretched hand.

Mallet finger/baseball finger: It is a disruption to the extensor tendon over the DIP joint. It occurs when a collision with a hard object (e.g., a ball) forces it to flex more than its normal range of motion.

Jersey finger: It is an avulsion injury of the flexor digitorum profundus at the insertion of the base of the distal phalanx. The ring finger most commonly involved.

Trigger finger: A nodule on the flexor tendon prevents it to move along the A1 pulley. This causes the finger to be stuck in a flexed position.

Boxer's fracture: It is a break in the neck of the metacarpal. It is caused by striking an object with a closed fist, as seen in boxing. The little finger is the most commonly affected.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 25-year-old female presented with pain in her right thigh and hips for three months. She was suspected to have hip tuberculosis. On examination, discrepancy in the length of her right limb was noticed. Which of the following stages of TB presents with apparent lengthening of the limb?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stage of synovitis

Apparent lengthening of the limb is seen in the stage of synovitis.

Tuberculosis of the hip occurs in three main stages based on the clinical manifestations:

Stages
Key findings
Position of the affected limb
Length of the affected limb

Stage 1
(Stage of synovitis)

There is effusion in the joint.

Patient usually does not present in this early stage

Flexion, abduction, external rotation
Apparent lengthening as the pelvis tilts downwards to compensate for the abduction

Stage 2
(Stage of arthritis)

Spasm of the powerful muscles around the hip.

Flexion, adduction, internal rotation
Apparent shortening as the pelvis tilts upwards to compensate for the adduction

Stage 3
(Stage of erosion)

Articular cartilage is destroyed

Acetabulum is eroded

Pathological dislocation/ subluxation of the hip

Flexion, adduction, internal rotation (exaggerated deformities)
True shortening as there is actual destruction of the bone

Some important radiological signs occurring in established cases of TB of the hip:

* Haziness: earliest radiological sign

* Lytic lesion

* Reduction of joint space and irregular outline of articular ends: because of the destruction of cartilage

* Wandering acetabulum: head may be lying out of the acetabulum

* Pestle and mortar appearance: sometimes, the acetabulum gets enlarged and deepened with the deformed head shifted medially.

* Sclerosis around the hip: seen if the disease is in the healing stage

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 26-year male presented to OPD with a deformity of the left hand. He had a past history of RTA in which he had injured the same limb 6 months back. There was hypothenar muscle atrophy and a fixed deformity where on opening his hand he is not able to extend the medial two fingers. Which of the following nerves is likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ulnar nerve

The given description is of a claw hand with hypothenar muscle atrophy classically seen in case of an ulnar nerve injury.

The ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals, adductor pollicis, interossei, and hypothenar muscles in the hand. The lumbricals are primarily responsible for the extension at the interphalangeal joints. Therefore, in ulnar nerve palsy, there is clawing of the medial two fingers.

In ulnar nerve palsy, only the medial two fingers develop clawing, while in a combined median and ulnar nerve palsy, all four fingers develop clawing.

The following tests are done to test the integrity of the ulnar nerve:

* Egawa's test - In a positive test, due to the weakness of the dorsal interossei, side-to-side movements of the middle finger is weak.

* Book test or Froment's sign - The patient is asked to hold a book between the thumb and index finger while the examiner attempt to pull it forcefully. In case of an ulnar nerve injury, the adductor pollicis is paralyzed and the patient attempts to hold the book with the flexor pollicis longus muscle supplied by the median nerve.

* Card test - In the case of weak palmar interossei, the examiner can pull out the card with ease.

Other options

Option B - In radial nerve palsy, the patient presents with a wrist drop due to paralyzed wrist extensors. In high lesions, there is sensory loss on the dorsum of the hand over the anatomical stuff box.

Option C - In median nerve injury, paralysis of opponens pollicis muscle leads to ape thumb deformity. A pointing finger deformity can also be seen due to paralyzed flexors of the fingers.

Option D - Long thoracic nerve supplies the serratus anterior muscle. Patients with injury to this nerve present with winging of the scapula.

Pearl PF1196: Seddon's classification of nerve injuries

Seddon's classification includes 3 groups

1. Neurapraxia
2. Axonotmesis
3. Neurotmesis

Neurapraxia:

Reversible physiologic conduction block. Occurs due to mechanical pressure causing segmental demyelination.

E.g.,Saturday night palsy, torniquet, and crutch palsy

Axonotmesis:

Axonal interruption. Conduction is lost but the nerve is in continuity and neural tubes are intact.

E.g.,Closed fractures and dislocations

Neurotmesis:

Division of the nerve trunk. Endoneurial tube destruction also occurs.

E.g., Complete section of nerve in open fractures

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presented to your OPD with genu varum and softening of skull bones. There is bony depression over the chest. What is the most likely deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin D deficiency

The clinical scenario with genu varum, craniotabes and Harrison groove of the chest with the given lab parameters suggests rickets caused by vitamin D deficiency.

Rickets occurs due to a nutritional deficiency in vitamin D. Decrease in vitamin D levels leads to decreased calcium and phosphate due to reduced absorption. The decreased calcium stimulates increased parathyroid hormone(PTH) production. ALP level is increased as it is involved in bone mineralization.

Clinical features of rickets include:

* General features include malnourishment, abdominal distension, proximal muscle weakness, etc.

* Head: Softening of the skull bones, called craniotabes, delayed closure of fontanels.

* Chest: Rachitic rosary, i.e. widening of the costochondral junctions that give the feeling of rosary beads on palpation. Harrison's groove, a horizontal groove in the lower chest, may appear from the inward pull of the softened ribs by the diaphragm during respiration.

* Vertebral column abnormalities like scoliosis, kyphosis, and lordosis

* In the distal extremities widening of the wrists and ankles, varus/ valgus deformities, windswept deformity (valgus on the side and varus on the contralateral side), anterior tibial bowing.

The laboratory findings in rickets show normal/decreased serum calcium, decreased phosphorous, elevated PTH, and increased ALP levels

Metabolic bone disorders due to nutritional deficiencies include:

* Vitamin D deficiency leads to Rickets- in children

* Osteomalacia- in adults

* Secondary hyperparathyroidism

* Vitamin C deficiency leads to scurvy

Other options:

Option A: Vitamin A deficiency- can lead to night blindness and recurrent childhood infections- diarrhoea, and respiratory infections.

Option C: Vitamin C deficiency - can lead to scurvy which has manifestations due to poor collagen synthesis- dry skin, poor wound healing, swelling of the knee and ankle, and radiographic findings of a radiolucent band (Trümmerfeld zone) under a white line of Fränkel.

Option D: Vitamin K deficiency- can be seen in neonates due to non-colonised gut, and in adults with chronic antibiotics-lead to manifestations of clotting disorders- purpura, ecchymoses.

Pearl PF1660: Radiological features of rickets

Radiological features of rickets:

* Loss of provisional zone of calcification: earliest radiological finding of rickets.

* Delayed appearance of the epiphysis

* Widening of growth plate: normal width of growth is 2-4mm. It is increased in cases of rickets due to excessive accumulation of uncalcified osteoid at the growth plate.

* Cupping of metaphysis: normally metaphysis meets epiphysis as a smooth line of sclerosis. But in rickets the line is absent and the metaphyseal ends appear irregular and the cartilage accumulating in the growth plate creates a depression in the metaphysis causing cupping.

* Fraying: indistinct margins of the metaphysis

* Bowing of diaphysis, with thinning of cortices

* In healing rickets, zone of calcification becomes denser.

The above features are prominent at the growth plates where growth is greatest:

* Knee: distal femur, proximal tibia

* Wrist: especially the ulna

* Anterior rib ends: rachitic rosary

The below image shows bowing of legs in rickets.

Pearl PF0382: Important Clinical Features of Rickets

Pearl PF1801: Radiological features of scurvy

Radiological features of scurvy:

* Generalised osteopenia

* Pencil-point cortex: Cortical thinning

* Periosteal reaction due to subperiosteal hemorrhage

* Scorbutic rosary: Expansion of the costochondral junctions

* Hemarthrosis

* Wimberger ring: Circular, opaque radiological shadow surrounding epiphyseal centers of ossification, which may result from bleeding

* Frenkel line: Dense zone of provisional calcification

* Trummerfeld zone: Lucent metaphyseal band underlying Frankel line

* Pelken spur: Metaphyseal spurs which result in cupping of the metaphysis

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 33-year-old male patient was brought to the trauma centre following a road traffic accident. He was walking on the street when a car hit him from the side and severely injured his left knee. An X-ray of the knee joint showing distal femur and proximal tibia-fibula was done. Identify the given fracture:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bumper fracture

The clinical vignette and the x-ray evidence a Bumper fracture.

Bumper fracture is the fracture of the tibial plateau resulting from impact with a car bumper. It is due to a forced valgus injury of the knee when the car hits from the side.

Other options:

Option A: Patellar Sleeve Fractures are rare injuries seen in children between 8 and 12 years of age characterized by separation of the cartilage "sleeve" from the ossified patella.

Option C: Pilon fracture refers to a comminuted intra-articular fracture of the distal tibia. These fractures are most often due to high-energy trauma such as a motor vehicle accident or a fall from a height

option D Chauffeur fracture:  The image shows a fracture of the radial styloid process, i.e., Chauffeur fracture. It is caused either by direct trauma to the wrist or traumatic radial deviation of the wrist

Pearl PF1909: Named fractures of the upper limb

Colle's fracture: Extra-articular fracture of the distal radius with dorsal angulation of the distal bone fragment.

Galeazzi fracture-dislocation: Fracture of the lower third of the radius and subluxation of the distal radio-ulnar joint.

Monteggia fracture-dislocation: Fracture of the shaft of the ulna with dislocation of a proximal radio-ulnar joint.

Barton’s fracture: Intra-articular fracture of the distal radius.

Rolando's fracture: Intra-articular comminuted fracture of the base of the first metacarpal with a T or Y configuration.

Smith's fracture: Reverse Colles' fracture. Extra-articular fracture of the distal one-third of the radius with palmar or ventral displacement (Image below).

Chauffeur's fracture or the Hutchinson fracture: Fracture of the radial styloid.

Essex–Lopresti lesion: Fracture of the radial head with disruption of the interosseous membrane and distal radial ulnar joint ligaments.

Nightstick fracture: Isolated fracture of radial or ulnar bone.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with decreased hearing. The skull radiograph shows the following appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Paget’s disease

The given clinical scenario and cotton wool skull appearance on the radiograph are suggestive of Paget's disease.

Paget's disease is a disease of bone remodelling. Normally, osteoclasts remove the old bones while osteoblasts form new bones. In this disease,  osteoclasts are more active than osteoblasts. leading to more bone absorption than normal. The osteoblasts try to keep up by making new bone, but they overreact and make excess bone that is abnormally large, deformed and fits together haphazardly.

Increased bone formation in Paget's disease may lead to the narrowing of the foramina of the skull. This causes compression of the cranial nerves which may lead to deafness, as seen in this patient. Deafness due to the narrowing of cranial nerve foramina is also seen in osteopetrosis. It can be differentiated from Paget's disease by the absence of lytic lesions of the bone.

Other skull radiological findings in Paget's disease:

* Osteoporosis circumscripta - Large well-defined lytic lesions involving the inner part of the outer table of the skull with an intact inner table

* Diploic widening

* Tam o' Shanter sign

Option A: In thalassemia, X-ray of the skull will show crew cut appearance.

Option C: In the skull X-ray, Multiple myeloma shows multiple well-defined, punched-out lytic lesions of various sizes scattered throughout the skull, giving the raindrop skull appearance, which is seen in multiple myeloma.

Option D: In Eosinophilic granuloma, the characteristic skull finding is the geographic skull and solitary or multiple lytic lesions, with a bevelled-edge appearance.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young child presented to the emergency with pain in the right hand after falling from a height. An X-ray of the distal forearm and hand was done. The radiological image shows a physeal plate injury with a fracture extending to the metaphyses with the sparing of the epiphysis. What is the type of Salter-Harris physeal injury mentioned above?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II

The type of Salter-Harris injury mentioned above is type II injury.

Type II fracture is an intraarticular fracture. In a type II Salter harris fracture, the fracture line traverses the epiphyseal plate and then into the metaphyses. This damages the growth plate and results in growth disturbance.

Salter-Harris classified epiphyseal injuries into 5 types as mentioned below.

Pearl PF2000: Types of Salter–Harris fractures- Mnemonic

There are nine types of Salter-Harris fractures. Among these, types I to V are more common.

The mnemonic "SALTER" can be used to help remember the first five types.

TYPE
MNEMONIC
DESCRIPTION

Type I
S = Slip/straight across
Transverse fracture through the growth plate

Type II
A = Away
The fracture lies away from the joint. A fracture through the growth plate and the metaphysis, sparing the epiphysis

Type III
L = Lower
The fracture is below the physis in the epiphysis.

Type IV
TE = Through Everything
A fracture through all three elements of the bone, the growth plate, metaphysis, and epiphysis

Type V
R = Rammed (crushed)
A compression fracture of the growth plate

Rarer types VI to IX have been added subsequently.

* Type VI - Injury to the perichondral structures

* Type VII - Isolated injury to the epiphyseal plate

* Type VIII - Isolated injury to the metaphysis, with a potential injury related to endochondral ossification

* Type IX - Injury to the periosteum that may interfere with membranous growth

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy presents with chronic swelling and pain over the upper tibia.There is no history of trauma. His radiographic image is shown below. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Brodie's abscess

The given clinical scenario of a child with prolonged swelling and pain over the upper tibia, along with a radiograph showing a lytic lesion with a dense sclerotic rim and minimal periosteal reaction, suggests the diagnosis of Brodie's abscess.

Brodie's abscess is a localized form of subacute osteomyelitis that occurs when organisms of low virulence infect an immunocompetent host. The abscess is walled off by the thickening of the surrounding bone trabeculae. It most commonly involves the metaphysis of the proximal tibia and distal femur.

The patient is typically a child or adolescent experiencing prolonged pain near a large joint for several weeks or months. Symptoms may include a limp, slight swelling, muscle wasting, and localized tenderness.

The typical radiographic finding is a circumscribed, round or oval radiolucent cavity measuring 1-2 cm in diameter, surrounded by a halo of sclerosis, with minimal or no periosteal reaction. The radioisotope scan shows markedly increased activity. MRI may be helpful in diagnosis. Open biopsy with curettage is indicated if there is any doubt in the diagnosis.

Differential diagnoses include:

* Cystic tuberculosis

* Eosinophilic granuloma

* Osteoid osteoma

* Ewing's sarcoma

Treatment:

* Immobilization and antibiotics (flucloxacillin and fusidic acid) intravenous for 4-5 days, followed by oral administration for another 6 weeks; healing may take up to 12 months

* Curettage is needed if the x-rays show no healing after conservative management.

The following X-ray and MRI images show Brodie's abscess of the radius in a patient.

Other options:

Option A: A Simple bone cyst is a solitary, usually unilocular cystic bone cavity lined by a fibrous membrane and filled with serous or serosanguinous fluid. Majority of cases are asymptomatic, and found incidentally.

Option B: Osteoid osteoma is a benign tumor formed of osteoid and woven bone. It is common in men and most commonly occurs in the diaphysis of the femur. It is characterized by night pains relieved by medication. Nidus of osteoid osteoma is seen in the cortex and hence CT is the investigation of choice.

Option D: Aneurysmal bone cysts are benign, locally destructive, multiloculated cysts filled with blood. They are eccentric, expansile, and lytic lesions. Most occur in patients younger than 20 years old. There is a slight female preponderance. The most common sites involved are the proximal humerus, distal femur, and proximal tibia.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 2-week-old infant is brought to the emergency department by his parents with complaints of lethargy and poor feeding. On clinical examination, the child has bruises over the chest, and X-rays reveal multiple fractures at different stages of healing, including long bone fractures around the knees, posterior rib fractures, and subdural hematomas on neuroimaging. The history given by the caregiver is inconsistent with the injuries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Battered baby syndrome

The clinical scenario of bruises over the chest, multiple fractures on different stages of healing and subdural hematoma on neuroimaging, along with an inconsistent history from the parents, is highly indicative of the battered baby syndrome.

The battered baby syndrome refers to a constellation of clinical findings suggestive of repetitive physical abuse in a child via non-accidental violence by a parent or a guardian. Additionally, there may be associated deprivation of nutrition, care, and affection. It is usually seen in children less than 3 years of age with a history of emotional or financial problems in the family.

Clinical features:

* Injuries of different ages and in different stages of healing

* Bruises may be seen on either side of the chest, behind the axillae, and down the anterior chest wall indicative of the hand impressions of the perpetrator.

* Violent shaking of a child leads to infantile whiplash syndrome. Repetitive and vigorous shaking of an infant gives rise to a triad of clinical findings—encephalopathy, retinal bleeds, and subdural hemorrhage.

* Multiple deformities of the long bones and ribs. Some characteristic fractures include the following:

* Knob fractures are a result of callus formation in healing ribs that have been damaged due to squeezing. Chest x-ray shows a "string of beads" appearance in the paravertebral gutter.

* Bucket-handle fractures are typical corner fractures near the metaphyseal regions of the long bones in the arms and legs.

As per the Standard Skeletal Survey for Suspected Child Abuse, the minimum X-ray views required in a case of suspected child abuse:

* AP views of the entire skeleton

* Dedicated

* views of hands and feet

* Lateral views of the axial skeleton—skull and spine.

Imaging Also Suggested

* Oblique views of ribs

* Oblique views of hands and feet

Other options:

Option A: Osteogenesis imperfecta, also known as brittle bone disease. Presents with wormian bones, multiple fractures, deafness and blue sclera.

Option C: Birth trauma due to forceps occurs around the time of delivery and would not explain fractures at different stages of healing in a 2-week-old infant.

Option D: Inconsistent with the clinical findings of the case.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 20-year-old athletic male presented after a road traffic accident. He has sustained the injury shown in the X-ray below. What is the next line of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Internal fixation

The given clinical vignette of a young male with a history of trivial injury (RTA) and X-ray showing a transverse break in the neck of the femur is suggestive of a fracture of the neck of the femur. In the above scenario, since the patient is young, the appropriate treatment is an internal screw fixation.

In fracture neck of femur, internal fixation is performed with a minimum of 3 cannulated screws.

Fracture neck of femur is more often seen in fifth to the sixth decade of life and generally occurs after trivial trauma. Examination of the affected limb will reveal external rotation, shortening of the limb, groin tenderness, pain with movement, and no active straight leg raising.

Treatment of fracture neck of femur depends on the age of the patient and duration of the injury.

In undisplaced fracture, fixation is performed with multiple screws. In a displaced fracture:

* For people less than age 60 years of age, internal fixation with multiple screws is performed

* For people greater than 60 years of age, having a:

* Hip with pre-existing arthritis, a total hip replacement is done

* Normal hip, a hemiarthroplasty is performed

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with a history of a fall on the posterior aspect of the shoulder. He has lacerations over the posterior shoulder and has sustained a fracture of the shaft of the humerus as shown in the X-ray below. Which nerve is most likely to be affected in this injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Radial nerve

In the above clinical scenario, the history and radiograph suggest a closed fracture of the shaft of the humerus. The radial nerve is commonly damaged in this condition.

It manifests as an inability to dorsiflex the wrist and digits (wrist drop and finger drop). Numbness occurs on the dorsoradial aspect of the hand and the dorsal aspect of the radial 31/2 digits.

Management of humerus shaft fractures:

* Conservative management using a hanging cast or U-slab for 2-3 weeks, followed by functional bracing

* Surgical fixation by compression plating, interlocking intramedullary nail, semi-flexible pins, or an external fixator is indicated in:

* Open fractures

* Pathological fractures

* Unstable humeral and forearm fractures (floating elbow)

* Radial nerve palsy

The X-ray below shows shaft of humerus fracture.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young athlete presents with a meniscal tear. Imaging reveals that the tear involves the white–white zone of the meniscus. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment modality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Meniscectomy

The white–white zone (avascular inner zone) meniscal tears heal poorly due to lack of blood supply, making meniscal repair ineffective and, leading to partial meniscectomy as the preferred treatment.

The menisci are divided into three zones depending on the perfusion of blood. The menisci are supplied by perimeniscal blood vessels from superior and inferior branches of medial and lateral genicular vessels.

Following birth, the menisci become increasingly avascular. By adulthood, only the peripheral 10% to 25% of the tissue is perfused. This gives rise to 3 distinct regions of the menisci:

* The peripheral relatively vascularised region is called the red-red zone (Zone 1)

* A zone of transition between the 2 zones, which is called the red-white zone (Zone 2)

* The completely avascular inner zone, known as the white-white zone (Zone 3)

There is a direct relationship between the vascularization and capacity of the tissue to heal, predisposing the white-white zone to permanent post-traumatic and degenerative lesions.

Other options:

Option B: Meniscal repair is suitable only in meniscal tears within the vascular zones.

Option C: Conservative management can be tried for minor tears in vascular zones, but a symptomatic white–white zone injury due to avascularity results in failure.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young man, a road traffic accident (RTA) patient with a fracture of the shaft of the femur, develops shortness of breath, a drop in SaO₂, and altered mental status 3 days later. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fat embolism

The clinical scenario of sudden onset breathlessness and altered mental status on 3rd day of following a femoral shaft fracture should raise suspicion of fat embolism.

Fat embolism is the presence of fat globules in vital organs and peripheral circulation after fracture of the long bone or other major trauma. Fat embolism is a frequent complication after limb fractures. In most adults with closed long bone fractures, fat globules larger than 10 μm circulate in the bloodstream, and histological evidence of fat can often be detected in the lungs and other internal organs.  Clinical features of fat embolism are usually seen within 72 hours.

Pathogenesis- release of free fatty acids by the action of lipases on the neutral fats and actual obstruction of small pulmonary vessels by fat globules.

Clinical features:

* Early signs are fever and tachycardia.

* Presenting features are of 2 types:

* Cerebral type: drowsiness, restlessness, disorientation.

* Pulmonary type: tachypnoea, tachycardia.

* Other features: petechial rash in front of neck/anterior axillary fold/ chest/ conjunctiva.

The classical clinical triad consists of

* respiratory distress

* petechial haemorrhages

* neurological abnormalities

Treatment of fat embolism is mainly supportive:

* Respiratory support (oxygen)

* Heparinization (increases lipoprotein lipase activity)

* Intravenous low molecular weight dextran

* Corticosteroids: To avoid pneumonitis

* Prompt stabilization of long-bone fractures

Other Options:

Option A: Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound(blackish) pain and crepitus

Option B: Sepsis, usually accompanied by fever, tachycardia, hypotension, and a source of infection.

Option C: Pulmonary embolism usually manifests as a sudden onset of shortness of breath, frequently accompanied by pleuritic chest pain and an increased heart rate.

Pearl PF1166: Gurd's criteria for diagnosing fat embolism syndrome

Major criteria

* Axillary or subconjunctival petechiae

* Hypoxemia with PaO2 <60 mmHg, FIO2 < 0.4

* CNS depression disproportionate to the hypoxemia

* Pulmonary edema

Minor criteria

* Tachycardia (HR >110 beats per minute)

* Pyrexia (temp >38.50C)

* Emboli visible in retina

* Fat globules in urine

* Fat globules in sputum

* Unexplanied drop in hematocrit or platelet count

* Increased ESR

At least one major criterion and four minor criteria are required to make a diagnosis of fat embolism syndrome.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An elderly patient presented after a fall in the bathroom. X-ray of the right hip shows the fracture depicted below. What is the most likely type of fracture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intertrochanteric fracture

In an elderly patient with a history of fall and X-ray clearly showing a fracture line running between the greater trochanter and the lesser trochanter of the femur points towards the Intertrochanteric fracture.

Fractures in the inter-trochanteric region of the proximal femur, involving either the greater or the lesser trochanter or both, are grouped as intertrochanteric fractures. In the elderly, the fracture is normally sustained by a sideways fall or a blow over the greater trochanter. In the young, it occurs following violent trauma, as in a road traffic accident.

Clinical features include a history of a fall or road accident, followed by pain in the region of the groin and an inability to move the leg. There will be swelling in the region of the hip, and the leg will be short and externally rotated. There is tenderness over the greater trochanter.

According to Kyle classification, there are 4 types of Intertrochanteric fractures:

* Type 1: Undisplaced, uncomminuted

* Type 2: Displaced, minimal comminuted, lesser trochanter fracture

* Type 3: Displaced, comminuted, greater trochanter fracture

* Type 4: Severely comminuted, subtrochanter extension(Also reverse oblique)

Complications include malunion and osteoarthritis.

Management:

The intertrochanteric fractures of the femur can be treated by intramedullary and extramedullary implants.

* Intramedullary implants include proximal femoral nail and gamma nail which are used in displaced/unstable intertrochanteric fractures of the femur. Compared to dynamic hip screws, the intramedullary fixation with proximal femoral nails has smaller incisions, decreased blood loss, decreased femoral neck shortening, and decreased risk of infection.

* Extramedullary implants include a dynamic hip screw which is used in undisplaced/stable inter-trochanteric fractures

Other options:

Option B: Subtrochanteric fracture occur between the inferior margin of the lesser trochanter and 5 cm below this point.

Option C:  Femoral head fractures are always seen in association with a dislocation or subluxation of the femoral head. Acetabular, femoral shaft and femoral neck fractures are often associated with femoral head fractures.

Option D: In the given X-ray, it is an oblique type of fracture.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Injury at which of the following marked sites causes failure of dorsiflexion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3

The site marked as '3' in the x-ray given above is the neck of the fibula. Injury at this site causes failure of dorsiflexion (foot drop) due to injury to the common fibular nerve (also known as the common peroneal nerve).

The common fibular nerve is derived from the dorsal branches of the 4th and 5th lumbar and 1st and 2nd sacral ventral rami. It runs obliquely along the lateral side of the popliteal fossa to the fibular head. It lies between the biceps femoris and the lateral head of the gastrocnemius. It then curves laterally around the neck of the fibula and gets divided into superficial and deep fibular nerves.

Superficial fibular nerve
Deep fibular nerve

Motor innervation

• Peroneus longus
• Peroneus brevis

• Extensor digitorum longus
• Extensor hallucis longus
• Tibialis anterior
• Peroneus tertius

Sensory innervation

• Lateral aspect of the lower leg
• Dorsum of the toes except for the lateral side of the 5th toe and the first interdigital web-space

• The first interdigital space

Injury to the common peroneal nerve (common fibular nerve) at the level of the neck of the fibula causes foot drop. Ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension, and eversion of the foot are lost, while the inversion and plantar flexion are usually preserved. Sensory innervation to the dorsum of the foot, including the first web space, is lost. The ankle reflex is usually preserved.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the doctor testing for in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior cruciate ligament

The test done in the image is the anterior drawer test. This is done to detect injuries to the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

Procedure:

* The patient is made to lie supine on the examining table. The hip is flexed to 45° and the knee is flexed to 90° with the foot flat on the table.

* The upper end of the tibia is held in both hands and tibia is gently pushed anteriorly. Increased displacement compared to the normal knee indicates injury to ACL.

Lachman test is also done to detect injuries to the anterior cruciate ligament. Here the leg is in slight external rotation and the knee is in the position between flexion and extension. One hand is placed to stabilise femur and another hand applies the anterior force to the proximal tibia.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old male patient presented with complaints of a gradually progressive swelling around his wrist joint for 3 months. Given below is the image of the swelling and the X-ray film. The biopsy of the lesion reveals giant cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteoclastoma

The clinical presentation and the X-ray showing an eccentric expansile lesion with a soap bubble appearance are suggestive of osteoclastoma or giant cell tumor(GCT).

Osteoclastoma usually affects young adults in the age group of 20-40 years. The most common location of the tumor is the distal femur, followed by the proximal tibia. Involvement of the distal end of the radius is also seen, and the tumor is more aggressive in this location.

Radiographic findings in GCT:

* A solitary, possibly loculated, lytic lesion in the epiphysis

* Eccentric location, most often subchondral

* Expansion of the overlying cortex

* Soap bubble appearance - The tumor is homogeneously lytic with trabeculae of the remnants of bone traversing it, giving it a loculated appearance called the soap bubble appearance

* No calcification within the tumor

* No or minimal reactive sclerosis around the tumor.

Treatment :

* Extended curettage and bone grafting.

* En bloc wide resection and reconstruction are done for advanced stages, local recurrence, and tumors not responding to other methods.

* Resection without reconstruction is done for lesions in expandable bones like the distal ulna, clavicle, etc.

* Irradiation and/or embolization are used for inoperable lesions in the spine and pelvis.

* Bisphosphonates have been shown to reduce the proliferation of osteoclasts and hence have been shown to stabilize local and metastatic disease.

* Denosumab is approved for use in unresectable tumors in skeletally mature patients.

Other options:

Option A: Ewing's sarcoma is a primary malignant tumor of the bone commonly involving the age group of 4-25 years. It commonly involves the diaphysis of the long bones like the femur, tibia, fibula, and humerus.

Radiographic findings: Onion-peel appearance due to deposition of periosteal reaction in layers is the typical finding.

Option B: Osteosarcoma is the most common non-hematologic primary malignancy of bone. It occurs most commonly in the second decade of life. It is typically metaphyseal. The distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus are the common sites.

Radiographic findings: The periosteal reaction is the typical finding, and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have a sunburst (sunray) appearance on X-ray.

Option D: Osteochondroma: are common benign bone tumors. The lesions consist of a bony mass, often in the form of a stalk, produced by endochondral ossification of a growing cartilaginous cap. The common sites of involvement are the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 67-year-old diabetic patient presented with swelling around the knee, restriction of movement and minimal or no pain. The x-ray of the knee is given below. The diagnosis is _________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Charcot arthropathy

The x-ray depicts severe joint destruction and instability, seen on (a) varus stress (b)Neutral (c) valgus stress on the patient's knee joint. There is h/o diabetes and minimal pain , which indicates a neuropathic cause like Charcot arthropathy.

Charcot arthropathy is a neuroarthropathy commonly associated with diabetes.

Though the exact pathogenesis of this disease is unclear, it is speculated that vascular, neurological, and metabolic changes associated with diabetes lead to this condition.

Points in favor of a diagnosis of Charcot arthropathy are:

* Swelling of ankle joint  associated with foot ulcer (possible diabetic foot ulcer)

* Instability of movement

* Movements beyond normal limits and a loose bag of bones feel

* X-ray that shows obvious bone destruction and the presence of irregular calcified masses

Charcot's arthropathy can also be caused by the following conditions:

* leprosy

* dialysis

* chronic alcoholism

* spinal cord injury

* syringomyelia

* meningomyelocele

* syphilis

Treatment for this condition is usually decided upon by a multidisciplinary team of health care professionals such as a physician, a rheumatologist, an orthopedician, and a physiotherapist.

Other options:

Rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis and psoriatic arthropathy present with pain.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient after sleeping whole night with the arm hanging over the back of the chair, wakes up with inability to extend his wrist. This is due to _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Neuropraxia

This is a case of saturday night palsy, which is a type of neuropraxia.

Neuropraxia is a reversible physiological block in nerve conduction. Saturday night palsy occurs when radial nerve is compressed in the arm from direct pressure against a firm object. It can occur when the person sleeps on the arm, often after alcohol intoxication. Therefore, it is known as Saturday night palsy or weekend palsy.

Other examples for neuropraxia include crutch palsy and tourniquet palsy.

Pearl PF1196: Seddon's classification of nerve injuries

Seddon's classification includes 3 groups

1. Neurapraxia
2. Axonotmesis
3. Neurotmesis

Neurapraxia:

Reversible physiologic conduction block. Occurs due to mechanical pressure causing segmental demyelination.

E.g.,Saturday night palsy, torniquet, and crutch palsy

Axonotmesis:

Axonal interruption. Conduction is lost but the nerve is in continuity and neural tubes are intact.

E.g.,Closed fractures and dislocations

Neurotmesis:

Division of the nerve trunk. Endoneurial tube destruction also occurs.

E.g., Complete section of nerve in open fractures

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with hip pain and true shortening of the limb which was diagnosed as tuberculosis of the hip. Which stage of the disease is he currently in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stage of advanced arthritis

In a patient with tuberculosis of the hip, true shortening of the limb is seen in the advanced arthritis.

Clinical features seen in the four stages of TB hip:

* Stage of synovitis presents with apparent lengthening of the limb due to abduction deformity.

* Stage of early arthritis presents with apparent shortening of the limb due to adduction deformity.

* Stage of advanced arthritis leads to true shortening of the limb because of the destruction of the articular cartilage of the femur and the acetabulum.

* Stage of arthritis with subluxation leads to true shortening of the limb. The destruction of acetabulum leads to dislocation of the femur head. This is also known as wandering acetabulum/ mortar and pestle hip because of the widened acetabulum and diminished size of femur head.

The TB of the hip finally results in fibrous ankylosis of the hip joint.

Note: The apparent length of the limb is measured from the umbilicus to the medial malleolus and the true length of the limb is measured from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial malleolus. The apparent length is increased when there is abduction deformity of the limb and decreased when there is adduction deformity of the limb.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young man is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. He was driving the car when the accident occurred. On examination, it is noted that the injured leg is shortened. The image of the pelvis radiograph is shown below. Which of the following nerve is most commonly damaged in the given condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sciatic nerve

The above radiograph shows that the femoral head of the left hip is displaced upwards and laterally, and the affected limb is in adduction. Also, the lesser trochanter is obscured. These features indicate posterior dislocation of the left hip joint. The nerve the most commonly injured in this type of dislocation is the sciatic nerve.

Posterior hip dislocation occurs when the knee of the passenger strikes the dashboard. The affected leg is shortened, and lies in an adducted, internally rotated and slightly flexed position.

Imaging shows the following features:

* Upward dislocation of the femoral head

* The size of the femoral head appears smaller compared to the unaffected side

* Adduction of the affected limb.

* The lesser trochanter may not be visible due to the internal rotation of the affected leg

Treatment- A pure hip dislocation should be reduced as early as possible to reduce the risk of osteonecrosis and subsequent osteoarthritis. Important maneuvers to reduce posterior hip dislocation are:

* Rochester method

* East Baltimore lift

* Allis

* Bigelow

* Stimson

Complications of posterior hip dislocation are:

* Injury to the sciatic nerve

* Injury to the superior gluteal artery

* Osteonecrosis of femoral head

* Secondary osteoarthritis

* Myositis ossificans

* Recurrent instability of the reduced dislocation

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The following clinical sign is elicited in a patient after an operation. Which of the following nerve is injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Median nerve

The given image shows pointing index sign, and is associated with median nerve injury at the forearm or elbow.

Pointing index sign results from inability to flex index finger and thumb due to paralysis of flexor digitorum superficialis and lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus.

Median nerve lesions can be high lesions or low lesions depending on the site of injury.

Low lesions - It occurs due to injuries at the distal third of the forearm such as carpal dislocation or cut wound of the wrist.  There is paralysis of the hand muscles and the patient is unable to abduct the thumb. There is also a loss of sensation over the radial three and a half digits. The forearm muscles supplied by the median nerve are spared in these lesions. Wasting of thenar eminence is seen in long-standing cases.

High lesions - It occurs due to injuries above the elbow such as forearm fractures or elbow dislocation. There is paralysis of the forearm muscles along with all the features of low lesions.

Muscles supplied by the median nerve are given in the table:

In the arm

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The splint depicted below is ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Foot abduction orthosis

The image shows a foot abduction orthosis called Dennin Browne splint which is used for correction of CTEV and club foot.

* The brace (foot abduction orthosis) consists of shoes mounted to a bar in a position of 70 degrees of external rotation and 15 degrees of dorsiflexion. The distance between the shoes is set at about 1 inch wider than the width of the infant’s shoulders.

* When the final cast (following serial casting) is removed, the infant is placed in a brace that maintains the foot in its corrected position (abducted and dorsiflexed).

*

* The brace is worn 23 hours each day for the first 3 months after casting and then while sleeping for 3 to 4 years. Frequent follow-up during the bracing period is essential. Example of a foot abduction brace- Dennis Browne splint.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about the condition shown in the image below?
options: It can be seen on the dorsal and volar aspect of wrist
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Less chances of recurrence

Image A shows a ganglion cyst of the wrist and image B shows the surgical excision of the cyst. Image B shows a swelling that is cystic, translucent, and filled with a fluid which is suggestive of a ganglion cyst. It has high rates of recurrence and thus , option A is false.

Ganglion cyst:

* It arises from the leakage of synovial fluid from a joint or tendon sheath and thus contains a glary, viscous fluid.

* It can appear anywhere in the wrist but the most common area is the dorsal surface of the scapholunate ligament.

* Usually appears as a painless, well-defined, cystic, transillumination positive, and non-tender swelling. If there is an impingement on a nearby nerve or structure it can cause pain.

* It disappears spontaneously, but the aspiration of the swelling or operative removal can be done for reassurance or when there is pressure on the nerve.

* If the swelling is near the radial artery or nerves then removal is done under ultrasound guidance.

* Even if treatment is done, the rates of recurrence are high.

Note:

A lipoma can be a differential here but it is not a transilluminant swelling and has a positive slip sign, i.e when palpated, the edge of the swelling slips under the finger.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30 year old male patient presented with complaints of a gradually progressive swelling around his wrist joint for 3 months. Given below is the image of the swelling and the X-ray film. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteoclastoma

The clinical presentation and the X-ray showing an eccentric expansile lesion with a soap bubble appearance are suggestive of osteoclastoma or giant cell tumor (GCT).

Osteoclastoma usually affects young adults in the age group of 20-40 years. The most common location of the tumor is the distal femur followed by the proximal tibia. Involvement of the distal end of the radius is also seen and the tumor is more aggressive in this location.

Radiographic findings in GCT:

* A solitary, possibly loculated, lytic lesion in the epiphysis

* Eccentric location, most often subchondral

* Expansion of the overlying cortex

* Soap bubble appearance - The tumor is homogeneously lytic with trabeculae of the remnants of bone traversing it, giving it a loculated appearance called soap bubble appearance

* No calcification within the tumor

* No or minimal reactive sclerosis around the tumor.

Treatment :

* Extended curettage and bone grafting.

* En-bloc wide resection and reconstruction are done for advanced stages, local recurrence, and tumors not responding to other methods.

* Resection without reconstruction is done for lesions in expandable bones like distal ulna, clavicle, etc.

* Irradiation and/or embolization are used for inoperable lesions in the spine and pelvis.

* Bisphosphonates have been shown to reduce the proliferation of osteoclasts and hence have been shown to stabilize local and metastatic disease.

* Denosumab is approved for use in unresectable tumors in skeletally mature patients.

Other options:

Ewing's sarcoma:

It is a primary malignant tumor of the bone commonly involving the age group of 4-25 years. It commonly involves the diaphysis of the long bones like the femur, tibia, fibula, and humerus.

Radiographic findings: Onion-peel appearance due to deposition of periosteal reaction in layers is the typical finding.

Osteosarcoma:

It is the most common non-hematologic primary malignancy of bone. It occurs most commonly in the second decade of life. It is typically metaphyseal. The distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus are the common sites.

Radiographic findings: The periosteal reaction is the typical finding and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have a sunburst (sunray) appearance on X-ray.

Osteochondroma:

Osteochondromas are common benign bone tumors. The lesions consist of a bony mass, often in the form of a stalk, produced by endochondral ossification of a growing cartilaginous cap. The common sites of involvement are the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 34 year old male presents with a history of progressive lower backache and early morning stiffness for the past 6 months. His symptoms are more severe in the morning and improve on exercise. He is a known case of ulcerative colitis. An X-ray of his lumbar spine is taken and is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ankylosing spondylitis

The given clinical scenario and X-ray image are suggestive of ankylosing spondylitis The clinical presentation of a young male with progressive lower backache, morning stiffness, a symptomatic improvement on exercise, and the X-ray showing the classical bamboo-spine appearance are features supportive of the diagnosis. It is an extraintestinal manifestation of ulcerative colitis.

Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory disease affecting the spine and sacroiliac joint. It is more common in young males and has a strong association with HLAB27.

Clinically, patients present with recurring backache which worsens in the early morning or with inactivity and improves with exercise. Later they develop fatigue, pain, joint swellings, and heel pain. Extra-articular manifestations include uveitis, aortic incompetence, carditis, and apical lobe fibrosis. Examination findings include loss of lumbar lordosis, increased thoracic kyphosis, diminished spinal movements, and decreased chest expansion.

X-ray findings:

* Erosion of sacroiliac joints - earliest sign

* Periarticular sclerosis (option B) in later stages

* Squaring of vertebrae due to flattening of normal anterior concavity of the vertebral body is the earliest vertebral change

* Bamboo spine appearance (option C) due to bridging of adjacent vertebrae

* Wedging of the vertebra (option D) leading to hyperkyphosis

Diagnostic criteria for ankylosing spondylitis:

* Insidious in onset

* Morning stiffness

* Symptoms begin early at the age <40 years

* Improvement with exercise

* Persistence for > three months

Treatment consists of maintaining posture and preserving mobility. Pain and stiffness can be controlled with anti-inflammatory drugs. In severe cases, TNF inhibitors are used. Surgery can be considered to correct the deformity.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 6-month-old child is brought to the OPD with a deformity as shown in the image given below. Which of the following is your line of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Manipulation and cast

The first line of management of the given image, congenital vertical talus deformity (CTEV), is manipulation and cast by Ponseti's method.

Congenital Vertical Talus deformity/Rocker-Bottom foot: It is a rare deformity usually affecting both feet where the medial arch is not only flat, it is also the most prominent part of the sole, producing the appearance of a rocker-bottom foot. The talus points almost vertically towards the sole.

Management:

* The first line management for CTEV is Ponseti's technique in which gradual correction of deformities is done by plaster cast. The sequence of correction is given as:

*         C- Cavus

*         A- Adduction

*         V- Varus

*         E- Equinus

*         Ponseti's method is the currently used method for conservative management of CTEV.

* When passive correction is not possible. ‘Reverse Ponseti’ technique (where the foot is stretched into plantar-flexion and inversion while counter pressure is applied to the medial aspect of the head of the talus), 4-5 plaster casts are usually required until the plantar-flexed talus is in line. This is followed by stabilization of the talonavicular joint with an open approach.

Following is the image of congenital vertical talus which has pre-operative, intraoperative and postoperative radiological images.

Ponseti's method is currently used for the conservative management of congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV), while Kite's method was previously followed. Conservative management is preferred for CTEV

Kite's method (Not used now)

Pearl PF1915: Age wise management of CTEV

Initial treatment starts with Ponseti's POP cast as early as possible, but within 1 year of age.

If deformity gets corrected:

* Dennis Brown splint is used till 1 year of age

* After 1 year upto 5 years CTEV shoes are used in day, and Dennis Brown splint is used at night

If deformity is not corrected or untreated previously:

* 1-3 years: Posteromedial soft tissue release (PMSTR)

* 3-5 years: Dillwyn Evans procedure

* 5-8 years: Dwyer osteotomy

* 8-10 years: Wedge tarsectomy

* >10 years: Triple arthrodesis, external fixators

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after sustaining a fall on their outstretched hand. The image given below shows the cast used to manage the patient's injury. Identify the fracture.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scaphoid fracture

The cast applied to a patient in the glass holding position is known as the scaphoid cast. It is used to treat scaphoid fractures.

To apply a scaphoid cast, the wrist is held in slight dorsiflexion and the thumb is in abduction and slight flexion as if the glass is being held between the index finger and thumb. It extends from just below the elbow to just proximal to the metacarpal necks of the digits. On the thumb, the cast extends to just proximal to the interphalangeal joint.

Scaphoid fracture presents with pain and swelling over the radial aspect of the wrist. A fall on an outstretched hand could result in such a fracture. The fracture can be confirmed (when an x-ray doesn't show a fracture) if there is pain elicited in the anatomical snuff box on the radial border of the wrist.

An oblique x-ray of the wrist should be able to show a scaphoid fracture.
