The above clinical scenario, the history and MRI scan are suggestive of spondylolisthesis.

Spondylolisthesis is the anterior displacement of a vertebra over another, usually at the lower lumbar spine. Occasionally, the displacement is backward (retrolisthesis). It is characterized by chronic back pain, lumbar lordosis, and step sign. Normally, spinous processes of adjacent vertebrae can be palpated on the back smoothly. In spondylolisthesis, a step-off or step sign can be felt over the spinous process at the affected level.

The Beheaded Scottish terrier sign (shown in the image below) on the x-ray is diagnostic. It is due to a break in the pars interarticularis of the vertebra.

It is usually managed conservatively based on symptoms with analgesics, temporary activity restriction, muscle relaxants, physical therapy, and strengthening exercises.

Other options:

Option A: Renal osteodystrophy is a complex condition that results from the kidneys' inability to maintain the proper levels of calcium and phosphate in the blood, leading to secondary hyperparathyroidism. The below image represents Rugger Jersey spine which is characteristic of hyperparathyroidism seen in renal osteodystrophy.

Option B: TB spine occurs secondary to a pulmonary or gastrointestinal primary and spreads through the Batson's plexus of veins (paravertebral plexus). It most commonly involves the dorso-lumbar region.

Option C: Spinal metastasis: Represents the spread of malignancy to the spine, causing bone destruction. MRI would demonstrate vertebral lesions, bone marrow involvement, or spinal cord compression, without evidence of vertebral slippage. The following image shows a radiograph of spinal metastasis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 58-year-old female patient presents with a pathological fracture of the hip and femur. Her serum calcium and phosphate are increased. DEXA scan confirms decreased bone density. Which of the following parameters will increase in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tartrate resistant acid phosphatase

In this patient, the pathological fracture and elevated serum calcium and phosphate suggest a possible metabolic bone disease such as Paget’s disease of bone. The parameter likely to be increased is TRAP (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase), which is a marker of osteoclast activity.

TRAP is an enzyme produced by osteoclasts, which are cells responsible for bone resorption. Elevated levels of TRAP are often seen in conditions with increased bone turnover, such as Paget’s disease, hyperparathyroidism, and certain bone malignancies.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A child sustained a fracture after a fall. An X-ray taken after fracture management is shown below. By which of the following mechanisms will fracture healing occur?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Primary healing

The clinical vignette describes a child sustaining a fracture, and the X-rays show compression plating. In this case, the fracture heals through primary healing without callus formation.

The stages of fracture healing are as follows:

1. Hematoma Stage (up to 7 days): The periosteum and soft tissues detach from the fracture ends, leading to ischemic necrosis. Some osteocytes die from lack of blood flow, while others transform into daughter cells that aid in healing.
2. Granulation Tissue Stage (2-3 weeks): Sensitized daughter cells differentiate into blood vessels, fibroblasts, and osteoblasts, forming soft granulation tissue that fills the fracture gap.
3. Callus Stage (4-12 weeks): Granulation tissue differentiates into osteoblasts that produce an intercellular matrix infused with calcium salts, forming a callus (woven bone), which is visible on X-rays around 3 weeks after the fracture.
4. Remodeling Stage (1-2 years): The woven bone is replaced by mature lamellar bone, known as the secondary callus, through a multicellular process of substitution.
5. Modeling Stage: The bone undergoes gradual strengthening and reshaping of its periosteal and endosteal surfaces, driven by local strains from weight-bearing stresses and muscle forces during normal activities.

Other options:

Option A: Secondary healing is more typical for fractures that have not been perfectly aligned or stabilized, where a callus is formed (soft callus forms first, followed by a hard callus as healing progresses).

Option C: Creeping osteogenesis refers to the process where new bone forms along the surface of existing bone, typically seen in the context of distraction osteogenesis or in cases where there is a gap that needs to be filled.

Option D: Intramembranous ossification is a type of bone formation that occurs primarily in flat bones and does not typically apply to the healing of fractures.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A child sustained an injury as shown in the below radiograph. What is the classification used and the grade used for this type of injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gartland's classification-type III

The given clinical features and X-ray image are suggestive of a supracondylar fracture of the humerus (extension type) and Gartland classification is used in this case. The extension type fracture which is displaced with no intact posterior cortex is type 3 as per this classification.

Gartland classification (in children):

• Type I: Undisplaced
• Type II: Displaced but posterior cortex is intact
• Type III: Displaced but no intact posterior cortex and distal fragment could be either displaced:

• Posteromedial
• Posterolateral

Supracondylar fracture of the humerus is most commonly seen in children of 5-7 years after a fall on an outstretched hand with the elbow in full extension. It is most commonly of extension type followed by flexion type. Gartland classification is used for supracondylar fractures. The three-point bony relationship is maintained in supracondylar fracture (option B). Three-point bony landmarks in the elbow are the tips of medial and lateral epicondyles and the olecranon.

Nerve and vessel injury:

• The most common nerve to be injured in extension type - anterior interosseous nerve > Median nerve > Radial nerve > Ulnar nerve. (AMRU)
• The most common nerve to be injured in the flexion type the ulnar nerve.
• The most common vessel to be injured - the brachial artery.

Radiological findings: An undisplaced fracture may show a triangular lucency like a sail of a yacht (sail sign), also called a fat pad sign. This is due to the fat pad around the elbow being pushed forward by the hematoma. Baumann’s angle (humeral-capitellar angle) can help in assessing the degree of medial angulation before and after reduction.

The most common complication of supracondylar fracture is malunion. This leads to cubitus varus or gunstock deformity. Malunion occurs due to improper reduction and not due to physeal damage, as the fracture is extraphyseal Other complications include myositis ossificans, compartment syndrome, and Volkmann ischemic contracture.

Undisplaced supracondylar humerus fractures are treated by an above-elbow plaster slab with the elbow in 90º flexion. Displaced fractures are treated by closed reduction and K-wire fixation since they tend to slip after reduction. Open fractures or those associated with brachial artery injury are treated by open reduction and internal fixation.

Other options:

Options A and D: Salter and Harris created a classification of physeal injuries for risk stratification.

• Type 3: Here, the fracture splits the epiphysis and then goes transversely in either direction into the hypertrophic layer of the physis. This leads to damage of the growth plate leading to growth disturbance.
• Type 4: The fracture splits the epiphysis and extends into the metaphysis. Displacement can occur in these types leading to asymmetrical growth.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A child with rickets not responding to treatment is being evaluated. Investigations show a serum calcium level of 9 mg/dL, low phosphate level of 2 mg/dL, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and normal parathyroid hormone levels with normal arterial blood gas levels. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypophosphatemic rickets

The given scenario indicates the diagnosis of hypophosphatemic rickets because of the following features:

• normal calcium levels (Normal: 9-11 mg/dL)
• normal parathyroid hormone levels
• decreased phosphate (Normal: 2.5-4.3 mg/dL)
• elevated levels of alkaline phosphatase (Normal: 33-96 U/L)
• normal arterial blood gas levels

Hypophosphatemic rickets:

X-linked dominant hypophosphatemic rickets are the most common genetic cause of rickets while the most common, overall is nutritional vitamin D deficiency. PHEX gene (phosphate-regulating endopeptidase on x chromosome) products are responsible for the inactivation of phosphatonin. Mutation of this PHEX leads to increased phosphatonin (FGF 23) levels, and hence, the excretion of phosphorous is increased. This is also associated with impaired renal tubular reabsorption of phosphate leading to its excess excretion.

The chart attached below summarizes the evaluation of hypophosphatemic rickets.

Other options:

Options A and C: In vitamin D-resistant rickets, the renal tubule’s inability to retain phosphate results in the loss of excessive phosphate through urine. Therefore, even normal or higher supplementations of vitamin D are not sufficient for bone mineralization.

• Vitamin D-dependent Type 1 rickets is due to decreased activation of vitamin D to its active form in the kidney.
• Vitamin D-dependent Type 2 rickets is due to resistance to vitamin D in peripheral tissues. This resistance to vitamin D can be overcome with high levels of this vitamin by supplementation.

Option D: Nutritional rickets occur due to a deficiency of vitamin D. This leads to low calcium levels in the blood. To raise the serum calcium, the secretion of the parathyroid hormone rises. The parathyroid hormone tries to raise the calcium levels by reabsorbing calcium in the kidneys and secreting phosphate in exchange leading to low phosphate levels and increasing bone resorption.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A fracture line passing through which of these will impair longitudinal growth of the bone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Epiphyseal plate

A fracture line passing through the epiphyseal plate (also known as the growth plate) will impair the longitudinal growth of the bone.

The epiphyseal plate is the area of growing tissue near the ends of the long bones in children and adolescents. It is responsible for bone lengthening (longitudinal growth). If the fracture involves the epiphyseal plate, it can disrupt this process and lead to growth disturbances or deformities.

Other options:

Option B: The epiphysis is the end of a long bone. While fractures involving the epiphysis can affect joint function, they don’t directly impair longitudinal growth unless the epiphyseal plate is involved.

Option C: The metaphysis is the region of bone between the diaphysis and the epiphysis, where bone growth in width occurs. A fracture here doesn’t directly impact longitudinal growth.

Option D: Diaphysis describes the shaft of the bone. A diaphyseal fracture typically affects the strength and structural integrity of the bone but doesn’t impair longitudinal growth.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient complains of decreased sensation in the lateral three-and-a-half fingers on the palmar side of the right hand, along with difficulty moving the upper phalanx of the thumb. Examination reveals thenar atrophy. Which of the following structures, when affected, lead to this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carpal tunnel

The most likely nerve injured here is the median nerve, which occurs in Carpal tunnel syndrome.

Carpal tunnel syndrome is the most common entrapment mononeuropathy caused by compression of the median nerve as it passes through the fibro-osseous carpal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum. Patients present with pain and paresthesia over the lateral 3 and a half digits. There may be a weakness of thumb opposition. In chronic cases, the thenar eminence is lost due to thenar atrophy. Carpal tunnel syndrome can be associated with rheumatoid arthritis, pregnancy, chronic renal failure, acromegaly, hypothyroidism, and gout. The diagnosis is usually made on clinical grounds but nerve conduction studies can confirm the diagnosis.

Other tests for CTS -

• Phalen's test - Elicited by holding the wrist flexed fully. The appearance of sensory symptoms within 60 seconds implies a positive test.
• Tinel's sign - Sensory symptoms reproduced by percussing over the median nerve imply a positive test.

The given image shows carpal tunnel syndrome:

Non-surgical Management of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: In mild to moderate cases of carpal tunnel syndrome, non-surgical management options can be explored to alleviate symptoms and improve function. These conservative treatments include:

1.

Wrist splinting: Wearing a wrist splint at night can help maintain the wrist in a neutral position, reducing pressure on the median nerve and providing relief from nocturnal symptoms.

2.

Activity modification: Identifying and modifying activities that exacerbate symptoms can help in managing carpal tunnel syndrome. For example, taking frequent breaks during repetitive tasks or adjusting the workstation ergonomics can be beneficial.

3.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs): Over-the-counter NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen, can help manage pain and inflammation associated with carpal tunnel syndrome.

4.

Corticosteroid injections: In some cases, corticosteroid injections into the carpal tunnel may provide temporary relief from symptoms by reducing inflammation and pressure on the median nerve.

5.

Physical and occupational therapy: Therapists can help patients learn exercises to stretch and strengthen the hand and wrist muscles, improving symptoms and function.

If conservative treatments do not provide sufficient relief or the condition worsens, surgical intervention, such as carpal tunnel release surgery, may be considered.

Other options:

Option A: High radial nerve injuries typically cause wrist drop due to weakness in wrist and finger extensors, with sensory loss in the dorsal aspect of the hand, not the lateral three and a half fingers on the palmar side.

Option B: High median nerve injuries can affect sensation in the lateral three-and-a-half fingers on the palmar side and impair thumb flexion and opposition, particularly at the proximal phalanx. There is a loss of pronation due to the paralysis of the pronator teres and pronator quadratus. Paralysis of flexor digitorum superficialis and lateral half flexor digitorum profundus results in loss of wrist flexion. Ape-like hand and pointing index are due to this injury.

Option C: High ulnar nerve injuries result in sensory loss in the medial one-and-a-half fingers (pinky and ring finger) and hand intrinsic muscle weakness, unrelated to thenar muscle involvement.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient met with road traffic accident and complained of severe back ache. The X-ray is shown below. What fracture does the patient have?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chance fracture

The X-ray shows a vertebral fracture with a horizontal fracture line passing through the body of the vertebra. This indicates Chance fracture.

Chance fracture is also known as seat-belt injury or the jack-knife injury. This injury is typically located in the upper lumbar spine in people involved in motor vehicle collisions while wearing a lap seat belt without a shoulder harness. The sudden deceleration causes flexion and posterior distraction of the spine. This causes the mid-lumbar spine to bend like a jack-knife around an axis anterior to the vertebral column.

There is a tear in the vertebra that passes transversely through the bones (bony Chance fracture), or the ligamentous structures (soft Chance fracture), or both. There is little or no crushing of the vertebral body. However, it is an unstable injury as the posterior and middle columns are distracted. Neurological damage is uncommon. Associated intra-abdominal injuries are seen in 50% of these injuries.

X-rays may show a horizontal fracture with the split running through the vertebra. It may involve the spinous process, the transverse processes, pedicles and the vertebral body. There may be opening up of the disc space posteriorly.

Most Chance fractures can be managed conservatively with bed rest and bracing. If posterior fixation is done, it will allow early mobilization. Ligamentous Chance fractures require posterior instrumented fusion.

Other options:

Option B: Burst fracture results from severe axial compression that explodes the vertebral body. The lateral view CT image showing the L4 vertebra burst fracture is given below.

Option C: Spinal compression fractures occur as a result of injury, common fall onto the buttock or pressure from normal activities, to the weakened vertebrae due to osteoporosis. Compression causes a short oblique fracture. The image showing the L4 vertebra compression fracture is given below:

Option D: Fracture of the spinous process of C7(Clay Shoveller's Fracture) is an example of an avulsion injury which may occur with severe voluntary contraction of the muscles at the back of the neck.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient sustained a fracture of the base of the fifth metatarsal in the right foot. He was advised below knee pop cast. How long should the cast be put?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 6-8 weeks

The given X-ray indicates a Jones fracture. Conservative management involves a short-leg non-weight bearing cast for 6-8 weeks.

A Jones fracture is typically caused by forced inversion of the foot, such as during a pothole injury, leading to the avulsion of the base of the fifth metatarsal. This injury is due to the pull of the peroneus brevis tendon or the lateral band of the plantar fascia, which inserts onto the base of the fifth metatarsal.

Surgical correction, such as intramedullary screw fixation, is recommended for faster healing in highly active individuals. Proximal avulsion fractures can generally be managed symptomatically with rest and support, followed by early mobilization and return to function.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young woman, following an intense workout involving heavy weight lifting, presents with lower back pain radiating to her right hip and extending down to her right ankle. MRI shows the following finding. Based on the location and radiation of her pain, which of the following nerve roots is most likely involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. L5

Based on the clinical presentation of lower back pain radiating to the right hip and ankle, along with an MRI showing L4-L5 disc prolapse, the likely nerve root involved is L5. In a typical L4-L5 disc herniation, the L5 nerve root is most commonly compressed.

Other options:

Option A: L4: Involvement typically causes symptoms around the knee and anterior lower leg, but not the ankle.

Option C: S1: Compression here causes symptoms in the posterior leg, calf, and heel, differing from this case's distribution of pain.

Option D: L3: Affects the anterior thigh, with no radiating pain below the knee.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An 18-year-old boy complains of fever and pain in the lower limb. There is a localised rise of temperature and tenderness in the region shown in the radiograph. ESR is raised. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ewing's sarcoma

The clinical features and radiograph showing onion peel type of periosteal reaction point towards a diagnosis of Ewing’s sarcoma.

Ewing's sarcoma is a malignant tumour that occurs more frequently in males, typically between 10 and 20 years of age and has a diaphyseal long-bone location. The femur is the most common long-bone site, followed by the tibia, humerus and fibula. Ewing’s sarcoma is believed to arise from mesenchymal stem cells in the bone marrow.

Pain is the earliest symptom, followed by swelling and a low-grade fever. Radiographically, an aggressive, permeative, poorly defined osteolytic lesion with cortical destruction, periosteal reaction and large, radiolucent soft-tissue mass may be found. Periosteal reaction is common in young patients with the lamellar ‘onion-skin’ appearance causing fusiform bone enlargement. Ewing’s sarcoma is composed of primitive, undifferentiated, small, round blue cells with large nuclei and scant cytoplasm. The characteristic translocation between chromosomes 11 and 22 results in a fusion gene, EWSR1-FL11, which is present in 90% of cases.

Preoperative chemotherapy frequently results in extensive tumour necrosis and shrinkage. Agents used in Ewing’s sarcoma include vincristine, ifosfamide, doxorubicin and etoposide. Wide excision may be combined with adjuvant radiotherapy if surgical margins are poor. A more favourable outcome is expected with younger age, distal appendicular sites, small tumour volume, normal ESR and greater chemotherapy necrosis response.

Other options:

Option A: Osteosarcoma has a periosteal reaction characterised as the Codman triangle. It can also be seen in Ewing’s sarcoma.

Option C: Giant cell tumor has a characteristic soap bubble appearance.

Option D: Acute osteomyelitis in children presents with fever, pain, refusal to bear weight, elevated WBC count, elevated CRP, and elevated ESR. During the first week, the X-ray appears to be normal and by the second week, a faint extracortical line may be visible due to periosteal new bone formation. This is a classic sign of early pyogenic osteomyelitis. A combination of regional osteoporosis with a localized segment of apparently increased density is an important late finding in this condition.

Chronic osteomyelitis presents with erythema, chronic pain, swelling, tenderness, and discharging sinus tract. X-ray shows sequestrum is a piece of devitalized bone that has been separated from its surrounding bone during the process of necrosis, involucrum is the thick sheath of periosteal new bone that surrounds the sequestrum and cloacae are openings in the involucrum that allow drainage of purulent and necrotic material out of the dead bone.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Following a road traffic accident, a patient with an intertrochanteric fracture of the femur was treated with the implant shown below. Identify the implant.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dynamic hip screw

The above radiograph shows an extramedullary implant called a dynamic hip screw.

Intertrochanteric fractures of the femur can be treated by:

• Extramedullary implants - dynamic hip screw
• Intramedullary implants - proximal femoral nail and gamma nail.

Dynamic hip screws are used in undisplaced intertrochanteric fractures, whereas proximal femoral nails are used in displaced intertrochanteric fractures.

The below image shows a dynamic hip screw.

Advantages of using a proximal femoral nail over a dynamic hip screw include:

• Smaller incisions
• Reduced blood loss
• Decreased femoral neck shortening
• Decreased risk of infection

Other options:

Option A: The below image shows a proximal femoral nail with locking and stabilization screws.

Option C: Austin Moore's implant is an older implant used in unipolar hemiarthroplasty. It can be identified by the fenestrations on the shaft of the prosthesis, as shown below.

Option D: Herbert screw is cannulated and threaded at both ends. It is designed for use in fractures of small articular bones such as carpals and scaphoid.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Patient presented with a twisting injury of the knee. Identify the test being performed.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lachman test

The image shows an examination being performed with the knee flexed to about 20 degrees which indicates that it is the Lachman test. The presence of free gliding indicates that it is a positive Lachman test.

Lachman test: The patient’s knee is flexed to 20 degrees.  The lower part of the thigh is grasped with one hand and the upper part of the leg with the other hand. The joint surfaces are shifted backward and forward upon each other.  If the knee is stable, there should be no gliding. The presence of gliding indicates the laxity of the anterior cruciate ligament.

Other options:

Anterior and posterior drawer test: The test is performed with the patient’s knees flexed to 90 degrees, and the feet resting on the examining bed. The examiner then grasps the upper part of the leg with both hands and rocks it forward and backward. Excessive anterior movement denotes anterior cruciate laxity (anterior drawer test) Excessive posterior movement denotes posterior cruciate laxity (posterior drawer test).

McMurray’s test: The test is used to identify torn meniscus. The knee is flexed as far as possible and the joint is stabilized with one hand. With the other hand, the examiner rotates the leg medially and laterally. If there is a clicking sound while rotating the leg, the test is positive. The sound is produced due to the trapping of the loose tag of the torn meniscus between the articular surfaces.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is this type of amputation called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Below knee amputation

The given image shows below-knee amputation.

By retaining the knee joint, a below-knee amputation allows for better mobility and function compared to an above-knee amputation. After surgery, patients can usually be fitted with a prosthetic limb, enabling them to walk with a relatively normal gait.

Other options:

Option A: Above-knee amputation (AKA): Surgical removal of the lower limb above the knee joint, typically at the femur, resulting in the loss of the knee and requiring a more complex prosthetic for ambulation.

Option C: Knee disarticulation: Amputation through the knee joint, preserving the femur while removing the tibia and fibula, allowing for better weight-bearing but with a longer residual limb than AKA.

Option D: Syme's amputation: Removal of the foot at the level of the ankle joint, preserving the heel pad for weight-bearing and creating a durable limb for ambulation without complex prosthetics.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy falls on his outstretched hand and sustains a supracondylar fracture of the humerus. On examination, he is unable to make "OK" sign with his thumb and index finger. Which of the following structures is most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Median nerve

This specifically indicates Anterior Interosseous Nerve (AIN) palsy, a branch of the median nerve

“OK Sign”

Normally:

• Thumb → flexed (FPL)
• Index finger → flexed (FDP)

Makes a neat circle

In injury:

• Cannot flex distal phalanges
• Forms a flat pinch instead of circle

Clinical Appearance of OK Sign Deficit

Pathophysiology-

Anterior Interosseous Nerve (AIN) is injured.

Branch of median nerve

Supplies:

• Flexor pollicis longus (FPL)
• Flexor digitorum profundus (lateral half)
• Pronator quadratus

Pure motor nerve (NO sensory loss)

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 32-year-old man presents with difficulty performing fine hand movements after sustaining a laceration near the medial aspect of his elbow. During examination, a video is shown. The patient is unable to maintain grip, and the card slips out easily. The abnormal finding on this test is most suggestive of injury to which of the following nerves?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ulnar nerve

The Card Test (Card Pinch Test) assesses the function of the palmar interossei muscles, which are responsible for finger adduction. These muscles are innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

• Positive test: Patient cannot hold the card between adjacent fingers against resistance.
• Indicates: Weakness/paralysis of the palmar interossei due to ulnar nerve palsy.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Median nerve: Injury causes thenar muscle weakness and impaired thumb opposition; assessed by the pen test or thumb opposition tests.
• B. Radial nerve: Injury produces wrist drop and impaired finger extension, not failure of finger adduction.
• D. Musculocutaneous nerve: Primarily supplies elbow flexors and does not control intrinsic hand muscles.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman, a data-entry operator, presents with a 5-month history of nocturnal tingling in the right hand that wakes her from sleep and is relieved by shaking the hand. Examination shows sensory blunting over the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle and radial half of the ring finger, with preserved sensation over the thenar eminence. There is mild wasting of the abductor pollicis brevis. Flexion of the wrist to 90° for 60 seconds reproduces her symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Carpal tunnel syndrome

Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is the most common entrapment neuropathy, caused by compression of the median nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum within the carpal tunnel.

It classically presents with numbness, tingling, and pain over the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger, often worsening at night. Advanced cases may develop thenar muscle weakness and atrophy, leading to impaired thumb opposition.

| Option | Why it's tempting | Why it's wrong — the discriminator

| ------ | ----------------- | ----------------------------------

| A. Pronator teres syndrome | Also, median nerve, also thumb–index–middle sensory loss | Palmar cutaneous branch is affected → thenar eminence sensation is LOST. Also: no nocturnal symptoms, pain in proximal forearm, aggravated by resisted pronation. Our patient has preserved thenar sensation

| C. Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome | Median nerve territory | AIN is purely motor — no sensory loss at all. Presents with inability to make the "OK" sign (FPL + FDP index weakness). Sensory findings exclude it

| D. C6 radiculopathy | Thumb/index tingling overlaps | Involves neck pain radiating, ↓ biceps/brachioradialis reflex, Spurling's positive, and does not respect the median distribution (spares the middle finger pattern, no APB-selective wasting)

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after sustaining a mid-shaft humerus fracture during a fall. On examination, he is unable to actively extend his wrist or his metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints, resulting in a “wrist drop” deformity. Which nerve has been injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Radial nerve

The radial nerve is the nerve most commonly injured in mid-shaft fractures of the humerus because it courses through the radial (spiral) groove along the posterior aspect of the humeral shaft.

Clinical features of radial nerve injury:

• Wrist drop due to paralysis of the wrist extensors.
• Inability to extend the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints due to paralysis of the extensor digitorum and other finger extensors.
• Weak thumb extension and abduction.
• Sensory loss over the posterior arm, posterior forearm, and dorsolateral aspect of the hand, especially the first dorsal web space.

Why not the other options?

• A. Axillary nerve: Injured in surgical neck fractures of the humerus or anterior shoulder dislocation; causes deltoid weakness, impaired shoulder abduction (15–90°), and sensory loss over the lateral shoulder (“regimental badge” area).
• B. Median nerve: Causes thenar weakness, loss of thumb opposition, and sensory loss over the lateral 3½ fingers; does not cause wrist drop.
• D. Ulnar nerve: Causes claw hand, weakness of finger abduction/adduction, and sensory loss over the medial 1½ fingers; commonly injured at the medial epicondyle or Guyon’s canal.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient complains that he often gets troubled at night during sleep by tingling and numbness that involves his lateral three digits. He further explains that symptoms are relieved as he lays his arms hanging from the bed. Correct regarding the condition is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CTS: Durkan test

Increased pressure in carpal tunnel

↓

Median nerve compression

↓

Sensory symptoms (lateral 3½ digits)

↓

Motor weakness (thenar muscles)

↓

Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

Night-time tingling and numbness in the lateral three digits, relieved by shaking or hanging the hand down, is classic for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) due to median nerve compression. The most sensitive clinical test is the Durkan compression test, where direct pressure over the carpal tunnel reproduces symptoms.

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Night symptoms | Wrist flexion during sleep

| Tingling/numbness | Median nerve distribution

| Relief on shaking | Improves circulation

| Thenar wasting | Late stage

Froment sign is for ulnar nerve palsy (adductor pollicis weakness), and Guyon canal syndrome affects the ulnar distribution, not the lateral three digits.

| Feature | CTS (Median) | Guyon Canal (Ulnar)

| ------- | ------------ | -------------------

| Nerve | Median | Ulnar

| Digits affected | Lateral 3½ | Medial 1½

| Night symptoms | ✅ Common | ❌ Rare

| Test | Durkan, Phalen | Froment

| Motor deficit | Thenar | Interossei

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient develops inability to extend the fingers while wrist extension is preserved following surgery for a fracture of the neck of the radius. Injury to which of the following nerves is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Posterior interosseous nerve

The posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) is the deep motor branch of the radial nerve that passes through the supinator muscle (Arcade of Frohse) near the neck of the radius.

Injury to the PIN results in loss of finger and thumb extension while wrist extension is preserved, because the extensor carpi radialis longus (and often extensor carpi radialis brevis) receive innervation proximal to the bifurcation of the radial nerve. Thus, patients present with finger drop without wrist drop. No sensory loss, as the PIN is a pure motor nerve

Why not the other options?

• A. Ulnar nerve: Injury causes clawing of the 4th and 5th digits, weak finger abduction/adduction, and a positive Froment’s sign, not isolated loss of finger extension.
• B. Radial nerve: Injury proximal to its bifurcation causes wrist drop along with inability to extend the fingers and sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand.
• D. Median nerve: Injury causes thenar weakness, loss of thumb opposition, and sensory loss over the lateral 3½ digits, not finger drop.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents after a fall with the fracture shown in the X-ray. Which nerve is most likely to be injured in this type of fracture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Radial nerve

The radial nerve is the most commonly injured nerve in shaft of humerus fractures, particularly at the junction of upper two-thirds and lower one-third of the shaft where the nerve pierces the lateral intermuscular septum (Halston Lewis sign).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents in the OPD complaining of unable to evert the ankle. Which of the following gait is present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stepping gait

| Finding | Interpretation

| ------- | --------------

| Unable to evert ankle | Weak peroneal muscles

| Foot tends to invert | Loss of lateral compartment function

| Likely nerve involved | Common peroneal nerve

This leads to: Foot drop → Stepping gait

| Function | Muscle | Nerve

| -------- | ------ | -----

| Dorsiflexion | Tibialis anterior | Deep peroneal

| Eversion | Peroneus longus/brevis | Superficial peroneal

| Gait | Cause | Key Feature

| ---- | ----- | -----------

| Stepping gait | Peroneal nerve palsy | Foot drop

| Waddling gait | Gluteus medius weakness | Pelvic sway

| Circumduction gait | Hemiplegia | Leg swings outward

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents to the clinic with a fracture of the humerus as shown in the image below. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ulnar nerve

The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus in the cubital tunnel, making it highly susceptible to injury in medial epicondyle fractures and elbow trauma. Injury results in sensory loss over the medial 1½ fingers and weakness of the interossei and ulnar two lumbricals, causing impaired finger abduction/adduction and, in severe cases, an ulnar claw hand.

FMGE/NEET PG Pearl

• Medial epicondyle fracture → Ulnar nerve injury.
• Lateral epicondyle fracture → May injure the radial nerve/posterior interosseous nerve.
• Supracondylar fracture → Most commonly injures the anterior interosseous nerve (median nerve branch).
• Surgical neck of humerus fracture → Axillary nerve injury.
• Midshaft humerus fracture → Radial nerve injury

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents to the orthopedic clinic with a fracture as shown in the image. Which nerve is most likely involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior interosseous nerve

Supracondylar fractures of the humerus commonly injure the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN), the most frequently affected branch of the median nerve. AIN palsy causes motor deficits without sensory loss, characterized by inability to make the “OK” sign due to paralysis of the flexor pollicis longus, the radial half of flexor digitorum profundus, and pronator quadratus.

FMGE/NEET PG Pearl

• Supracondylar fracture → Most common nerve injured: Anterior interosseous nerve (median nerve branch).
• AIN injury → Pure motor; no sensory deficit.
• Median nerve injury → Sensory loss over the lateral 3½ fingers and thenar weakness.
• Cubital tunnel/medial epicondyle injury → Ulnar nerve involvement.
• Radial nerve is more commonly injured in shaft fractures of the humerus.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with a characteristic deformity as shown below while attempting to make a fist. Injury to which of the following nerves is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Median nerve

The “pointing index” (hand of benediction) deformity is a classic sign of proximal median nerve injury. When the patient is asked to make a fist, the index and middle fingers remain extended, while the ring and little fingers flex normally. This occurs because of paralysis of the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS), the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus (FDP), and flexor pollicis longus (FPL), all of which are supplied by the median nerve.

• Median nerve injury proximal to the elbow causes:

• Inability to flex the index and middle fingers
• Inability to flex the thumb
• Pointing index (Hand of Benediction) when attempting to make a fist

Why not the other options?

• A. Ulnar nerve: Causes ulnar claw hand, involving hyperextension at the MCP joints and flexion at the IP joints of the 4th and 5th digits. It does not produce a pointing index deformity.
• B. Radial nerve: Causes wrist drop due to paralysis of the wrist and finger extensors. Finger flexion is preserved.
• D. Axillary nerve: Causes weakness of shoulder abduction and sensory loss over the regimental badge area, without hand deformities.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with meralgia paresthetica. Involvement of which nerve roots is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. L2, L3

Meralgia paresthetica is due to compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2–L3), causing burning and numbness over the lateral thigh. It is commonly compressed under the inguinal ligament from tight clothing, obesity, pregnancy, or hip flexion.

The nerve lies in the triangle of pain, making it vulnerable during laparoscopic hernia repair, and can also be stretched in the McRoberts position during obstetric maneuvers.

Lumbar plexus (L2–L3)

↓

Emerges lateral to psoas

↓

Crosses iliacus muscle

↓

Passes under inguinal ligament (near ASIS)

↓

Supplies anterolateral thigh

Compression point:

• Under inguinal ligament near ASIS

Common causes:

• Tight belts / Obesity /Pregnancy / Diabetes

Clinical Features

• Numbness over anterolateral thigh

| Nerve | Root Value | Area Supplied | Clinical Clue

| ----- | ---------- | ------------- | -------------

| Lateral femoral cutaneous | L2–L3 | Anterolateral thigh | Meralgia paresthetica

| Femoral nerve | L2–L4 | Anterior thigh + leg | Weak knee extension

| Obturator nerve | L2–L4 | Medial thigh | Weak adduction

| Ilioinguinal nerve | L1 | Groin | Inguinal pain

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient sustains a fracture at the neck of the humerus. Which nerve is most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Axillary nerve

The axillary nerve is the most commonly injured nerve in fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus because it winds around the surgical neck with the posterior circumflex humeral artery through the quadrangular space.

Injury results in:

• Weakness of shoulder abduction (15°–90°) due to deltoid paralysis
• Weakness of external rotation (teres minor)
• Loss of sensation over the lateral shoulder (“regimental badge” area)

Why not the other options?

• B. Radial nerve: Commonly injured in midshaft humeral fractures (spiral groove).
• C. Median nerve: More commonly injured in supracondylar fractures of the humerus.
• D. Ulnar nerve: Commonly injured in medial epicondyle fractures or elbow trauma.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A video demonstrates a patient attempting to extend the wrist. Which peripheral nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Radial nerve

• The hallmark finding of radial nerve injury is wrist drop, which occurs due to paralysis of the wrist and finger extensors located in the posterior compartment of the forearm.
• The flickering movement of the index finger indicates that the extensor muscles are severely weakened but may have minimal residual function due to partial innervation or incomplete nerve injury. This finding is still consistent with radial nerve palsy.

Common causes include:

• Mid-shaft fracture of the humerus (injury in the radial groove)
• Compression neuropathy ("Saturday night palsy")
• Crutch palsy
• Posterior interosseous nerve injury (finger drop with preserved wrist extension)

Why not the other options?

• B. Ulnar nerve: Causes clawing of the ring and little fingers, loss of finger abduction/adduction, Froment sign, and hypothenar wasting. Wrist drop is not a feature.
• C. Median nerve: Causes ape thumb, thenar wasting, loss of thumb opposition, and difficulty making the "OK" sign (anterior interosseous nerve lesion), but not wrist drop.
• D. Musculocutaneous nerve: Primarily affects elbow flexion and forearm supination; wrist and finger extension remain intact.

High-yield pearl

Differentiate common upper limb nerve injuries:

| Nerve | Classic clinical sign

| ----- | ---------------------

| Radial nerve | Wrist drop due to loss of wrist and finger extensors

| Ulnar nerve | Ulnar claw, loss of finger abduction/adduction

| Median nerve | Ape thumb, thenar wasting, loss of opposition

| Axillary nerve | Loss of shoulder abduction, flattened shoulder

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young female patient complains of low back pain radiating to the right hip, back of the thigh, leg, and ankle after an intense workout of lifting some heavy weights. MRI shows the following finding. Which nerve root is most likely to be involved here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. L5

Key clues:

• Heavy lifting → disc prolapse
• Pain radiates:

• Low back → hip → posterior thigh → leg → ankle

The sagittal lumbar MRI shows a posterolateral disc herniation at the L4–L5 level.

• In lumbar disc prolapse, the disc typically herniates posterolaterally
• It compresses the traversing (lower) nerve root, not the exiting one

👉 Therefore:

• L4–L5 disc herniation → compresses L5 nerve root

L5 dermatome:

• Lateral thigh
• Lateral leg
• Dorsum of foot

Pain radiating to ankle + leg strongly suggests L5

| Root | Pain Area | Reflex | Motor Deficit

| ---- | --------- | ------ | -------------

| L3 | Anterior thigh | — | Hip flexion

| L4 | Medial leg | Knee ↓ | Knee extension

| L5 | Lateral leg + dorsum foot | Normal | Foot dorsiflexion ↓

| S1 | Posterior leg + lateral foot | Ankle ↓ | Plantarflexion ↓

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Correctly match the statement regarding the splint shown in image.
options: Knuckle bender splint; Ulnar Nerve Palsy
Dynamic cock up splint; Radial Nerve Palsy
Turn buckle splint; Volkmann’s Ischemic Contracture
Knuckle bender splint; Median Nerve Palsy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dynamic cock up splint; Radial Nerve Palsy

The splint shown is a dynamic cock-up splint, which uses elastic traction to extend the wrist and MCP joints in patients with radial nerve palsy (wrist drop). It allows active finger flexion while passively assisting extension, improving hand function during nerve recovery.

Radial nerve injury

↓

Loss of extensor muscle function

↓

Wrist flexes due to unopposed flexors

↓

Wrist drop

Knuckle-bender splints are for ulnar/median nerve palsies, and turn-buckle splints are used to gradually correct contractures such as in Volkmann ischemic contracture.

| Nerve Injury | Deformity | Splint Used

| ------------ | --------- | -----------

| Radial nerve | Wrist drop | Dynamic cock-up splint ✅

| Ulnar nerve | Claw hand | Anti-claw splint

| Median nerve | Ape hand | Opponens splint

| Volkmann contracture | Flexion deformity | Turnbuckle splint

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Fracture at which site in leg will cause failure of dorsiflexion of foot?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Proximal fibular neck

Injury to the proximal neck of fibula causes paralysis of dorsiflexion of the foot because around this portion, the common peroneal nerve winds, which supplies the dorsiflexors of the foot.

Fracture at fibular neck

↓

Common peroneal nerve injury

↓

Loss of anterior compartment muscles

↓

Loss of dorsiflexion

↓

Foot drop

| Muscle | Function

| ------ | --------

| Tibialis anterior | Dorsiflexion

| Extensor hallucis longus | Great toe extension

| Extensor digitorum longus | Toe extension

| Site | Nerve Affected | Deficit

| ---- | -------------- | -------

| Fibular neck | Common peroneal | Foot drop ✅

| Popliteal fossa | Tibial nerve | Loss of plantarflexion

| Thigh | Sciatic nerve | Complete leg weakness

| Ankle | Distal nerves | Limited deficit

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the muscle along with its correct action.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dorsal interossei – abduction

The dorsal interossei are four intrinsic muscles of the hand that abduct the fingers away from the midline (middle finger) and also assist the lumbricals in flexing the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and extending the interphalangeal (IP) joints. They are innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve (C8–T1).

FMGE/NEET PG Pearl

• DAB → Dorsal interossei ABduct the fingers.
• PAD → Palmar interossei ADduct the fingers.
• Palmar interossei are 3 muscles; dorsal interossei are 4 muscles.
• Ulnar nerve injury weakens finger abduction and adduction and produces a positive card (paper) test due to interossei muscle paralysis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Injury at which of the marked anatomical areas would most likely result in difficulty with dorsiflexion of the foot?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. C

Injury at the neck of fibula damages the common peroneal nerve

This nerve supplies the anterior compartment of leg

Responsible for dorsiflexion of foot

Injury leads to:

• Loss of dorsiflexion
• Foot drop
• High-stepping gait

The common peroneal nerve is most vulnerable to injury at the neck of fibula (area A), where it winds around the bone superficially, and injury at this site causes foot drop with inability to dorsiflex the foot and high stepping gait.

Trauma at fibular neck

↓

Common peroneal nerve injury

↓

Paralysis of anterior compartment muscles

↓

Loss of dorsiflexion

↓

Foot drop

| Muscle | Action

| ------ | ------

| Tibialis anterior | Dorsiflexion

| Extensor hallucis longus | Great toe extension

| Extensor digitorum longus | Toe extension

| Nerve | Injury Site | Deficit | Clinical Sign

| ----- | ----------- | ------- | -------------

| Common peroneal | Fibular neck | Loss of dorsiflexion | Foot drop

| Tibial nerve | Popliteal fossa | Loss of plantarflexion | Cannot stand on toes

| Femoral nerve | Inguinal region | Loss of knee extension | Weak quadriceps

| Sciatic nerve | Posterior thigh | Whole leg weakness | Severe deficit

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Neuropraxia is a type of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Physiological conduction block

Neuropraxia is the mildest form of peripheral nerve injury (Seddon classification) and is characterized by a transient physiological conduction block without structural disruption of the axon or connective tissue. Recovery is complete and spontaneous, usually within days to weeks.

• Neuropraxia results in a temporary conduction block due to focal demyelination.
• The axon, endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium remain intact, allowing complete recovery.

Why not the other options?

• A. Endoneurium disruption: Seen in axonotmesis or more severe nerve injuries, not neuropraxia.
• B. Nerve trunk damage: Refers to severe nerve injury, typically neurotmesis.
• D. Axonal discontinuity: Characteristic of axonotmesis and neurotmesis, not neuropraxia.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which action will be impacted in PIN Palsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Extension of fingers

| Feature | Meaning

| ------- | -------

| PIN palsy | Branch of radial nerve

| Pure motor nerve | No sensory loss

| Affects | Finger extensors

So the key deficit: Inability to extend fingers

• Branch of radial nerve that Runs through supinator muscle
• Runs through supinator muscle
• Supplies:

• Extensor digitorum
• Extensor pollicis

Finger drop WITHOUT wrist drop

Why?

• Wrist extensors (ECRL, ECRB) are supplied before PIN branch
• So:

• Wrist extension → preserved (sometimes weak)
• Finger extension → lost

| Feature | Radial Nerve Injury | PIN Injury

| ------- | ------------------- | ----------

| Wrist extension | ❌ Lost | ✔️ Preserved

| Finger extension | ❌ Lost | ❌ Lost

| Sensory loss | ✔️ Present | ❌ Absent

| Level | High lesion | Deep branch

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which muscle is affected if the patient is unable to make an "OK" sign?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Flexor pollicis longus

Patient tries to make a circle with: Thumb + index finger

Normal: Forms a perfect round “O”

Abnormal: Forms a flattened pinch (triangle)

This indicates: Anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) palsy

Anterior interosseous nerve lesion affects flexor pollicis longus, preventing thumb IP flexion, producing Kiloh‑Nevin sign. Abductor pollicis brevis abducts thumb, lumbricals flex MCP/extend IP, opponens pollicis performs opposition.

| Muscle | Function

| ------ | --------

| Flexor pollicis longus (FPL) | Flexes thumb IP joint

| FDP (index finger) | Flexes DIP joint

| Pronator quadratus | Forearm pronation

| Muscle | Function | Role in OK Sign

| ------ | -------- | ---------------

| FPL | Thumb IP flexion | ✅ Critical

| FDP (index) | Finger DIP flexion | Also involved

| APB | Thumb abduction | ❌ No

| Opponens | Thumb opposition | ❌ No

| Lumbricals | MCP flexion | ❌ No

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding Neuropraxia?
options: Axon is damaged but the nerve sheath is intact
Axon, endoneurium, perineurium and epineurium are damaged
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myelin sheath is damaged

Neuropraxia-

• Mildest form of nerve injury (Seddon classification)
• Typically caused by:

• Compression (Saturday night palsy )
• Mild ischemia
• Stretch injury

Core pathology:

• Focal demyelination
• Axon remains intact

Normally:

• Myelin sheath → enables saltatory conduction

In neuropraxia:

• Myelin damaged
• Axon intact

Result:

• Conduction block
• No transmission of impulse across lesion

BUT:

• No Wallerian degeneration (because axon intact)

| Feature | Neuropraxia | Axonotmesis | Neurotmesis

| ------- | ----------- | ----------- | -----------

| Myelin | Damaged | Damaged | Damaged

| Axon | Intact | Damaged | Damaged

| Connective tissue | Intact | Intact (early) | Disrupted

| Wallerian degeneration | No | Yes | Yes

| Recovery | Complete, rapid | Slow, variable | None (needs surgery)

| Example | Compression | Crush injury | Cut injury

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presented with knee pain following a fall from the stairs. The physical and radiological evaluation revealed injury to the marked structure. Identify the structure:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tibial tuberosity

Osgood-Schlatter Disease

• Repetitive microtrauma at tibial tuberosity
• Painful swelling in adolescents
• Chronic version of same stress mechanism

Acute → Avulsion fracture

Chronic → Osgood-Schlatter

| Structure | Location | Attachment | Injury Type | Typical Age

| --------- | -------- | ---------- | ----------- | -----------

| Tibial tuberosity | Anterior tibia | Patellar tendon | Avulsion fracture | Children/adolescents ✅

| Medial tubercle | Medial condyle | Ligaments | Rare trauma | Any

| Gerdy’s tubercle | Lateral tibia | IT band | Segond fracture | Adults (ACL injury)

| Anterior intercondylar area | Between condyles | ACL | ACL avulsion | Sports injuries

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy from a rural area is brought to the orthopedic clinic by his parents. He has a history of a congenital foot deformity that was never treated during infancy. On physical examination, he has a fixed, rigid equinovarus deformity of his right foot. He walks on the lateral border of his foot and has significant pain with ambulation. Radiographs demonstrate severe structural adaptation of the tarsal bones with degenerative changes in the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints. Because the patient has passed the window for soft tissue correction, surgical management is planned to provide a stable, painless, plantigrade foot. Which of the following surgical procedures is the definitive treatment of choice for this patient?
options: Ponseti casting and percutaneous Achilles tenotomy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Triple arthrodesis

Triple arthrodesis is the treatment of choice for neglected, rigid congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) in older children and adolescents who have completed the window for soft tissue correction.

It involves fusion of three joints:

• Subtalar joint (talocalcaneal)
• Talonavicular joint
• Calcaneocuboid joint

Indications:

• Age >10–12 years with skeletal maturity approaching
• Rigid, fixed deformity
• Painful gait
• Degenerative changes in the tarsal joints
• Failure or absence of early treatment

Why not the other options?

• A. Ponseti casting + percutaneous Achilles tenotomy: First-line treatment for newborns and infants with flexible clubfoot.
• B. Turco posteromedial soft tissue release: Used in young children (typically <2–4 years) with resistant deformity; ineffective in long-standing rigid deformities.
• D. Ilizarov external fixator alone: Can gradually correct severe neglected deformities but is generally an adjunct; definitive treatment for rigid, arthritic clubfoot is triple arthrodesis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 2-week-old infant is brought with a history of a single fall. X-ray examination reveals multiple fractures involving different bones. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Battered baby syndrome

Multiple rib fractures in a non-ambulatory infant with an inconsistent history strongly suggests battered baby syndrome (non-accidental trauma). This must be differentiated from osteogenesis imperfecta, which presents with blue sclera, dentine defects, and a family history of brittle bones.

Repeated physical abuse

↓

Forceful shaking / twisting / impact

↓

Fragile infant bones subjected to abnormal forces

↓

Multiple fractures (different ages)

↓

Battered Baby Syndrome

| Fracture Type | Significance

| ------------- | ------------

| Metaphyseal (corner / bucket-handle) | MOST specific

| Posterior rib fractures | Squeezing injury

| Skull fractures | Direct trauma

| Long bone fractures | Twisting

| Feature | Battered Baby | Osteogenesis Imperfecta

| ------- | ------------- | -----------------------

| Cause | Abuse | Genetic (Type I collagen defect)

| Fractures | Multiple, different stages | Recurrent but uniform

| Other signs | Bruises, neglect | Blue sclera, teeth defects

| History | Inconsistent | Family history

| Legal aspect | Yes | No

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: An 8-year-old child presents with a painless limp. A pelvic X-ray is performed and is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Perthes disease

Perthes disease in school-age children presents with painless limp and characteristic X-ray findings of femoral head flattening, fragmentation, and sclerosis due to avascular necrosis.

Key Radiological Signs:

• Increased density (sclerosis) of femoral head
• Fragmentation
• Flattening (collapse) of femoral head
• Crescent sign (subchondral fracture)
• Joint space may appear widened early

| Feature | Perthes | TB Hip | SCFE | DDH

| ------- | ------- | ------ | ---- | ---

| Age | 4–10 yrs | Any | 10–16 yrs | Infants

| Pain | Mild/painless | Painful | Painful | Variable

| Pathology | AVN | Infection | Slip | Dysplasia

| X-ray | Sclerosis + fragmentation | Erosions | Slip | Dislocation

| Key sign | Flattened head | Phemister triad | Ice cream sign | Shenton line break

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the classification used and grade of the shown injury in a child:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gartland’s classification Type III

| Type | Description

| ---- | -----------

| Type I | Undisplaced

| Type II | Displaced with intact posterior cortex

| Type III | Completely displaced (no cortical contact)

| Type IV | Multidirectional instability

Gartland Type III supracondylar fracture is completely displaced with no cortical contact. Salter‑Harris is for epiphyseal injuries, not supracondylar fractures. Type IV is intraoperative finding with periosteum torn both sides.

Complications:

• Brachial artery injury → pulseless hand
• Median nerve injury (especially AIN)
• Compartment syndrome → Volkmann ischemic contracture

| Feature | Gartland Type III | Gartland Type II | Salter-Harris

| ------- | ----------------- | ---------------- | -------------

| Region | Supracondylar | Supracondylar | Growth plate

| Displacement | Complete | Partial | Variable

| Cortex | No contact | Posterior intact | Involves physis

| Age group | Children | Children | Children

| Key clue | Fully displaced elbow | Tilted fracture | Epiphyseal injury

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The longitudinal growth of the bone is affected by fracture of which region of the bone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Epiphyseal plate

Epiphyseal plate (physis) controls longitudinal growth. Fractures here (Salter‑Harris) can cause growth arrest. Diaphysis provides strength, epiphysis forms joints, metaphysis is vascular but not growth center.

The epiphyseal plate has 5 zones:

| Zone | Function

| ---- | --------

| Resting | Reserve cells

| Proliferative | Rapid cell division

| Hypertrophic | Cell enlargement

| Calcification | Matrix calcifies

| Ossification | Bone formation

Growth happens mainly at proliferative zone

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following features is not associated with Achondroplasia?
options: [Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
[Option image — not included in this edition]
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. [image not included in this edition]

Vertical Acetabular Roof is not a radiological feature associated with achondroplasia. Achondroplasia is the most common skeletal dysplasia, characterized by rhizomelic shortening (shortened proximal limbs) due to a mutation in the FGFR3 gene. The classic radiological features include bullet-shaped vertebrae, champagne glass pelvis, and metaphyseal flaring.

Other Options:

• Bullet Shaped Vertebra - This is a characteristic finding in achondroplasia\, showing posterior scalloping of the vertebral bodies\, giving them a bullet-like appearance.
• Champagne Glass Pelvis - This is a hallmark pelvic configuration in achondroplasia with narrow greater sciatic notch and flared iliac wings that resembles a champagne glass.
• Trumpet Bone - While not always called by this specific name\, the metaphyseal flaring with V-shaped metaphysis (Chevron sign) in achondroplasia gives long bones a trumpet-like appearance.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: 60-year-old man with a history of pulmonary TB taking ATT now presents with back pain. What would be the appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Biopsy

The MRI shows spondylodiscitis involving the thoracolumbar spine, most likely Pott spine (spinal tuberculosis).

Key MRI findings visible:

• Destruction/collapse of adjacent vertebral bodies.
• Narrowing and destruction of the intervertebral disc space.
• Large paravertebral/prevertebral soft tissue collection (cold abscess).
• Epidural extension causing compression of the thecal sac/spinal canal.
• Gibbus/kyphotic deformity may be beginning due to vertebral collapse.

Since patient is already on ATT and has progressed to have Pott spine, confirmation by biopsy/CBNAAT/culture.

Treatment:

• Antitubercular therapy (ATT)
• Surgical decompression/stabilization if:

• neurological deficit
• instability
• severe deformity
• large abscess
• failure of medical treatment

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with chronic, aching low back pain that is worse in the morning and improves with activity. On physical examination, the patient is placed in a supine position. The examiner flexes, abducts, and externally rotates the patient’s hip, placing the ipsilateral ankle on the contralateral knee. This maneuver reproduces the patient’s deep gluteal pain. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for this positive provocative test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sacroiliitis

The FABER (Patrick) test is performed by placing the hip in Flexion, ABduction, and External Rotation (figure-of-four position). Pain reproduced over the posterior pelvis or deep gluteal region indicates sacroiliac (SI) joint pathology, most commonly sacroiliitis.

In a young adult with chronic inflammatory low back pain (morning stiffness that improves with activity), a positive FABER test strongly suggests sacroiliitis, which is a hallmark of axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis).

Clinical features of sacroiliitis:

• Inflammatory back pain (<45 years of age)
• Morning stiffness lasting >30 minutes
• Improvement with exercise and worsening with rest
• Buttock or deep gluteal pain
• Positive FABER and SI joint compression tests
• Bilateral sacroiliitis on imaging in ankylosing spondylitis

Why not the other options?

• A. Lumbar disc herniation: Causes radicular pain with a positive straight-leg raise test, not a positive FABER test.
• B. Osteoarthritis of the hip: FABER may cause groin pain due to hip pathology rather than posterior SI joint pain; pain worsens with activity.
• D. Trochanteric bursitis: Causes localized tenderness over the greater trochanter and lateral hip pain, not SI joint pain.

Presence of lower back pain and stiffness since months, raised levels of ESR and CRP, mild restriction of chest movements and chest expansion, with history of red eye are suggestive of presence of ankylosing spondylitis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient complains of frequent episodes of red, painful eyes, stiffness, and back pain. He has sacroiliitis and anterior uveitis, according to the examination. Which HLA is frequently involved among the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. HLA B27

| Clue | Interpretation

| ---- | --------------

| Young adult (35 yrs) | Typical age group

| Chronic back pain + stiffness | Inflammatory back pain

| Sacroiliitis | Hallmark of spondyloarthropathy

| Anterior uveitis (red painful eye) | Extra-articular feature

Diagnosis points to: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS)

And the genetic association:  HLA-B27

HLA-B27 is like a genetic “ID card” for spondyloarthropathies:

• Present in \~90–95% of ankylosing spondylitis
• Associated with:

• Reactive arthritis
• Psoriatic arthritis
• Enteropathic arthritis

• Chronic inflammation at entheses (ligament insertions)
• Leads to:

• Fibrosis
• Ossification

• Spine becomes rigid → “Bamboo spine”

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 70-year-old woman presents with severe back pain. CT of the lumbar spine is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spondylolisthesis

Spondylolisthesis is defined as anterior displacement of one vertebra over another, often due to degeneration or bilateral defects in the pars interarticularis—seen as a “Scotty dog with a collar” on oblique X-ray views.

Key Radiological Signs:

• Anterior displacement (“step-off”)
• Misalignment of vertebral bodies
• Narrowed disc space (degenerative type)
• Possible osteophytes

| Type | Cause | Typical Age

| ---- | ----- | -----------

| Isthmic | Pars defect (spondylolysis) | Young

| Degenerative | Facet + disc degeneration | Elderly (MOST LIKELY HERE)

| Traumatic | Fracture | Any

| Pathological | Tumor/infection | Variable

Meyerding Classification

| Grade | Slip %

| ----- | ------

| I | <25%

| II | 25–50%

| III | 50–75%

| IV | >75%

| Feature | Spondylolisthesis | Compression Fracture | Spondylolysis | TB Spine

| ------- | ----------------- | -------------------- | ------------- | --------

| Alignment | Shift present | Normal | Normal | May collapse

| Vertebral shape | Normal | Wedge | Normal | Destroyed

| Key sign | Step-off | Height loss | Scotty dog collar | Gibbus

| Age group | Elderly | Elderly | Young | Any

| Cause | Degeneration | Osteoporosis | Stress fracture | Infection

questions.text: A patient presented with severe back ache and the following x-ray after an RTA. Diagnose the fracture present.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chance fracture

Sudden deceleration (RTA)

↓

Torso flexes over seatbelt

↓

Posterior elements distracted

↓

Horizontal splitting of vertebra

↓

Chance fracture

Chance fracture is a flexion‑distraction injury involving all three spinal columns, classically seatbelt injury. Burst fracture involves anterior + middle columns, compression fracture affects anterior body, spinous process fracture is isolated posterior injury.

Key feature:

• Horizontal fracture line
• Extends through:

• Spinous process
• Pedicles
• Vertebral body

| Feature | Chance Fracture | Burst Fracture | Compression Fracture | Spinous Process Fracture

| Fracture line | Horizontal | Comminuted | Wedge | Isolated posterior

| Posterior elements | Disrupted | Intact/variable | Intact | Involved only

| Neurological risk | Moderate | High | Low | Minimal

| Classic clue | Seatbelt injury | Canal compromise | Osteoporosis | Local pain

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: All are true about Ankylosing spondylitis except:
options: HLA B27 is associated in 90% cases
It is non-erosive and only joints are affected
Involvement of sacroiliac joint is earliest sign
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is non-erosive and only joints are affected

AS is a disease of entheses (ligament insertions), not just joints:

• Causes:

• Bone erosion initially
• Then new bone formation

• Leads to:

• Syndesmophytes
• Fusion → ankylosis

AS is:

• Inflammatory
• Erosive
• Affects joints + entheses + extra-articular systems

| Feature | Description

| ------- | -----------

| HLA-B27 | Present in \~90%

| Earliest sign | Sacroiliitis

| Gender | M > F

| Pathology | Erosive + inflammatory

| Spine | Bamboo spine

✨ Earliest sign → Sacroiliitis

✨ HLA-B27 strongly associated

✨ Erosive disease initially (important trap)

✨ Extra-articular:

• Uveitis
• Aortic regurgitation

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Hangman’s fracture is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Traumatic spondylolisthesis of axis vertebra (C₂)

Hangman’s fracture is a traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis (C2 vertebra) caused by bilateral fractures through the pars interarticularis (pedicles) of C2. It classically results from forceful hyperextension and axial loading of the cervical spine, as seen in road traffic accidents or judicial hanging.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Traumatic spondylolisthesis of atlas vertebra (C₁): C1 fracture is known as a Jefferson fracture, caused by axial loading.
• C. Traumatic spondylolisthesis of thoracic vertebra (T₁): This is not termed a Hangman’s fracture.
• D. Traumatic spondylolisthesis of lumbar vertebra (L₁): Lumbar spondylolisthesis is unrelated to Hangman’s fracture.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Schober’s test is used in the assessment of which one of the following clinical conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ankylosing spondylitis

Schober’s test is a bedside clinical test used to assess lumbar spine flexion and is an important screening tool for ankylosing spondylitis (AS). Reduced lumbar flexion reflects inflammatory involvement of the sacroiliac joints and spine, which is characteristic of axial spondyloarthritis.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Rheumatoid arthritis: Primarily affects peripheral joints (MCP, PIP, wrists) and is not assessed using Schober’s test.
• B. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): Causes non-erosive arthritis but does not produce the characteristic restriction of lumbar spine mobility.
• D. Psoriasis: Cutaneous psoriasis does not require Schober’s test, although axial psoriatic arthritis may rarely show reduced spinal mobility.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which is the earliest imaging modality used to detect ankylosing spondylitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MRI sacroiliac joint

MRI of the sacroiliac joints is the earliest imaging modality to detect ankylosing spondylitis, capable of demonstrating active inflammatory changes (bone marrow edema) years before structural changes appear on radiographs.

MRI Findings:

• Bone marrow edema (STIR hyperintensity) ⭐
• Active inflammation
• Early erosions
•

X-ray Findings:

• Joint space narrowing
• Sclerosis
• Fusion
• Bamboo spine (late stage)

Early inflammation

↓

Bone marrow edema (MRI visible)

↓

Erosions develop

↓

Sclerosis (X-ray visible)

↓

Fusion → Bamboo spine

| Modality | Role | Sensitivity

| -------- | ---- | -----------

| MRI SI joint ⭐ | Detects early inflammation | Highest

| X-ray | Detects late structural changes | Low early

| CT | Shows bony detail | Late

| Bone scan | Functional, non-specific | Less specific
